q_0137.rationale: Table 12.3 gives 0.2 mg intravenously over 15 seconds for reversal of moderate sedation or general anesthesia, repeated at 60-second intervals up to four additional times, to a maximum total dose of 1 mg. For suspected benzodiazepine overdose the regimen starts at 0.2 mg over 30 seconds and escalates through 0.3 mg and then 0.5 mg doses at 1-minute intervals to a cumulative dose of 3 mg.
q_0137.trap: (C) swaps the two ceilings, and the swap is easy because both regimens open with the same 0.2 mg dose. The difference between the 1 mg and the 3 mg ceiling is the cleanest discriminator between the two indications.

q_0138.topic: sedative-hypnotic interactions and black box warnings
q_0138.stem: A patient taking a benzodiazepine mentions that she drinks a large glass of grapefruit juice every morning. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Decreased benzodiazepine metabolism, with prolonged effect and possible toxicity
Increased benzodiazepine metabolism, with loss of therapeutic effect
No interaction, since grapefruit affects only the oral anticoagulants
An additive CNS depressant effect contributed by the juice itself
q_0138.rationale: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice alter drug metabolism by inhibition of the cytochrome P-450 system and can result in prolonged effect, increased effect, and toxicity (p. 186). Table 12.4 groups grapefruit juice with the azole antifungals, verapamil, diltiazem, protease inhibitors, and macrolide antibiotics under decreased benzodiazepine metabolism and prolonged benzodiazepine action.
q_0138.trap: (B) runs the interaction backwards. Inhibition slows metabolism, so more drug stays in the body longer; only induction produces the loss of effect described there.

q_0139.topic: sedative-hypnotic interactions and black box warnings
q_0139.stem: A patient stabilized on a benzodiazepine is started on rifampin for tuberculosis, and within days he reports that the benzodiazepine no longer seems to work. What explains this?
options: Rifampin inhibits benzodiazepine metabolism, causing accumulation and tolerance
Rifampin increases benzodiazepine metabolism, decreasing benzodiazepine effects
Rifampin displaces the benzodiazepine from its receptors, acting as an antagonist
Rifampin adds to CNS depression, masking the benzodiazepine effect
q_0139.rationale: Table 12.4 lists rifampin with increased metabolism and decreased benzodiazepine effects. Rifampin is the one row of that table that runs against all the others, which is why it is printed there; the chapter also names rifampin as reducing the efficacy of ramelteon by speeding its metabolism (p. 188).
q_0139.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — it applies the grapefruit and azole direction to an inducer. Inducers speed metabolism and cause treatment failure; inhibitors slow it and cause toxicity.

q_0140.topic: sedative-hypnotic interactions and black box warnings
q_0140.stem: A patient takes a benzodiazepine nightly. According to this chapter, which of the following would prolong or increase the benzodiazepine's effect? Select all that apply.
options: An azole antifungal
Grapefruit juice
Rifampin
An opioid analgesic
Verapamil
q_0140.rationale: Table 12.4 assigns decreased benzodiazepine metabolism and prolonged benzodiazepine action to the azole antifungals, verapamil, diltiazem, protease inhibitors, macrolide antibiotics, and grapefruit juice, and assigns additive effects with increased CNS depression to the CNS depressants, which the chapter exemplifies with alcohol, opioids, and muscle relaxants.
q_0140.trap: (C) is the single row in Table 12.4 that goes the other way — increased metabolism and decreased benzodiazepine effects. A learner who sorts the whole table into one bucket keeps it.

q_0141.topic: sedative-hypnotic interactions and black box warnings
q_0141.stem: A prescriber orders an opioid analgesic and a benzodiazepine together for a postoperative patient. Which statement reflects the 2016 FDA black box warning?
options: The combination is absolutely prohibited in every patient
The combination should be used only if no other alternatives are available, because of extreme sleepiness, respiratory depression, coma, and death
The warning applies only when the opioid is given intravenously
The warning concerns complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving
q_0141.rationale: The 2016 warning covers all opioids and all benzodiazepines regarding the risk of combined use, and states that they should be used "only if no other alternatives are available," with risks including extreme sleepiness, respiratory depression, coma, and death (p. 186). The assessment section operationalizes it by watching for severe decreases in blood pressure, respiratory rate, reflexes, and level of consciousness.
q_0141.trap: (D) is the 2019 warning, which belongs to the nonbenzodiazepines. It is the most memorable of the three, so it gets attached to the wrong box; three warnings, three years, three different scopes.

q_0142.topic: sedative-hypnotic interactions and black box warnings
q_0142.stem: A patient asks which drugs carry the FDA warning about complex sleep behaviors, including sleepwalking, sleep-driving, and engaging in other activities while not fully awake. Which answer is correct?
options: The entire benzodiazepine class
The nonbenzodiazepines zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon
All barbiturates
The orexin receptor antagonists
q_0142.rationale: The 2019 warning names complex sleep behaviors for the nonbenzodiazepines zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon (p. 184). The late-2020 warning is the one covering the entire benzodiazepine class, and it concerns the risk for abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal.
q_0142.trap: (A) crosses the years. It is the correct scope for the 2020 dependence warning and the wrong scope for the 2019 sleep-behavior warning, and the two collapse together because they were issued about a year apart.

q_0143.stem: Table 12.2 lists temazepam, triazolam, zolpidem, and eszopiclone together in one table of sedative-hypnotics, and a student concludes that all four are benzodiazepines. Which correction is accurate?
options: All four are benzodiazepines, since they appear in the same table and share schedule IV status
Zolpidem and eszopiclone are classified as miscellaneous hypnotic drugs that share many characteristics with the benzodiazepines but are chemically distinct from them
Only temazepam is a benzodiazepine; triazolam is a barbiturate
Classification depends on the duration column, not on the drug
q_0143.rationale: The footnote to Table 12.2 states that these drugs "share many characteristics with the benzodiazepines but are classified as miscellaneous hypnotic drugs," and the chapter describes zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon as functioning much like benzodiazepines but chemically distinct from them (pp. 184 and 185). The Clinical Pearl supplies the naming cue: many benzodiazepines end in "pam."
q_0143.trap: (A) is exactly the error the chapter's own Key Points make when they list eszopiclone, ramelteon, zaleplon, and zolpidem as short-acting benzodiazepines. The rows and the footnote have to be read together, and the shared schedule IV status makes the merge feel safe.

q_0144.stem: A woman is discharged after a hysterectomy with a new prescription for zolpidem 10 mg at bedtime. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
options: Review the adverse effects with her and reinforce the bedtime timing
Suggest a glass of wine at bedtime if the drug alone is not effective
Contact the prescriber to question the dose
Help her locate a pharmacy that stocks the drug
q_0144.rationale: The FDA now recommends doses of 5 mg as a maximum dose for women, or 5 to 10 mg for men, because of the risk for next-morning impairment (p. 188). A 10 mg dose for a female patient is twice the recommended maximum.
q_0144.trap: (A) is the safe-looking choice, and it is wrong precisely because teaching about a dose the FDA capped at half leaves the hazard in place. (B) fails on a separate rule: alcohol is an additive CNS depressant, and Box 12.1 says it fragments sleep rather than producing it.

q_0145.stem: A patient with a history of alcohol and sedative misuse needs help falling asleep. Which drug in this chapter is described as an option for patients likely to abuse CNS depressants, and why?
options: Temazepam, because it is intermediate acting and therefore less reinforcing
Ramelteon, because it is not a controlled substance, is technically not a CNS depressant, and does not lead to withdrawal symptoms
Suvorexant, because the orexin receptor antagonists are not scheduled
Phenobarbital, because its long half-life smooths withdrawal
q_0145.rationale: Ramelteon is structurally similar to melatonin and works as an agonist at melatonin receptors in the CNS; it is "technically not a CNS depressant" and is "not classified as a controlled substance because of its lack of observed dependency risk" (p. 188). The nursing sections add that it does not carry the potential for abuse or dependence and does not lead to withdrawal symptoms, so it may be an option for patients likely to abuse CNS depressants.
q_0145.trap: (C) is the closest wrong answer, because suvorexant is also a newer non-benzodiazepine hypnotic with an unfamiliar mechanism. Suvorexant is a schedule IV drug; ramelteon is the only unscheduled hypnotic in this chapter.

q_0146.stem: Suvorexant is ordered for a patient with insomnia. Which explanation of its mechanism is accurate?
options: It blocks orexin receptors, opposing hypothalamic neuropeptides that promote wakefulness
It agonizes melatonin receptors and resets the circadian rhythm
It potentiates GABA at the brainstem reticular formation
It decreases calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle fibers
q_0146.rationale: Suvorexant is the first drug in a new class called the orexin receptor antagonists. Orexin A and orexin B are hypothalamic neuropeptides that play a key role in promoting wakefulness and regulating the sleep-wake cycle, and orexin antagonists compete with the physiologic effects of orexin (p. 188).
q_0146.trap: (B) is the ramelteon mechanism, and the two are the chapter's easiest swap because both are newer hypnotics that do not work through GABA. Suvorexant blocks a wake-promoting peptide; ramelteon agonizes a sleep-promoting receptor.

q_0147.stem: A patient is starting suvorexant. Which statements should the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Take the drug about 30 minutes before bedtime
Take the drug 2 hours before bedtime, because of its slow onset
Be cautious about daytime somnolence and unconscious nighttime behaviors
This drug is less likely than other hypnotics to interact with alcohol
The drug is available over the counter if a refill runs out
q_0147.rationale: Suvorexant's profile gives a 30-minute onset, and the chapter's dosing rule is to match the teaching time to the onset column, since a drug with an onset of 30 to 60 minutes is dosed 60 minutes before bedtime (p. 194). The safety concerns regarding daytime somnolence and unconscious nighttime behaviors are stated verbatim (pp. 188 and 196).
q_0147.trap: (E) is defeated by one phrase in the profile: suvorexant is a schedule IV drug, and a scheduled drug is never sold over the counter. (B) fabricates a pharmacokinetic that contradicts the 30-minute onset printed in that same profile.

q_0148.subtopic: site of action, duration groups, and schedules
q_0148.stem: A patient asks how phenobarbital differs from a benzodiazepine in where it acts. Which description fits the barbiturates?
options: They act primarily on the brainstem in an area called the reticular formation, reducing nerve impulses traveling to the cerebral cortex
They act on the hypothalamic, thalamic, and limbic systems
They act at the neuromuscular junction
They antagonize orexin receptors in the hypothalamus
q_0148.rationale: Barbiturates are CNS depressants that act primarily on the brainstem in an area called the reticular formation, and they work by reducing the nerve impulses traveling to the cerebral cortex; they also potentiate the action of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and raise the seizure threshold (p. 189).
q_0148.trap: (B) is the benzodiazepine site. Both classes are CNS depressants that involve GABA, so the anatomic site is the only thing separating them and it is the detail most often traded between them.

q_0149.subtopic: site of action, duration groups, and schedules
q_0149.stem: A patient is scheduled for a short surgical procedure requiring anesthesia induction, and the neurosurgical team also wants intracranial pressure reduced. Which barbiturate duration group does Table 12.5 assign these purposes to?
options: Ultrashort acting, such as methohexital and thiopental
Short acting, such as pentobarbital and secobarbital
Intermediate acting, such as butabarbital
Long acting, such as phenobarbital and mephobarbital
q_0149.rationale: The ultrashort-acting barbiturates methohexital and thiopental are used for anesthesia for short surgical procedures, anesthesia induction, control of convulsions, and reduction of intracranial pressure in neurosurgical patients (p. 189). The long-acting group is used for epileptic seizure prophylaxis, and the short- and intermediate-acting groups carry the identical printed indication of sedation and control of convulsive conditions.
q_0149.trap: (D) picks the group whose drug names are most familiar, since phenobarbital is the prototype. Because the short and intermediate groups share word-for-word identical indications, any item separating the four tiers must be answered on the drug names rather than on the stated purpose.

q_0150.subtopic: site of action, duration groups, and schedules
q_0150.stem: A nurse assumes that the shorter a barbiturate's duration of action, the more restrictive its controlled-substance schedule will be. Which fact from Table 12.7 defeats that assumption?
options: Phenobarbital is long acting and is schedule C-II
Thiopental is ultrashort acting but only schedule C-III, and methohexital is ultrashort acting but only schedule C-IV
Butabarbital is intermediate acting and is unscheduled
All barbiturates share a single schedule, the same one as the benzodiazepines
q_0150.rationale: Table 12.7 places pentobarbital and secobarbital, both short acting, at schedule C-II, the tightest in the chapter, while the two ultrashort-acting drugs sit lower — thiopental at C-III and methohexital at C-IV. Phenobarbital, the long-acting prototype, is C-IV, the same schedule as the benzodiazepines.
q_0150.trap: (A) inverts phenobarbital's schedule, which is C-IV rather than C-II. Tables 12.5 and 12.7 have to be read as independent lists, because the intuitive duration-tracks-schedule rule fails on two of the seven drugs.

q_0151.stem: A woman taking oral contraceptives is started on phenobarbital. What should the nurse teach her?
options: The contraceptive will be more effective, so its dose may be reduced
Phenobarbital accelerates the metabolism of the contraceptive, so she should use an additional method of contraception as a backup
Phenobarbital has no meaningful effect on oral contraceptives
She should stop the contraceptive entirely, since the combination causes clot formation
q_0151.rationale: Barbiturates as a class are notorious enzyme inducers: they increase the activity of hepatic microsomal or cytochrome P-450 enzymes, causing many drugs to be metabolized more quickly, which usually shortens their duration of action (pp. 189 and 190). With oral contraceptives the printed result is accelerated metabolism of the contraceptive drug and possible unintended pregnancy, and the chapter advises an additional method of contraception as a backup.
q_0151.trap: (D) borrows the clot-formation outcome, which belongs to the anticoagulant row, and attaches it to the wrong drug. Induction lowers the other drug's level, so the victim drug fails at its own job: the anticoagulant stops preventing clots and the contraceptive stops preventing pregnancy.

q_0152.stem: A patient stabilized on a barbiturate is also taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. How does this interaction differ from the barbiturate's other listed interactions?
options: It causes the barbiturate itself to have prolonged effects, rather than causing the other drug to fail
It causes accelerated metabolism of the monoamine oxidase inhibitor
It produces purely additive CNS depression, exactly as alcohol does
It has no clinical significance and requires no monitoring
q_0152.rationale: The interaction table gives monoamine oxidase inhibitors the result of prolonged barbiturate effects. Every other listed interaction is either additive CNS depression, as with alcohol, antihistamines, benzodiazepines, opioids, and tranquilizers, or induction-driven failure of the other drug, as with the anticoagulants and the oral contraceptives (p. 190).
q_0152.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item — it applies the induction direction, in which the other drug loses effect, to the one row where the arrow points back at the barbiturate.

q_0153.stem: A patient is admitted after a phenobarbital overdose. Which measures does this chapter identify as part of management? Select all that apply.
options: Maintenance of an adequate airway, assisted ventilation, and oxygen administration if needed
Alkalinization of the urine, raising the pH
Forced diuresis using a diuretic such as furosemide
Administration of flumazenil as the specific antidote
Activated charcoal, which recent clinical data support as improving outcome
q_0153.rationale: Barbiturate overdose treatment is mainly symptomatic and supportive, with the mainstays being maintenance of an adequate airway, assisted ventilation, and oxygen administration if needed, along with fluid and pressor support. Because phenobarbital and mephobarbital are relatively acidic, alkalinizing the urine keeps the drug in the urine and prevents it from being resorbed back into the circulation, and alkalinization along with forced diuresis using diuretics such as furosemide can hasten elimination (p. 189).
q_0153.trap: (D) offers the benzodiazepine antidote for a barbiturate, which trades on both drugs being CNS depressants; the barbiturates have no antidote. (E) is named and then dismissed in the same sentence of the chapter, which states that recent clinical data do not support charcoal because no improvement in clinical outcome has been shown.

q_0154.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis is prescribed baclofen for spasticity, and a family member asks how the drug works on the muscles. Which explanation is accurate?
options: It acts directly on the muscle fiber by decreasing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Its beneficial effects are thought to come from its sedative effects rather than from direct muscle relaxation, because it acts in the CNS
It blocks transmission at the muscle-nerve junction
It increases the force of muscle contraction to overcome spasm
q_0154.rationale: Most muscle relaxants are centrally acting because their site of action is the CNS — the brainstem, thalamus, and basal ganglia, and also the spinal cord. Their beneficial effects are thought to come from their sedative effects rather than from direct muscle relaxation, and they have no direct effects on muscles, nerve conduction, or muscle-nerve junctions (p. 191).
q_0154.trap: (A) is dantrolene's mechanism, the one direct-acting drug in the chapter. Because every drug in the section is called a muscle relaxant, crediting a centrally acting agent with direct muscle action is the reflex error.

q_0155.stem: A patient develops malignant hyperthermia during general anesthesia. Which muscle relaxant is indicated, and why is it the only one that fits?
options: Baclofen, because it can be delivered by an implantable pump
Cyclobenzaprine, because it is the most commonly used drug in the class
Dantrolene, because it acts directly on the excitation-contraction coupling of muscle fibers rather than at the level of the CNS
Diazepam, because it is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant
q_0155.rationale: Only one compound, dantrolene, acts directly on skeletal muscle; it works on the excitation-contraction coupling of muscle fibers and not at the level of the CNS, by decreasing the amount of calcium released from storage sites in the sarcoplasmic reticula of muscle fibers. Intravenous dantrolene is used for the management of skeletal muscle spasms that accompany the crisis condition known as malignant hyperthermia (p. 191).
q_0155.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — it offers a centrally acting drug for a crisis occurring in the muscle fiber itself. Baclofen's pump and test dose are real facts attached to the wrong problem.

q_0156.subtopic: the two profiled relaxants and their adverse effects
q_0156.stem: Two centrally acting muscle relaxants are on a unit's formulary. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: Baclofen is available with an implantable pump requiring an initial test dose and relieves hiccups; cyclobenzaprine is related to the tricyclic antidepressants and commonly causes marked sedation
Cyclobenzaprine is the drug given by implantable pump; baclofen is the one related to the tricyclic antidepressants
Baclofen acts directly on muscle fibers, while cyclobenzaprine acts centrally
Only cyclobenzaprine is listed for spasticity
q_0156.rationale: Baclofen's injectable form is for use with an implantable baclofen pump device, and a test dose must be administered initially to test for a positive response; baclofen has also been shown to be effective in relieving hiccups (pp. 191 and 192). Cyclobenzaprine is structurally and pharmacologically related to the tricyclic antidepressants, is the most commonly used drug in this class to reduce spasms after musculoskeletal injuries, and very commonly produces marked sedation (p. 192).
q_0156.trap: (B) swaps the two drugs' signature facts, which is easy because both are centrally acting, both are dosed three times daily, and the dosages table lists spasticity for both.

q_0157.subtopic: the two profiled relaxants and their adverse effects
q_0157.stem: A patient receiving a skeletal muscle relaxant is being monitored for adverse effects. Which is the priority concern?
options: Hypertension
Peripheral edema
Blurred vision
CNS depression
q_0157.rationale: The adverse effects of the muscle relaxants are an extension of their effects on the CNS and skeletal muscles, and include generalized CNS depression manifested as sedation, somnolence, ataxia, and respiratory and cardiovascular depression (p. 191). Implementation escalates this: frequent monitoring of airway, breathing, and circulation is warranted, and early identification of toxicity is critical (p. 194).
q_0157.trap: (A) has the vital-sign direction backwards. The chapter lists hypotension among the less common adverse effects, not hypertension, so the option is inverted rather than merely unlisted.

q_0158.subtopic: the two profiled relaxants and their adverse effects
q_0158.stem: A patient takes the first dose of a newly prescribed muscle relaxant at home. Which teaching addresses the chapter's stated window of greatest risk?
options: The greatest risk for hypotension is usually within 1 hour of dosing, so change positions purposefully and slowly and ambulate cautiously
The greatest risk for hypotension occurs 8 to 12 hours after dosing, so avoid all morning activity
There is no hypotension risk with the centrally acting agents
Early dizziness and drowsiness mean the drug is failing and the dose should be doubled
q_0158.rationale: "The greatest risk for hypotension... is usually within 1 hour of dosing, so caution must be taken with activity" (p. 194); the patient is taught to change positions purposefully and slowly to prevent syncope or dizziness and to ambulate cautiously.
q_0158.trap: (D) misreads the chapter's reassurance about early effects. Euphoria, lightheadedness, dizziness, drowsiness, fatigue, confusion, and muscle weakness are common early in treatment and are generally short lived because patients grow tolerant to them — tolerance to the adverse effects, not loss of benefit, and never grounds for increasing the dose.

q_0159.topic: cns depressant administration and sleep hygiene teaching
q_0159.stem: A nurse prepares to give intravenous diazepam. Which action is correct?
options: Dilute the drug in 50 mL of normal saline and infuse it over 30 minutes
Inject it slowly, taking at least 1 minute for each 5 mg, through the infusion tubing as close as possible to the vein insertion site
Mix it in the same syringe with the ordered analgesic to reduce the number of injections
Choose a small vein in the hand so the site is easy to observe
q_0159.rationale: Intravenous diazepam must be injected slowly, at least 1 minute for each 5 mg given, through the infusion tubing as close as possible to the vein insertion site. It must not be mixed or diluted with other solutions or drugs in a syringe or infusion container, small veins are not to be used, and intraarterial administration and extravasation must be avoided (p. 194).
q_0159.trap: (A) applies the barbiturate rule to diazepam. Barbiturates require dilution with normal saline; diazepam must not be diluted at all, and swapping the two rules is the error the chapter's own page layout invites.

q_0160.topic: cns depressant administration and sleep hygiene teaching
q_0160.stem: A barbiturate is ordered intravenously. Which administration rule applies?
options: Give it undiluted by rapid intravenous push to reach a therapeutic level quickly
Dilute it with normal saline and give it no faster than 1 mg/kg/min
Give it no faster than 1 minute for each 5 mg
Add it to a running infusion of hydrocortisone
q_0160.rationale: Intravenous administration of a barbiturate requires dilution of the drug with normal saline, and most of these drugs are not to be given any faster than 1 mg/kg/min. Too rapid an infusion of a barbiturate may produce profound hypotension and marked respiratory depression, and the Key Points warn that too rapid an infusion may precipitate respiratory or cardiac arrest (pp. 194 and 196).
q_0160.trap: (C) is the mirror error of the previous item — it is diazepam's fixed time-per-dose rule, whereas the barbiturate rule is weight based. (D) names one of the chapter's stated incompatibilities, listed alongside amphotericin B and hydromorphone.

q_0161.topic: cns depressant administration and sleep hygiene teaching
q_0161.stem: A patient taking phenobarbital has a serum level of 46 mcg/mL and is found with cold, clammy skin and a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: The level is therapeutic, and the findings are unrelated to the drug
The level is above the therapeutic range, and the findings are the chapter's described signs of toxicity
The level is subtherapeutic, and the dose should be increased
The respiratory rate is within the acceptable range for this drug
q_0161.rationale: The therapeutic level of phenobarbital must range between 15 and 40 mcg/mL, and patients with serum levels greater than 40 mcg/mL may experience toxicity manifested by cold and clammy skin, a respiratory rate of less than 10 breaths/min, and other signs of severe CNS depression (p. 194).
q_0161.trap: (D) treats a rate of 8 as acceptable by rounding toward the printed threshold. The chapter's cutoff is a rate of less than 10, so a rate of 8 is already inside the toxic description rather than approaching it.

q_0162.topic: cns depressant administration and sleep hygiene teaching
q_0162.stem: A hospitalized patient tells the nurse she cannot fall asleep. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the ordered sedative-hypnotic
Offer valerian tea
Encourage her to walk the halls for exercise
Provide a restful environment and decrease exposure to loud noises
q_0162.rationale: The chapter states in four separate places that nonpharmacologic measures come before drug therapy, and gives the reason directly: benzodiazepines and other drugs are used only when nonpharmacologic methods fail (p. 194). Decreasing exposure to loud noises is itself an item in Box 12.1.
q_0162.trap: (B) looks nonpharmacologic because it is herbal, but valerian is a drug with hepatotoxicity and CNS depressant interactions of its own. (C) is contradicted by Box 12.1's instruction to avoid exercise late in the evening.

q_0163.topic: cns depressant administration and sleep hygiene teaching
q_0163.stem: A nurse teaches a patient the nonpharmacologic measures in Box 12.1. Which instructions belong to that box? Select all that apply.
options: Keep fixed bed and wake times in order to reset your internal clock
Avoid daytime napping
Avoid caffeine within 6 hours of bedtime
Have a glass of wine in the evening to help you fall asleep
If you are still awake 20 minutes after going to bed, get up and do something relaxing until you feel drowsy
q_0163.rationale: Box 12.1 lists a set sleep pattern with fixed bed and wake times to reset the internal clock, avoiding daytime napping, avoiding stimulants such as caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol close to bedtime with no caffeine within 6 hours of bedtime, and getting up after 20 minutes awake to engage in a relaxing activity before returning to bed once drowsy (p. 195).
q_0163.trap: (D) is the trap the box itself sets up: alcohol is listed among the things to avoid in the evening "because rather than putting you to sleep, it actually results in fragmented sleep." Alcohol is never a correct sleep intervention in this chapter, in any form.

q_0164.stem: A drug monograph states that only 35% of an oral dose reaches the systemic circulation, because the liver inactivates the rest before it gets there. Which branch of pharmacology does that statement belong to?
options: Pharmacodynamics
Pharmaceutics
Pharmacokinetics
Pharmacotherapeutics
q_0164.rationale: Pharmacokinetics is the study of what happens to a drug from the time it is put into the body until the parent drug and all metabolites have left it — absorption into, distribution and metabolism within, and excretion from the body. How much drug survives hepatic metabolism is a kinetic fact.
q_0164.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the two words differ by four letters. Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body.

q_0165.stem: The same monograph states that the drug slows heart rate by binding beta-1 receptors and reducing the rate at which cardiac cells contract. Which branch of pharmacology does that statement belong to?
options: Pharmacokinetics
Pharmacodynamics
Pharmaceutics
Pharmacognosy
q_0165.rationale: Pharmacodynamics is the study of the biochemical and physiologic interactions of drugs at their sites of activity; it examines the effect of the drug on the body. Receptor binding at the site of action is the definition case.
q_0165.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. Nothing here describes the drug's journey through the body — it describes what the drug does once it has arrived.

q_0166.stem: A pharmacist explains that micronized glyburide reaches its maximum concentration peak faster than nonmicronized glyburide, because the smaller particle size dissolves more quickly. Which science does this observation belong to?
options: Pharmaceutics
Pharmacokinetics
Pharmacotherapeutics
Pharmacoeconomics
q_0166.rationale: Pharmaceutics is the study of how various dosage forms influence the way in which the drug affects the body, and dosage form determines the rate at which dissolution occurs. Micronized versus nonmicronized glyburide is the chapter's own example.
q_0166.trap: (B) sounds defensible because dissolution feeds absorption, but Fig. 2.2 orders the three phases pharmaceutical, then pharmacokinetic, then pharmacodynamic. Anything decided by the dosage form before the body gets involved is pharmaceutic.

q_0167.stem: A discharge list reads "ibuprofen (Motrin) 400 mg," and the package insert gives the same drug as 2-p-isobutylphenyl propionic acid. Which of these names is the registered trademark?
options: ibuprofen, because it is the name used in most official drug compendiums
Motrin, because it is the commercial name given to the product by its manufacturer
2-p-isobutylphenyl propionic acid, because it uniquely identifies the molecule
Both ibuprofen and Motrin, because both are proprietary
q_0167.rationale: The trade or proprietary name is the drug's registered trademark, indicating that its commercial use is restricted to the owner of the patent. Trade names are created with marketability in mind, which is why they are shorter and easier to pronounce than generic names.
q_0167.trap: (A) is chosen by students who assume the name printed first is the official, protected one. The generic name is the official compendium name and is explicitly not protected by trademark.

q_0168.stem: The same patient asks who decides what a drug's generic name will be. Which response is accurate?
options: The manufacturer chooses it, with marketability in mind
The United States Adopted Names Council assigns it, and it is not protected by trademark
The FDA assigns it at approval and protects it for the life of the patent
It is derived from the drug's chemical composition and molecular structure
q_0168.rationale: The generic or nonproprietary name is given to a drug by the United States Adopted Names Council. It is much shorter and simpler than the chemical name and is not protected by trademark.
q_0168.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — marketability drives the trade name, not the generic one. (D) describes the chemical name, which is the one that states composition and molecular structure.

q_0169.stem: A formulary committee designates one drug in a class as the preferred agent and substitutes it for the others, even though the drugs do not contain the same active ingredient, on the ground that all have been proven to produce the same therapeutic effect. Which term names this practice?
options: Bioequivalence
Therapeutic equivalence
Biosimilarity
Off-label substitution
q_0169.rationale: Therapeutic equivalence is the practice of choosing one drug in a class of several as the preferred agent even though the drugs do not have the same active ingredients; the drugs must have been proven to have the same therapeutic effect before one can be substituted for another.
q_0169.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because the two terms differ by one word. Bioequivalence requires the same active ingredient at the same concentration with the same bioavailability. The phrase "do not contain the same active ingredient" is what rules it out here.

q_0170.stem: A pharmacist substitutes a generic tablet for the brand-name product, noting that the two contain the same active ingredient at the same concentration and have the same bioavailability. Which term names this relationship?
options: Therapeutic equivalence
Bioequivalence
Prototypical substitution
Off-label substitution
q_0170.rationale: If two drug products have the same bioavailability and the same concentration of active ingredient, they are said to be bioequivalent — the chapter's own example is a brand-name drug and the same generic drug.
q_0170.trap: (A) is the mirror error. Therapeutic equivalence is the looser, formulary-level standard that spans drugs with different active ingredients; bioequivalence is the strict same-ingredient, same-bioavailability match.

q_0171.stem: A patient asks why a newly approved drug costs so much more than an older one in the same class. Which statements about drug patents are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The patent life of a newly discovered drug molecule is normally 17 years
The research process for new drug development normally requires about 10 of those years
The manufacturer generally has the remaining 7 years for sales profits
After the patent expires, other manufacturers may make generics with the same active ingredient and the price usually decreases substantially
The 17 years begins at FDA approval, giving the manufacturer 17 years of marketing exclusivity
q_0171.rationale: Patent life is normally 17 years, development consumes about 10, roughly 7 remain for sales profits, and generic competition after expiration usually drops the price substantially.
q_0171.trap: (E) confuses patent life with the post-approval remainder, and it is the version that sounds most generous to the manufacturer. The clock runs on the molecule from discovery, which is exactly why only about 7 of the 17 years earn anything.

q_0172.stem: A prescriber orders a drug for an indication that does not appear in the manufacturer's labeling. Which statement is accurate?
options: This is illegal, and the nurse should refuse to administer the drug
This is off-label prescribing; only the manufacturer's written labeling is restricted to FDA-approved indications
This is off-label prescribing, which the FDA prohibits once a drug has an approved indication
This means the drug has not completed FDA approval for any indication
q_0172.rationale: The FDA permits only FDA-approved indications to be described in the manufacturer's written information, or labeling. Prescribers may at times choose to use drugs for non-FDA-approved indications, which is known as off-label prescribing, and previously off-label indications often become approved over time.
q_0172.trap: (A) reads the labeling restriction as a restriction on practice. What is regulated is what the manufacturer may claim in print, not what the prescriber may judge appropriate.

q_0173.stem: Four oral formulations of the same drug are stocked. Which will be absorbed most rapidly?
options: Enteric-coated tablet
Oral soluble wafer
Suspension
Capsule
q_0173.rationale: Table 2.1 ranks oral disintegration forms, buccal tablets, and oral soluble wafers as the fastest-absorbed oral preparations, ahead of liquids and elixirs, suspensions, powders, capsules, tablets, coated tablets, and enteric-coated tablets.
q_0173.trap: (C) is the strong second choice, because liquids are already dissolved and genuinely do beat every solid form. The wafer beats the liquid because nothing has to dissolve at all.

q_0174.stem: Of those same four formulations, which will be absorbed most slowly?
options: Enteric-coated tablet
Oral soluble wafer
Suspension
Capsule
q_0174.rationale: An enteric coating prevents the tablet from being broken down in the acidic pH of the stomach, so the drug is not absorbed until it reaches the higher, more alkaline pH of the intestines. That property produces slower dissolution and therefore slower absorption.
q_0174.trap: (D) is the reflex pick for anyone ranking by how solid the form looks. A plain capsule sits in the middle of Table 2.1; the enteric-coated tablet is last because the delay is engineered, not incidental.

q_0175.stem: A patient who has trouble swallowing is prescribed a tablet whose name ends in XL. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Crush the tablet and mix it into applesauce
Instruct the patient to chew the tablet thoroughly before swallowing
Consult the pharmacist about an alternative dosage form
Dissolve the tablet in 3 ounces of orange juice
q_0175.rationale: SR, SA, CR, XL, and XT all mark extended-release formulations, which must not be crushed, because crushing could cause accelerated release of drug from the dosage form and possible toxicity. The chapter directs consultation with a pharmacist or other suitable source whenever a question exists.
q_0175.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because the chapter does endorse applesauce and pudding — but as a vehicle for capsule contents and granules that are sprinkled, not as permission to crush an extended-release tablet. The soft food is the delivery method, not the authorization.

q_0176.stem: A patient asks why an enteric-coated tablet cannot be chewed. Which explanation is correct?
options: Chewing releases the whole dose at once, which can cause toxicity
Chewing destroys a coating that protects the stomach lining from the drug and protects the drug from stomach acid
Chewing makes the drug dissolve too slowly to be absorbed at all
Chewing converts the drug into an inactive metabolite before absorption
q_0176.rationale: The chapter names both purposes of an enteric coat in one sentence — protecting the stomach lining from the local effects of the drug, and protecting the drug from being prematurely disrupted by stomach acid. A stem may want either half.
q_0176.trap: (A) is the extended-release rationale attached to the wrong dosage form. One prohibited action, two different harms: crushing an extended-release form dumps the dose and risks toxicity, while destroying an enteric coat removes acid protection.

q_0177.stem: A patient with acute chest pain receives sublingual nitroglycerin rather than an oral tablet. Which statement best explains the choice?
options: Sublingual tissue absorbs slowly, which prolongs the drug's duration of action
The area under the tongue is highly vascular, so absorption is rapid, and the drug bypasses the liver while remaining systemically bioavailable
Sublingual administration is a topical route and therefore produces only local effects
Sublingual drugs undergo a first-pass effect that converts them to their active form
q_0177.rationale: Sublingual drugs are absorbed into the highly vascularized tissue under the tongue, absorbed rapidly because the area has a large blood supply, and bypass the liver while still being systemically bioavailable.
q_0177.trap: (D) turns the first-pass effect into an activation step. The first pass inactivates, which is why it reduces bioavailability to less than 100%. Metabolism that activates a drug is the separate case of a prodrug.

q_0178.stem: Which routes deliver drug to the systemic circulation without a first pass through the liver? Select all that apply.
options: Oral
Sublingual
Intravenous
Transdermal
Intramuscular
q_0178.rationale: Box 2.2 lists hepatic arterial, oral, portal venous, and rectal as first-pass routes. Sublingual, buccal, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, transdermal, inhaled, intranasal, intraarterial, intraocular, intravaginal, and aural are all non-first-pass.
q_0178.trap: (A) is the single first-pass route in this list, and it is the one most often let through, because oral feels like the default rather than a special case. Anything draining into the portal circulation is first-passed.

q_0179.stem: A patient receives an acetaminophen suppository. Which statement about the rectal route is accurate?
options: Rectal administration is topical and therefore completely avoids the first-pass effect
Rectal administration leads to both first-pass and non-first-pass effects, because some drug reaches the portal vein while some is absorbed into perirectal tissue
Rectal administration is handled identically to oral administration
Rectal administration produces 100% bioavailability
q_0179.rationale: All topical routes avoid first-pass effects with the exception of rectal administration. Because the rectum is part of the GI tract, some drug is absorbed into capillaries feeding the portal vein, while some is absorbed locally into perirectal tissues. Box 2.2 footnotes rectal on both lists.
q_0179.trap: (A) states the general topical rule and stops one clause early. The chapter names the exception in the same sentence as the rule, and rectal is the one route that appears on both sides of Box 2.2.

q_0180.subtopic: route choice and conditions that alter absorption
q_0180.stem: A trauma patient is in shock with decreased cardiac output and urine output under 30 mL/hr, and needs a drug to take effect immediately. Which route should the nurse anticipate?
options: Intramuscular
Subcutaneous
Intravenous
Oral
q_0180.rationale: The parenteral route is the fastest route by which a drug can be absorbed, and drugs injected intravenously are immediately placed into solution in the bloodstream, so 100% absorption is assumed to occur immediately. Intramuscular and subcutaneous doses are absorbed over a period of several hours.
q_0180.trap: (A) is the common miss, because intramuscular is also parenteral and feels fast. Intramuscular and subcutaneous absorption both depend on blood flow to the tissue, and perfusion is precisely what has failed in this patient — decreased blood flow decreases absorption.

q_0181.subtopic: route choice and conditions that alter absorption
q_0181.stem: A nurse reviews the timing of a patient's medications with respect to food. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Alendronate is taken on an empty stomach with at least 6 ounces of water
Taking an enteric-coated medication with a large amount of food may cause it to be dissolved by acidic stomach contents
The presence of food may enhance the absorption of some fat-soluble drugs
Macrolides and oral opioids are often taken with food to minimize gastrointestinal irritation, even though they are specified for an empty stomach
Anticholinergic drugs speed gastrointestinal transit time and increase the absorption of acid-susceptible drugs
q_0181.rationale: Box 2.1 places alendronate and risedronate on an empty stomach with at least 6 ounces of water, and carbamazepine, iron, hydralazine, lithium, propranolol, spironolactone, NSAIDs, and theophylline with food. Macrolides and oral opioids are its third category — specified for an empty stomach but often given with food for tolerability.
q_0181.trap: (E) reverses the anticholinergic effect in both halves of the sentence. Anticholinergic drugs slow GI transit time, which may reduce the amount absorbed for acid-susceptible drugs.

q_0182.subtopic: route choice and conditions that alter absorption
q_0182.stem: A patient has had a large portion of the small intestine resected and now has short bowel syndrome. Which effect on oral drug therapy should the nurse anticipate?
options: Increased absorption, because transit time is shortened
Decreased absorption, because the surface available for absorption is reduced
No change, because absorption occurs primarily in the stomach
Increased first-pass effect, because the liver receives more drug
q_0182.rationale: The chapter lists surgical alteration of GI anatomy among the factors that alter absorption, naming short bowel syndrome from small-intestine resection and bariatric surgery, where stomach contents are delivered to the intestines more rapidly than usual in what is called gastric dumping.
q_0182.trap: (C) mislocates absorption. Orally administered drugs are absorbed through the mucosa of the stomach and the small or large intestine, and the small intestine is the highly vascularized surface that resection removes.

q_0183.stem: A patient with extensive burns and a low serum albumin is receiving a highly protein-bound drug at a standard dose and develops signs of toxicity. Which explanation is correct?
options: Low albumin leaves a larger fraction of free, pharmacologically active drug
Low albumin leaves more drug bound to protein and therefore more active
Low albumin slows hepatic metabolism of the drug
Low albumin increases the drug's distribution into adipose tissue
q_0183.rationale: Only drug molecules not bound to plasma proteins can freely distribute to extravascular tissue and reach the site of action, and the unbound portion is the pharmacologically active one. Conditions causing low albumin, such as extensive burns and malnourished states, result in a larger fraction of free drug and raise the risk for toxicity.
q_0183.trap: (B) inverts the rule, and it is the intuitive inversion, because "bound to a carrier" sounds like "being delivered." Bound drug is stuck in the bloodstream in a complex too large to cross the capillary wall, and it is doing nothing.

q_0184.stem: A patient stabilized on warfarin, which is highly protein bound, is started on amiodarone, which is also highly protein bound. Which effect should the nurse anticipate, and in which pharmacokinetic phase does it occur?
options: Decreased effect of both drugs, in the absorption phase
Higher levels of free warfarin and amiodarone with increased actions of both, in the distribution phase
Decreased metabolism of warfarin with toxic accumulation, in the metabolism phase
Prolonged plasma levels of both drugs, in the excretion phase
q_0184.rationale: Table 2.10 gives warfarin with amiodarone as its distribution-phase example: both drugs compete for protein-binding sites, producing higher levels of free, unbound drug and increasing the actions of both, which is harmful.
q_0184.trap: (C) names a plausible outcome with the wrong mechanism, and it is the reflex answer because most interactions in this chapter turn out to be enzyme interactions. Competition for albumin is displacement, not enzyme competition, and the phase label is what this item is testing.

q_0185.stem: A drug is described as highly water-soluble, or hydrophilic. What should the nurse expect?
options: A large volume of distribution and low blood concentrations
A small volume of distribution and high blood concentrations
A large volume of distribution and high blood concentrations
Extensive distribution into adipose tissue
q_0185.rationale: Highly water-soluble drugs have a smaller volume of distribution and high blood concentrations. Volume of distribution is a theoretical volume describing the compartments — blood, total body water, body fat, other tissues and organs — into which a drug may distribute.
q_0185.trap: (A) is the lipophilic pattern, and it is the more commonly chosen inversion, because "distributes widely" sounds like it should mean higher levels. Water-soluble drugs stay in the water compartment, which is small, so the concentration there is high.

q_0186.stem: A drug is described as highly fat-soluble, or lipophilic. What should the nurse expect?
options: A small volume of distribution and high blood concentrations
A large volume of distribution and low blood concentrations
A small volume of distribution and low blood concentrations
Distribution confined to the intravascular space
q_0186.rationale: Fat-soluble drugs have a larger volume of distribution and low blood concentrations, because they disperse out of the blood into fat and other tissues.
q_0186.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. The relationship is inverse in both directions, and the practical danger is reading a low blood level on a lipophilic drug as "not enough drug on board."

q_0187.subtopic: sites that are hard to reach
q_0187.stem: An antibiotic reaches therapeutic serum concentrations but fails to clear an infection in bone. Which explanation does the chapter give?
options: Bone is protected by a physiologic barrier similar to the blood-brain barrier
Bone has a poor blood supply, which makes drug distribution to it difficult
Bone tissue metabolizes drugs faster than other tissues
Bone binds drug to albumin more tightly than plasma does
q_0187.rationale: The chapter names two kinds of hard-to-reach site and gives one example of each: sites with a poor blood supply, such as bone, and sites with physiologic barriers, such as the brain with its blood-brain barrier. Heart, liver, kidneys, and brain receive drug rapidly, while muscle, skin, and fat receive it more slowly.
q_0187.trap: (A) transfers the brain's reason onto bone. There is no bone-blood barrier in this chapter; the obstacle is perfusion, which is a different problem with a different set of solutions.

q_0188.stem: A patient stable on a maintenance drug is started on rifampin, and within two weeks the original drug is no longer controlling their symptoms. What has most likely happened?
options: Rifampin inhibited the cytochrome P-450 enzymes, so the drug accumulated
Rifampin induced the cytochrome P-450 enzymes, speeding metabolism and lowering drug levels
Rifampin displaced the drug from albumin, increasing the free fraction
Rifampin blocked renal tubular secretion of the drug
q_0188.rationale: Rifampin and phenytoin are the chapter's named P-450 inducers, and barbiturates also increase metabolism. Enzyme inducers stimulate drug metabolism, often by stimulating the formation of new microsomal enzymes, which causes decreased pharmacologic effects.
q_0188.trap: (A) is the reflex answer for anyone who hears "enzyme interaction" and reaches for accumulation. An inducer speeds metabolism, so there is less drug present and the failure is therapeutic, not toxic.

q_0189.stem: A patient stable on a maintenance drug is started on ketoconazole, and within a week shows signs of toxicity from the original drug. What has most likely happened?
options: Ketoconazole induced the cytochrome P-450 enzymes, speeding metabolism
Ketoconazole inhibited the cytochrome P-450 enzymes, so the drug accumulated and its effects were prolonged
Ketoconazole increased the drug's volume of distribution
Ketoconazole increased renal excretion of the drug
q_0189.rationale: Ketoconazole is the chapter's named P-450 inhibitor. Decreases in drug metabolism result in accumulation of the drug and prolongation of its effects, which can lead to drug toxicity.
q_0189.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. The word "inhibitor" misleads because it sounds like it should reduce the drug's effect — it reduces enzyme activity, which raises drug levels.

q_0190.stem: Which conditions and drugs decrease drug metabolism? Select all that apply.
options: Renal insufficiency
Slow acetylator status
Barbiturates
Obstructive jaundice
Starvation
q_0190.rationale: Table 2.6 sorts in two directions. Cardiovascular dysfunction, renal insufficiency, starvation, obstructive jaundice, slow acetylator status, and ketoconazole all decrease metabolism; only fast acetylator status, barbiturates, rifampin, and phenytoin increase it.
q_0190.trap: (C) is the one entry here from the increased side, and it slips through because barbiturates are sedatives and sedation reads as "slowing." Barbiturates belong with rifampin and phenytoin as agents that stimulate metabolism, not with the disease states that impair it.

q_0191.stem: A patient is described as a slow acetylator. What is the clinical consequence?
options: Metabolism of certain drugs is increased, risking therapeutic failure
Metabolism of certain drugs is reduced, so the drug accumulates and toxicity is more likely
Red blood cells hemolyze when the patient is exposed to oxidizing drugs
Renal excretion of the drug is accelerated
q_0191.rationale: Table 2.6 lists slow acetylator status under genetic constitution with decreased metabolism, and fast acetylator status with increased metabolism. Reduced metabolism means the drug accumulates.
q_0191.trap: (C) is the other genetic host factor this course teaches, and it is the substitution students make under time pressure. G6PD deficiency makes red cells break down; slow acetylation makes drug pile up. They are not interchangeable.

q_0192.stem: A prodrug is ordered for a patient with severe hepatic impairment. Why is the nurse concerned?
options: The prodrug is already active and will accumulate to toxic levels
The prodrug is inactive until biochemical reactions convert it to an active metabolite, and impaired metabolism may leave it ineffective
The prodrug will bypass the first-pass effect entirely
The prodrug will be excreted unchanged by the kidney before it can act
q_0192.rationale: A prodrug is an inactive drug dosage form that is converted to an active metabolite by various biochemical reactions once it is inside the body, and the liver is the organ most responsible for drug metabolism. Cefuroxime axetil is the course's worked example, hydrolyzed in the liver to its active cefuroxime form.
q_0192.trap: (A) treats every metabolic problem as an accumulation problem, which is the correct instinct for most drugs and exactly backwards here. With a prodrug the failure runs the other way: no metabolism means no active drug.

q_0193.stem: A drug's peak level is 100 mg/L, and the level measured 8 hours later is 50 mg/L. Approximately how long after the peak will this drug be considered effectively removed from the body?
options: 16 hours
24 hours
40 hours
80 hours
q_0193.rationale: A fall from 100 to 50 mg/L over 8 hours makes the half-life 8 hours. After about five half-lives most drugs are considered effectively removed, with approximately 97% eliminated — five times 8 hours is 40 hours.
q_0193.trap: (B) is what you get by stopping at three half-lives, where Table 2.7 shows 88% removed. Eighty-eight percent feels like "most of it is gone," but the chapter's threshold is five half-lives and 97%.

q_0194.stem: A drug with a half-life of 24 hours is started at a fixed dose on a fixed schedule. When should the nurse expect steady-state blood levels?
options: After the first dose, once absorption is complete
After about four to five half-lives, so roughly 4 to 5 days
After one half-life, so roughly 24 hours
Never, because drugs with long half-lives do not reach steady state
q_0194.rationale: Steady state is the physiologic state in which the amount of drug removed via elimination equals the amount absorbed with each dose, and this plateau typically occurs after four to five half-lives. A drug with an extremely long half-life takes much longer to reach steady-state blood levels.
q_0194.trap: (C) collapses the plateau into a single half-life. Both of this chapter's milestones are counted in half-lives — about five to clear a drug out, four to five to build up to steady state — and the shared unit is what makes them swappable.

q_0195.stem: A patient's therapeutic drug monitoring returns a peak level above the reference range and a trough level below it. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The high peak risks toxicity and the low trough risks a period below therapeutic levels
The high peak risks a period below therapeutic levels and the low trough risks toxicity
Both values indicate toxicity
Peak and trough describe drug effects only, never drug concentrations
q_0195.rationale: If the peak blood level is too high, drug toxicity may occur, ranging from intensified drug effects such as excessive sedation to damage to vital organs. If the trough blood level is too low, the drug may not be at therapeutic levels to produce a response.
q_0195.trap: (B) inverts the two ends of the same curve, which is the whole reason monitoring measures both. (D) is half true and therefore tempting: onset, peak, duration, and trough all describe drug effects, but peak and trough are also used for concentrations measured from blood samples.

q_0196.stem: A drug undergoes active tubular reabsorption in the nephron. What is the effect on that drug?
options: It is taken back up into the systemic circulation rather than eliminated
It is moved from the surrounding vasculature into the nephron for elimination
It is passively filtered at the glomerulus
It is conjugated into a more water-soluble metabolite
q_0196.rationale: In active tubular reabsorption, substances present in the nephron are taken back up into the systemic circulation and transported away from the kidney, in what the chapter calls an attempt by the body to retain needed substances.
q_0196.trap: (B) is the definition of active tubular secretion, and the two are swapped constantly because both are "active tubular" processes. Reabsorption returns drug to the body; secretion pushes more into the nephron. This is the transporter probenecid blocks, which is why it keeps penicillin in the blood.

q_0197.stem: A fat-soluble drug persists in a patient far longer than its elimination rate alone would predict. It is taken up by the liver, released into bile, reabsorbed from the intestine, returned to the liver, and secreted into bile again. Which process is this?
options: First-pass effect
Enterohepatic recirculation
Active tubular reabsorption
Protein binding
q_0197.rationale: Drugs eliminated by biliary excretion are taken up by the liver, released into the bile, and eliminated in the feces, but fat-soluble drugs in the bile may be reabsorbed into the bloodstream, returned to the liver, and again secreted into the bile. Enterohepatically recirculated drugs persist in the body for much longer periods.
q_0197.trap: (A) is chosen because both processes involve the liver and the gut. The first-pass effect happens once, on the way in, and reduces bioavailability; recirculation happens repeatedly, on the way out, and prolongs the drug.

q_0198.stem: A patient receives naloxone after an opioid overdose. Naloxone binds the opioid receptor, produces no response, and prevents the opioid from binding. How is naloxone classified?
options: Agonist
Partial agonist
Antagonist
Substrate
q_0198.rationale: Table 2.8 defines an antagonist as a drug that binds to the receptor with no response and prevents the binding of agonists. Antagonists are also called inhibitors.
q_0198.trap: (B) is picked by students who reason that some effect must be occurring, since the patient visibly improves. A partial agonist binds and produces a diminished response; naloxone's benefit comes from producing no response at all while blocking the opioid.

q_0199.stem: A drug binds its receptor and produces the full expected cellular response. How is it classified?
options: Antagonist
Agonist
Competitive antagonist
Noncompetitive antagonist
q_0199.rationale: An agonist binds to and stimulates the activity of one or more receptors in the body, and Table 2.8 states simply that the drug binds the receptor and there is a response.
q_0199.trap: (A) is the inversion this chapter warns about most directly, because both agonists and antagonists bind. Fig. 2.7 makes the point visually: the antagonist occupies the site and produces a blocked response. The distinction is what happens after binding, not whether attachment occurs.

q_0200.stem: A patient who took a long-acting opioid is given naloxone, improves, then deteriorates again 45 minutes later. Which property of naloxone explains why repeat dosing is required?
options: It is a noncompetitive antagonist and permanently inactivates the receptor
It is a competitive antagonist, so the remaining opioid can reoccupy the receptor as naloxone's level falls
It is a partial agonist whose diminished response wears off
It induces the P-450 enzymes that metabolize the opioid
q_0200.rationale: A competitive antagonist competes with the agonist for binding to the receptor, and if it binds there is no response. Because the competition is for the same site, the balance shifts back as the antagonist is cleared. Naloxone and naltrexone are competitive antagonists with strong affinity for the opioid receptors.
q_0200.trap: (A) describes the noncompetitive pattern, in which the drug combines with a different part of the receptor and inactivates it, so more agonist does not help. If naloxone worked that way, redosing would be unnecessary — which is exactly the clinical error this distinction prevents.

q_0201.stem: A drug is described as having very high affinity for its receptor. What does this tell the nurse?
options: The drug will produce a strong therapeutic response
The drug attaches to and binds the receptor strongly; among agonists that predicts a greater response, but an antagonist with high affinity produces no response at all
The drug must be an agonist, since only agonists bind receptors
The drug has a high therapeutic index
q_0201.rationale: Affinity is the degree to which a drug attaches to and binds with a receptor, and the drug with the best fit and strongest affinity elicits the greatest response. Affinity describes the strength of attachment; whether a response follows is a separate question, which is why naloxone can be a strong-affinity antagonist.
q_0201.trap: (A) conflates affinity with intrinsic activity, and the lock-and-key figure invites it by pairing "the better the fit" with "the better the response." Binding strongly and producing an effect are two different claims.

q_0202.stem: An antibiotic kills bacteria by causing formation of a defective cell wall that ruptures the cell. Which mechanism of action is this?
options: Receptor interaction
Enzyme interaction
Nonselective interaction with cellular processes
Competitive antagonism
q_0202.rationale: Drugs with nonspecific mechanisms of action do not interact with receptors or enzymes; their main targets are cell membranes and cellular processes such as metabolic activities. By incorporating into a normal metabolic process they cause a defect in the final product — an improperly formed cell wall that results in cell death through cell lysis, or the lack of a necessary energy substrate leading to cell starvation. Some cancer drugs and antibiotics work this way.
q_0202.trap: (B) is the chapter's other non-receptor mechanism and the closer distractor: in a selective enzyme interaction the drug inhibits, more commonly, or enhances, less commonly, a specific enzyme. The clue is the target — a defective structural product rather than a catalyzed reaction.

q_0203.stem: A patient takes a beta blocker daily to keep blood pressure within a target range and prevent end-organ damage. Which type of therapy is this?
options: Palliative
Maintenance
Supportive
Supplemental
q_0203.rationale: Maintenance therapy does not eradicate preexisting problems but prevents progression of a disease or condition, and it is used for chronic illnesses. Hypertension is the chapter's own example: maintenance therapy keeps blood pressure within given limits, which prevents certain end-organ damage.
q_0203.trap: (D) is the closest miss, because a daily drug feels like something the body is being supplied with. Supplemental, or replacement, therapy supplies a substance the body cannot make or does not make in sufficient quantity — insulin, or iron in iron-deficiency anemia. A beta blocker replaces nothing.

q_0204.stem: A patient who is vomiting and has diarrhea receives intravenous fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration while the illness resolves. Which type of therapy is this?
options: Supportive
Supplemental
Maintenance
Prophylactic
q_0204.rationale: Supportive therapy maintains the integrity of body functions while the patient is recovering from illness or trauma. The chapter's examples are fluids and electrolytes for a vomiting patient with diarrhea, and fluids, volume expanders, or blood products for a patient who has lost blood during surgery.
q_0204.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because fluid is being supplied, and supplemental therapy also supplies something. Supplemental therapy replaces a substance the body cannot produce in adequate quantity as an ongoing deficit; supportive therapy holds body functions steady through a temporary insult.

q_0205.stem: A patient in the final stages of cancer receives high-dose opioid analgesics. The family asks whether starting these means treatment has been abandoned. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Palliative therapy is begun only after all curative treatment has been stopped
Palliative therapy focuses on relief from symptoms, pain, and stress, and can be provided along with curative treatment
Palliative therapy is a form of maintenance therapy that prevents disease progression
Palliative therapy is limited to the last 48 hours of life
q_0205.rationale: Palliative therapy makes the patient as comfortable as possible and focuses on providing relief from the symptoms, pain, and stress of a serious illness, with the goal of improving quality of life for both patient and family. It is typically used in the end stages of an illness when attempts at curative therapy have failed, but it can be provided along with curative treatment.
q_0205.trap: (A) is the widespread assumption the chapter explicitly contradicts in the same paragraph where it names the typical timing. "Typically used at the end stages" is not the same claim as "only after curative therapy stops."

q_0206.stem: A patient is given an antibiotic before the surgical incision is made, to prevent a postoperative infection. Which type of therapy is this?
options: Empiric
Prophylactic
Supportive
Maintenance
q_0206.rationale: Prophylactic therapy is provided to prevent illness or another undesirable outcome during a planned event. The chapter's examples are preoperative antibiotic therapy, with the antibiotic given before the incision is made, and disease-specific vaccines for travel to areas where a disease is endemic.
q_0206.trap: (A) is the reflex answer, because both types start before any organism has been identified. The deciding fact is that this patient has no infection — prophylaxis prevents, while empiric therapy treats something already present.

q_0207.stem: A patient arrives with signs of pneumonia. Cultures are drawn, and an antibiotic active against the organism most commonly associated with that infection is started before results return. Which type of therapy is this?
options: Prophylactic
Empiric
Palliative
Supplemental
q_0207.rationale: Empiric therapy is based on clinical probabilities and involves drug administration when a pathologic condition has a high likelihood of occurrence based on the patient's initial presenting symptoms — the chapter's example is an antibiotic active against the most commonly associated organism, started before culture and sensitivity reports are available.
q_0207.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, and the culture is what gives it away. You do not draw cultures on a patient who has no infection; the pending culture means illness is present and the choice is a probability judgment, not prevention.

q_0208.stem: A patient is started on warfarin, and the nurse notes that it has a low therapeutic index. What does this mean for the plan of care?
options: The drug is unusually safe and rarely associated with overdose
The difference between a therapeutically active dose and a toxic dose is small, so closer monitoring is required
The drug requires a loading dose to reach steady state
The drug has low bioavailability by the oral route
q_0208.rationale: The therapeutic index is the ratio of a drug's toxic level to the level that provides therapeutic benefits, and it determines the safety of the therapy. With a low therapeutic index the difference between an active dose and a toxic dose is small, which brings a greater likelihood of an adverse reaction and requires closer monitoring. Warfarin and digoxin are the chapter's examples.
q_0208.trap: (A) inverts the scale, and the inversion is built into the wording — "low" sounds like low risk. The index is a ratio, so a small ratio means the therapeutic and toxic doses sit close together.

q_0209.stem: A different drug is described as having a high therapeutic index. What does this indicate?
options: The drug is more dangerous and needs frequent serum levels
The drug has a wide margin between therapeutic and toxic levels and is rarely associated with overdose events
The drug reaches toxic levels after a single dose
The drug must be given intravenously to be safe
q_0209.rationale: Drugs with a high therapeutic index are rarely associated with overdose events, and the chapter's example is amoxicillin.
q_0209.trap: (A) is the mirror error. Consistent monitoring belongs to the low-index drugs — warfarin, digoxin, and the aminoglycosides and vancomycin taken up in Chapter 39 — precisely because their margin is narrow.

q_0210.stem: A patient has needed steadily larger doses of an analgesic over several months to obtain the same relief, and reports no craving and no withdrawal when a dose is late. Which term describes this?
options: Psychological dependence
Physical dependence
Tolerance
Idiosyncratic reaction
q_0210.rationale: Tolerance is a decreasing response to repeated drug doses, or reduced response to a drug after prolonged use. Dependence, by contrast, is a physiologic or psychological need for a drug.
q_0210.trap: (B) is the standing confusion in this course, and it is not the student's fault: Chapter 10's key terms call tolerance the same thing as physical dependence, while this chapter keeps them separate. When a stem turns on the distinction, this chapter's version is the more precise one — tolerance is a decreasing response, dependence is a need.

q_0211.stem: A patient with an opioid use disorder develops tachycardia and other physical symptoms when the drug is withheld, and describes an obsessive desire for its euphoric effects. Which terms apply? Select all that apply.
options: Physical dependence, shown by withdrawal symptoms when the drug is withheld
Psychological dependence, also known as addiction
Tolerance, defined as a physiologic need to avoid withdrawal
An idiosyncratic reaction to the opioid
Dependence, defined as a physiologic or psychological need for a drug
q_0211.rationale: Physical dependence is the physiologic need for a drug to avoid physical withdrawal symptoms, with tachycardia in an opioid-addicted patient as the chapter's example. Psychological dependence, also known as addiction, is the obsessive desire for a drug's euphoric effects and typically involves recreational use of drugs such as benzodiazepines, opioids, and amphetamines.
q_0211.trap: (C) attaches the definition of physical dependence to the word tolerance, which is the substitution this chapter exists to prevent. Tolerance is a decreasing response to repeated doses, not a need to avoid withdrawal.

q_0212.stem: Two antibiotics with similar actions are given together, and the combined effect is greater than the sum of their individual effects. Which term names this?
options: Additive effects
Synergistic effects
Antagonistic effects
Incompatibility
q_0212.rationale: Synergistic effects are drug interactions in which the effect of a combination of two or more drugs with similar actions is greater than the sum of the individual effects — the chapter's arithmetic is 1 + 1 is greater than 2. Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and an aminoglycoside plus a beta-lactam are the course's worked examples.
q_0212.trap: (A) is the reflex answer for any beneficial combination. Additive means the combination equals the sum, 1 + 1 = 2. The word "greater" in the stem is doing all the work.

q_0213.stem: A tetracycline is given together with a bactericidal antibiotic, and the combined effect is less than the sum of the individual effects. Which term names this?
options: Additive effects
Synergistic effects
Antagonistic effects
Incompatibility
q_0213.rationale: Antagonistic effects are interactions in which the effect of a combination is less than the sum of the individual effects, 1 + 1 equals less than 2, usually caused by an antagonizing, blocking, or reducing effect of one drug on another.
q_0213.trap: (D) is chosen because both terms sound like drugs working against each other. Incompatibility is a physical or chemical event between two parenteral drugs mixed together — a precipitate, haziness, or color change — not a diminished pharmacologic effect in the patient.

q_0214.stem: A patient taking simvastatin asks whether grapefruit juice is a problem. Which response is accurate, and why?
options: Grapefruit juice increases metabolism of the drug, so the drug becomes less effective
Grapefruit juice decreases metabolism of the drug, so drug levels and effects increase
Grapefruit juice binds the drug in the gut, so less is absorbed
Grapefruit juice has no effect on statins
q_0214.rationale: Table 2.9 gives grapefruit juice with amiodarone, buspirone, carbamazepine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, several calcium channel blockers, simvastatin, and atorvastatin, with the result listed as decreased metabolism of drugs and increased effects.
q_0214.trap: (A) reads "decreased" as "less drug effect," which is the direction most students assume, because the word sits right next to the juice. What is decreased is the enzyme activity, so the drug accumulates and the effect is stronger.

q_0215.stem: A patient on warfarin begins eating large servings of leafy green vegetables daily. Which effect should the nurse anticipate?
options: Increased anticoagulant effect and bleeding risk
Decreased anticoagulant effect
Chemical binding of warfarin, preventing absorption
Hypertensive crisis
q_0215.rationale: Table 2.9 lists leafy green vegetables with warfarin and gives the result as a decreased anticoagulant effect from warfarin.
q_0215.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because bleeding is the outcome students associate with warfarin teaching, so any change gets read as more bleeding. (D) belongs to aged cheese and wine with monoamine oxidase inhibitors, the other food row in the same table.

q_0216.stem: Match each drug interaction to the pharmacokinetic phase in which it occurs. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Antacid with levofloxacin — absorption, because the antacid binds the drug in the gut
Warfarin with amiodarone — distribution, because the drugs compete for protein-binding sites
Erythromycin with cyclosporine — metabolism, because the drugs compete for the same hepatic enzymes
Amoxicillin with probenecid — excretion, because probenecid inhibits secretion of amoxicillin into the kidneys
Antacid with levofloxacin — metabolism, because the antacid inhibits P-450 enzymes
q_0216.rationale: Table 2.10 gives exactly one example per phase, and marks the first three harmful and the probenecid pairing as potentially beneficial, since it elevates and prolongs plasma levels of amoxicillin.
q_0216.trap: (E) reassigns the antacid interaction to the metabolism phase, and it is tempting because the chapter states that most drug interactions involve competition for metabolizing enzymes. This one is the exception the table uses to teach the absorption phase — binding in the gut, before anything is absorbed.

q_0217.stem: A patient took a sleep medication and reports feeling restless and being unable to sleep at all that night. There is no rash, swelling, or respiratory involvement. How should this reaction be classified?
options: Allergic reaction
Idiosyncratic reaction
Pharmacologic reaction
Synergistic effect
q_0217.rationale: An idiosyncratic reaction is an abnormal and unexpected response to a medication, other than an allergic reaction, that is peculiar to an individual patient. A response opposite to the drug's intended effect in one individual fits that definition.
q_0217.trap: (A) is the default label students apply to any unexpected reaction. An allergic reaction is an immunologic hypersensitivity reaction involving immunoglobulins, and nothing in this stem points to the immune system. (C) would require an extension of the drug's normal effect — excessive sedation, not the reverse.

q_0218.stem: A nurse omits a scheduled dose of a patient's antihypertensive, and the patient's blood pressure rises. Which term best describes what has occurred?
options: An adverse drug reaction, because the outcome occurred at a therapeutic dose
An adverse drug event, because it is an undesirable occurrence related to failing to administer a prescribed medication
An idiosyncratic reaction, because the response was peculiar to this patient
Neither, because no drug was given
q_0218.rationale: An adverse drug event is any undesirable occurrence related to administering or failing to administer a prescribed medication, and it is the broadest of the chapter's four overlapping terms. A medication error is any preventable adverse drug event, and it may or may not cause patient harm.
q_0218.trap: (D) is the intuitive answer, since nothing entered the patient. The definition of an adverse drug event explicitly includes failing to administer, which is what separates it from an adverse drug reaction — the narrower term, restricted to responses at therapeutic dosages.
