Japanese patients require higher dosages of antimanic drugs
Chinese patients require lower dosages of antipsychotics
The comparison group for all of these responses is White patients
q_0437.rationale: The box lists lower haloperidol dosages for Asian patients, better response to lower antidepressant dosages for Asian and Hispanic patients, and lower antipsychotic dosages for Chinese patients. Its footnote reads, "Note: The comparison group for all responses is Whites." The body text adds that Japanese and Taiwanese patients may require lower dosages of lithium.
q_0437.trap: (C) is the one option taken from the wrong side of its row. The box says Japanese patients "require lower dosages of antimanic drugs." Reading these rows for drug class while skipping the direction word is what loses this item, and an option that states an absolute dose requirement rather than a relative one has also dropped the comparator that makes the claim mean anything.

q_0438.stem: A nurse is preparing to give a first dose to a patient who recently immigrated. Which action does the chapter direct before that medication is administered?
options: Apply the health beliefs listed for the patient's cultural group in the chapter's table of common practices
Withhold the drug until a family member confirms what the patient believes
Complete a cultural assessment covering language needs, health beliefs, past medicine use, herbal and home remedies, over-the-counter drugs, religious practices, community support, and dietary habits
Document that a cultural assessment is not indicated for a first dose
q_0438.rationale: The chapter's checklist directs a thorough cultural assessment before any medication is administered, covering languages spoken and the need for an interpreter, health beliefs and practices, past uses of medicine, herbal and folk and home remedies or supplements, over-the-counter drug use, usual responses to illness, responsiveness to medical treatment, religious practices and beliefs, support from the patient's cultural community, and dietary habits.
q_0438.trap: (A) is the assumption the chapter explicitly forbids in the most important sentence of the section: "consult with the patient rather than assume that the patient holds certain beliefs because he or she belongs to a certain ethnic group." The table exists to describe variation, not to predict an individual.

q_0439.stem: An older adult Asian patient is admitted for drug therapy. Which cultural issue does the chapter tie most directly to that therapy?
options: Hospital diets will be unacceptable to this patient
The use of herbal products may be an important practice for this patient
X-ray studies will be refused by this patient
Hospitalization will be valued mainly as an opportunity for socialization
q_0439.rationale: The assessment checklist names "use of herbal treatments, folk remedies, home remedies, or supplements" as a required question, and the body text warns that alternative therapies such as herbal and homeopathic remedies "can inhibit or accelerate drug metabolism" and therefore alter a drug's response. The chapter also notes that a diet high in fat "has been documented to increase the absorption of some drugs."
q_0439.trap: (A), (C), and (D) are group-level assumptions rather than assessment findings, and none has a pharmacologic mechanism attached to it. The herbal option is the only one the chapter connects to drug metabolism.

q_0440.stem: A nurse is writing discharge medication instructions for a patient whose first language is Chinese. Which approach does the chapter specifically recommend?
options: Use contractions so the instructions stay short and conversational
Give general instructions and let the patient work out the specifics
Rely on a family member to translate rather than requesting an interpreter
Write "cannot," "will not," and "do not" instead of the contractions "can't," "won't," and "don't"
q_0440.rationale: The chapter notes that some languages, such as Chinese, "do not have numerous verb tenses" compared with English, so "very precise instructions must be included in patient education," and it states that avoiding contractions "is important with patients from other countries to prevent confusion."
q_0440.trap: (A) inverts the chapter's own instruction, and it pulls because plain conversational English is usually the teaching advice. Here precision outranks informality. (B) breaks the same requirement for very precise instructions from the other side.

q_0441.stem: A unit adopts Leininger's Sunrise Model to structure its cultural assessments. How many major areas does the chapter say this model covers?
options: Four, matching the columns of the chapter's table of common cultural practices
Nine, matching the provisions of the ANA Code of Ethics
Seven, including educational, economic, familial and social, political, technologic, religious and philosophic, and cultural values, beliefs, and practices
Three, matching the bodies that regulate drug therapy
q_0441.rationale: Box 4.3 states that the Sunrise Model "focuses on seven major areas of cultural assessment, including educational, economic, familial and social, political, technologic, religious and philosophic, and cultural values, beliefs, and practices." Other tools are named in the same box by author and year only.
q_0441.trap: (B) borrows the nine provisions of the ANA Code of Ethics, and (D) borrows the FDA, DEA, and state law trio. Numbers lifted from a different list in the same chapter are the standard distractor for any counted item here.

q_0442.subtopic: the tragedies and the acts they produced
q_0442.stem: Over 100 people died in the United States after ingesting a sulfanilamide preparation made with diethylene glycol, a component of automobile antifreeze, which had never been tested for toxicity. Which legislation did this produce, and what did it require?
options: The Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962, requiring proof of therapeutic efficacy
The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, requiring data proving drug safety and establishing the investigational new drug application process
The Durham-Humphrey Amendment of 1951, establishing legend drugs
The Controlled Substance Act of 1970, establishing the schedules
q_0442.rationale: Table 4.1 credits the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938 with requiring manufacturers to "provide data proving drug safety" with FDA review and with establishing the investigational new drug application process, and names the sulfanilamide elixir tragedy as its prompt.
q_0442.trap: (A) is the reflex pick for anyone who remembers only that a tragedy produced a law. The pairing is chronological and it is the mnemonic: the earlier disaster produced the earlier, weaker requirement, which was safety alone.

q_0443.subtopic: the tragedies and the acts they produced
q_0443.stem: Pregnant women in Europe who took thalidomide, a sedative-hypnotic, gave birth to seriously deformed infants. Which US legislation followed, and what did it add?
options: The Sherley Amendment of 1912, prohibiting fraudulent claims
The Orphan Drug Act of 1983, promoting research on drugs for rare diseases
The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, establishing the investigational new drug application process
The Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962, requiring manufacturers to demonstrate both therapeutic efficacy and safety
q_0443.rationale: Table 4.1 pairs the Kefauver-Harris Amendments with the thalidomide tragedy and states they required manufacturers to "demonstrate both therapeutic efficacy and safety" of new drugs.
q_0443.trap: (C) is the mirror error of the previous item. An option crediting Kefauver-Harris with the investigational new drug process has the two acts crossed; that process came from the 1938 act, and efficacy is what 1962 added on top of safety.

q_0444.stem: A drug label carries the statement "Caution—Federal law prohibits dispensing without a prescription." Which act required that legend, and what does the term legend drug mean?
options: The Durham-Humphrey Amendment of 1951, and legend drug means prescription drug
The Durham-Humphrey Amendment of 1951, and legend drug means nonprescription drug
The Federal Food and Drugs Act of 1906, and legend drug means a drug with addicting potential
The Harrison Narcotic Act of 1914, and legend drug means a narcotic
q_0444.rationale: Table 4.1 states that the Durham-Humphrey Amendment "established legend drugs or prescription drugs" and required the quoted legend on the label. The key term gives legend drugs as "another name for prescription drugs," while over-the-counter drugs are the ones available without a prescription.
q_0444.trap: (B) keeps the correct act and flips the definition, which is the error the word itself invites. "Legend" here means the printed caution required on the label, not "legendary" or "listed."

q_0445.stem: A caller identifying himself as a hospitalized patient's grandson telephones the unit and asks for her diagnosis and prognosis. Which understanding guides the nurse's response?
options: The privacy rule applies only to written records, so verbal information may be shared with family
Diagnosis may be released but payment information may not
HIPAA requires health care providers, insurers, public health authorities, employers, and schools to protect individually identifying health information, and severe fines may follow a breach
HIPAA binds only clinicians, so information a school or employer holds may be released freely
q_0445.rationale: The chapter states HIPAA "requires all health care providers, health and life insurance companies, public health authorities, employers, and schools to maintain patient privacy regarding protected health information," which "includes any individually identifying information such as patients' health conditions, account numbers, prescription numbers, medications, and payment information." The key term adds that if confidentiality is breached, "severe fines may be imposed."
q_0445.trap: (D) narrows the covered entities down to clinicians, which is the usual misreading of HIPAA. The chapter's own list names employers and schools right alongside providers, which is why this act reaches so much further than the chart.

q_0446.stem: A patient brings in an herbal product whose label reads "For depression." What does the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act require of that product's manufacturer?
options: To prove both safety and efficacy before marketing, as for any prescription drug
At least to ensure the product's safety, though not necessarily its efficacy, and to make no unsubstantiated claims such as "Known to cure depression"
To prove efficacy only, since supplements are presumed safe
Nothing, because dietary supplements are entirely unregulated
q_0446.rationale: The chapter states the 1994 act requires manufacturers "at least to ensure their safety (although not necessarily their efficacy)" and prohibits "any unsubstantiated claims" in product labeling, and gives this exact worked example: a label "may read 'For depression' but cannot read 'Known to cure depression.'" Chapter 7 develops this framework further.
q_0446.trap: (A) applies the drug standard to a supplement, which is the reflex assumption. The FDA has less regulatory authority over vitamin, herbal, and homeopathic preparations precisely because they are designated dietary supplements rather than drugs.

q_0447.subtopic: who is enrolled in each phase
q_0447.stem: A pharmaceutical company begins the first human testing of a new antihypertensive. Who receives the drug, and what is being determined?
options: Small numbers of volunteers who have hypertension, to determine effectiveness
Large numbers of patients with hypertension, to detect rare adverse effects
The general population after marketing, to compare the drug against an existing agent
Small numbers of healthy subjects, to determine the optimal dosage range and the pharmacokinetics of the drug
q_0447.rationale: Phase I uses "small numbers of healthy subjects rather than those who have the disease" and is designed "to determine the optimal dosage range and the pharmacokinetics of the drug and to ascertain if further testing is needed." Blood tests, urinalyses, vital signs, and specific monitoring tests are performed. All of this follows preclinical in vitro and animal studies, which rule many compounds out before any human is dosed.
q_0447.trap: (A) is the reflex pick, and it is the single most counterintuitive fact in the sequence: the first humans to receive a new drug do not have the disease it treats. Volunteers who have the disease enter at phase II.

q_0448.subtopic: who is enrolled in each phase
q_0448.stem: The same drug moves on to a study enrolling a small number of volunteers who actually have hypertension. What is this phase determining?
options: The optimal dosage range and pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers
The drug's effectiveness and any adverse effects, with therapeutic dosage ranges refined
Infrequent or rare adverse effects in large numbers of patients
Postmarketing comparison against another drug in the same therapeutic category
q_0448.rationale: Phase II uses "small numbers of volunteers who have the disease that the drug is designed to diagnose or treat," to "determine the drug's effectiveness and identify any adverse effects," and "therapeutic dosage ranges are refined during this phase."
q_0448.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. The switch from healthy subjects to subjects who have the disease is the boundary between phases I and II, and the change in purpose follows from it.

q_0449.subtopic: reaching the market and staying watched
q_0449.stem: A drug is being studied in large numbers of patients followed by medical research centers, with objectives of establishing clinical effectiveness, safety, and dosage range. What happens when this phase is complete?
options: The manufacturer submits an investigational new drug application so that human testing may begin
The drug automatically enters a further trial phase before any marketing can occur
The manufacturer submits a new drug application, and the drug goes on the market if the FDA approves it
The drug is marketed immediately with no further FDA review
q_0449.rationale: Phase III uses large numbers of patients and provides information about "infrequent or rare adverse effects," with the three objectives of establishing "clinical effectiveness, safety, and dosage range." After phase III the FDA receives a report and the company submits a new drug application, and the drug is put on the market once that application is approved.
q_0449.trap: (A) swaps the two applications, which is the most common error here because both are applications to the same agency. The investigational new drug application comes first and permits study in humans; the new drug application comes after phase III and permits marketing.

q_0450.subtopic: reaching the market and staying watched
q_0450.stem: Six months after a drug reaches the market, reports of severe adverse effects never seen during the trials begin arriving. Which phase does this belong to, and why did the effects appear only now?
options: Phase III, because rare adverse effects are its stated purpose
Phase II, because adverse effects are identified there
Phase I, because pharmacokinetics were established there
Phase IV, because these are postmarketing studies and severe effects may appear for the first time once a drug is used in the larger general population
q_0450.rationale: Phase IV consists of "postmarketing studies that are voluntarily conducted by pharmaceutical companies to obtain further proof of the therapeutic and adverse effects," with data gathered "for at least 2 years after the drug's release," often comparing the new drug with another in the same therapeutic category. The chapter notes that some drugs pass every trial phase without problems and then produce severe adverse effects in the general population.
q_0450.trap: (A) pulls because phase III is the phase whose stated purpose is infrequent or rare adverse effects. Timing settles it: anything happening after the drug is on sale is by definition after phase III.

q_0451.topic: investigational study design and informed consent
q_0451.stem: In a drug study, the subjects do not know whether they are receiving the investigational drug or the placebo, but the investigator does know. What is this design called, and whose bias does it minimize?
options: A double-blind investigational drug study, minimizing bias on the part of both investigator and subjects
An open-label study, which minimizes no bias at all
A blinded investigational drug study, minimizing bias on the part of research subjects
A postmarketing study, minimizing investigator bias
q_0451.rationale: The key term defines a blinded study as one in which "the subjects are purposely unaware" of whether they receive the drug or a placebo, and states that this "serves to minimize bias on the part of research subjects." The body text confirms that in a blinded study the subject does not know but "the investigator does know."
q_0451.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because both terms contain the word blind. Count who is unaware: one party is blinded, two parties is double-blind.

q_0452.topic: investigational study design and informed consent
q_0452.stem: In a second study, neither the research staff nor the subjects know which subjects receive the real drug. What is this design called, and what does it add?
options: A double-blind investigational drug study, minimizing bias on the part of both the investigator and the subject
A blinded investigational drug study, minimizing bias on the part of the subject only
A placebo-free design, since blinding removes the need for a placebo
A preclinical design, since the researchers are not yet involved
q_0452.rationale: The key term defines a double-blind study as one in which "both the investigator(s) and the subjects" are purposely unaware, minimizing bias "on the part of both." Dosage forms often look identical except for a secret code, which is revealed at the end of the study and can be broken earlier by the principal investigator in a clinical emergency.
q_0452.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item. Both definitions turn on the word bias, which is why the chapter gives bias its own key term, defined as "any systematic error in a measurement process."

q_0453.topic: investigational study design and informed consent
q_0453.stem: A nurse is asked to obtain informed consent for a drug study. Which set of requirements matches the chapter?
options: Explain purpose, procedures, benefits, and risks; the document is written in a language the patient understands and is dated and signed by the patient and at least one witness
Explain purpose and benefits only; the document is signed by the patient alone
Explain risks only; the document is signed by the prescriber and a witness
Explain purpose, procedures, benefits, and risks; the document is signed once therapy has begun
q_0453.rationale: The chapter requires that the "purpose of the study, the procedures to be used, the possible benefits, and the risks involved" be explained, and that the document be "written in a language understood by the patient" and "dated and signed by the patient and at least one witness." Obtaining consent may be carried out by a nurse or other health care professional depending on how the study is designed.
q_0453.trap: (D) keeps all four content elements intact and breaks only the timing, which is the half people stop reading. Consent "must be obtained more than a given number of days or hours before certain procedures are performed and must always be obtained when the patient is fully mentally competent."

q_0454.topic: investigational study design and informed consent
q_0454.stem: A patient enrolled in an investigational drug study tells the nurse she wants to stop participating. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Once therapy has begun she cannot withdraw until the study period ends
Any individual may decline to participate or quit the study at any time, without affecting delivery of any previously agreed-upon health care services
Withdrawing means she forfeits the right to bring any future legal action
Withdrawal requires the prescriber's written approval
q_0454.rationale: Informed consent "is always voluntary," participants must be "informed volunteers and not be coerced to participate in any way," and any individual "can either decline to participate or quit the study at any time without affecting the delivery of any previously agreed-upon health care services."
q_0454.trap: (A) and (C) both contradict the chapter directly, and both appear among the distractors in its own review question on informed consent. Consent is a permission that can be withdrawn, not a waiver of the patient's rights.

q_0455.topic: investigational study design and informed consent
q_0455.stem: A patient with a life-threatening illness asks why some drugs reach patients faster than others. Which explanation matches the chapter?
options: Expedited approval skips the preclinical phase so human testing can start sooner
Expedited approval was created for the COVID-19 pandemic and has no earlier precedent
Expedited approval removes the need for a new drug application entirely

Expedited approval accelerates the usual process for life-threatening diseases; AIDS was the first major public health crisis for which the FDA granted it, allowing use of drugs that showed promise during early phase I and phase II trials
q_0455.rationale: The key term defines expedited drug approval as "acceleration of the usual investigational new drug approval process by the FDA, usually for drugs used to treat life-threatening diseases," and the chapter states that AIDS "was the first major public health crisis for which the FDA began granting expedited drug approval." The rofecoxib recall in 2004 later made the process controversial and reduced the number of drugs approved through it.
q_0455.trap: (B) picks the most recent example the chapter names. COVID-19 vaccines and drugs were approved under Emergency Use Authorization, and even there the chapter states the product "must first be proven safe and effective."

q_0456.stem: A newly hired nurse reads that a drug on the unit carries a black box warning and asks whether the drug has been taken off the market. What is the accurate answer?
options: The drug has been withdrawn and may no longer be dispensed
The warning applies only to investigational drugs still in trials

The drug can still be prescribed; the black box warning is the strictest FDA warning, indicating that serious adverse effects have been reported, so the prescriber must be aware of the risk and the patient must be warned
The drug may now be given only under an approved protocol
q_0456.rationale: A black box warning is "the strictest warning from the FDA," indicating "that serious adverse effects have been reported" with the drug. The chapter states plainly, "The drug can still be prescribed," though the prescriber must be aware of the potential risk and the patient must be warned. The warning text is bordered in solid black, which is where the name comes from.
q_0456.trap: (A) confuses the warning with the withdrawal mechanism. Removal from the market is a recall; a black box warning is a warning, not a withdrawal. (D) borrows the dispensing restriction that belongs to schedule I controlled substances.

q_0457.stem: A drug product is recalled because its use carries a reasonable probability of serious adverse health effects or death. Which class is this, and where does it sit on the scale?
options: Class III, the most serious type of recall
Class II, because the effects may be temporary or medically reversible
Class I, the least serious type of recall
Class I, the most serious type of recall
q_0457.rationale: A class I recall is "the most serious type of recall," in which use "carries a reasonable probability of serious adverse health effects or death." Class II is less severe, with temporary or medically reversible effects and a low probability of lasting major harm, and class III is least severe.
q_0457.trap: (A) inverts the direction of the scale, which is worth guarding against because plenty of clinical severity scales run the other way. Recall classes run from I as the worst down to III, the same direction as the controlled substance schedules.

q_0458.stem: A manufacturer recalls a product whose use is not likely to result in any significant health problems. Which class is this?
options: Class III
Class I
Class II
Class IV
q_0458.rationale: Class III is the least severe recall class, defined as use that "is not likely to result in any significant health problems." The chapter gives three recall classes, not four.
q_0458.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item. (D) invents a fourth class by borrowing the length of the five-schedule controlled substance list; the recall system stops at three.

q_0459.stem: A nurse observes an unexpected adverse event with a recently approved drug. Which program does the chapter name for reporting it, and what kind of program is it?
options: MedWatch, a mandatory federal reporting system carrying penalties for nonreporting
MedWatch, a voluntary program in which professionals are encouraged to report any adverse events seen with newly approved drugs
A required postmarketing trial the nurse must enroll the patient into
The Drug Enforcement Agency, which collects all adverse event reports
q_0459.rationale: MedWatch is described as "a voluntary program in which professionals are encouraged to report any adverse events seen with newly approved drugs."
q_0459.trap: (A) keeps the right program and makes it mandatory, which is how most people assume drug safety reporting must work. The chapter's word is voluntary, the same word it uses for the phase IV postmarketing studies that gather the same kind of information.

q_0460.stem: Two controlled substances both carry high abuse potential and severe physical and psychological dependency potential, yet they sit in different schedules. What separates them?
options: The schedule I drug has a higher abuse potential than the schedule II drug
The schedule I drug produces only psychological dependency
The schedule II drug may be sold over the counter in some states
The schedule I drug has no currently accepted medical use, while the schedule II drug has an accepted medical use
q_0460.rationale: Table 4.2 gives both schedule I and schedule II as high abuse potential with severe physical and psychological dependency; medical use is the only column that differs, listing none for schedule I and accepted for schedule II. The body text states that schedule I drugs have "no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse" while schedule II drugs have "a medical use and a high potential for abuse."
q_0460.trap: (A) assumes every step down the ladder must also lower abuse potential, which is true of every pair except this top one. Read Table 4.2 across the row, not down the column. (C) belongs to schedule V.

q_0461.stem: A nursing student asks how to tell a schedule III drug from a schedule IV drug by its dispensing rules. What should the nurse explain?
options: Schedule III allows five refills and schedule IV allows none
The dispensing rules cannot distinguish them, because both allow a written or oral prescription that expires in 6 months with no more than five refills; only abuse and dependency potential differ
Schedule IV expires in 6 months while schedule III expires in 12 months
Schedule III requires a written prescription only, the same as schedule II
q_0461.rationale: Table 4.3 gives schedule III and schedule IV identical dispensing restrictions: "written or oral prescription that expires in 6 months; no more than five refills in a 6-month period; container must have warning label." Table 4.2 is what separates them, with abuse potential less than schedule II for the one and less than schedule III for the other.
q_0461.trap: (A) manufactures a distinction where the tables give none, which is what a test taker does when a question seems to demand that two adjacent categories differ on the axis being asked about. Here the honest answer is that this axis does not separate them.

q_0462.stem: A prescriber telephones an order for oxycodone to the unit and asks that it be refillable twice. Which response is correct?
options: A schedule II drug may be telephoned in routinely and refilled up to five times in 6 months
A schedule II drug may be refilled but never telephoned in
A schedule II drug requires a written prescription with no refills; telephoning is permitted for major emergencies only, and a written prescription is then required within 72 hours
A schedule II drug may be telephoned in, and the prescription then expires in 6 months
q_0462.rationale: Table 4.3 gives schedule II restrictions as "written prescription only; no prescription refills," with a container warning label, and its footnote states such drugs are "legally permitted to be telephoned in for major emergencies only. If telephoned in, written prescription is required within 72 hours."
q_0462.trap: (A) applies the schedule III and IV rules one rung too high. Five refills in 6 months belongs to the schedules below; no refills at all is the schedule II signature, and this is the order to question.

q_0463.stem: One patient is discharged on a codeine and acetaminophen combination product and another on codeine alone. How are the two scheduled?
options: The combination is schedule II and codeine alone is schedule III
Both are schedule II, because both contain codeine
The combination is schedule III and codeine alone is schedule II
Both are schedule V, because combination opioid products contain limited quantities
q_0463.rationale: Table 4.3 lists codeine among the schedule II examples and "codeine with selected other medications (e.g., acetaminophen)" among the schedule III examples. Chapter 10 states the same from the drug side: the combination "is classified as a Schedule III controlled substance," while codeine not combined with other drugs "is classified as a Schedule II."
q_0463.trap: (A) is the reflex inversion, because adding a second drug feels as though it ought to raise the level of control. The combination product sits at the lower schedule, not the higher one.

q_0464.stem: A patient asks how an antitussive containing a small amount of an opioid can be sold without a prescription in her state. What explains this?
options: Antitussives are never classified as controlled substances
Every schedule V drug is prescription-only nationwide, so the product must be mislabeled
The product was moved to schedule IV, which permits over-the-counter sale
Schedule V drugs may be dispensed by written prescription or over the counter depending on state law, and consist of preparations containing limited quantities of certain opioids
q_0464.rationale: Table 4.3 gives schedule V dispensing as "written prescription or over the counter (varies with state law)," with examples being medications "generally for relief of coughs or diarrhea containing limited quantities of certain opioid controlled substances." The body text adds that schedule V drugs have lower potential for abuse than schedule IV.
q_0464.trap: (B) reflects the widespread assumption that "controlled substance" always means "requires a prescription." The lowest schedule is the exception, and the chapter also notes that a drug such as gabapentin may carry a higher schedule in some states than in others.

q_0465.stem: A nursing student reviews the controlled substance schedules. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: There are five classes of controlled substances, designated from C-I to C-V
Schedule I drugs may be dispensed only with an approved protocol
In 2014 hydrocodone was rescheduled from schedule III to schedule II
Schedule IV examples include phenobarbital, benzodiazepines such as diazepam and lorazepam, and tramadol
Schedule III drugs may be dispensed over the counter depending on state law
q_0465.rationale: The chapter states that the Controlled Substance Act "requires the scheduling of every controlled drug" and that there are "five classes of controlled substances, designated from C-I to C-V." Table 4.3 gives "only with approved protocol" for schedule I and lists phenobarbital, benzodiazepines, and tramadol among the schedule IV examples, and the chapter records that in 2014 hydrocodone "was rescheduled from C-III to C-II," which Chapter 10 confirms.
q_0465.trap: (E) moves the over-the-counter provision up two rungs. That provision belongs to schedule V alone, and only as state law allows. Note also that the 2014 change made hydrocodone stricter even though its schedule number went down, which is the direction most people reverse.

q_0466.stem: A nurse fails to give the care a reasonably prudent nurse would render under similar circumstances, and a patient is harmed. Which term names this, and why?
options: Negligence only, because malpractice applies solely to physicians
Fraud, because a professional standard was breached
Malpractice, because it is a special type of negligence committed by a professional with specialized education and training
Neither, because a licensed nurse is not held to a legal standard of care
q_0466.rationale: Negligence is "the failure to act in a reasonable and prudent manner" or failure of the nurse to give the care that a "reasonably prudent (cautious) nurse would render or use under similar circumstances." Malpractice is "a special type of negligence" or the failure of a professional with specialized education and training to act in a reasonable and prudent way. Every malpractice case is negligence; not every negligence case is malpractice.
q_0466.trap: (A) restricts malpractice to medicine, which is the common lay understanding of the word. The definition turns on specialized education and training, not on which profession holds it.

q_0467.stem: A visitor in the hallway fails to act in a reasonable and prudent manner and a patient is injured. Which term applies?
options: Negligence, but not malpractice
Malpractice, because harm resulted
Malpractice, because it happened inside a health care facility
Neither, because only documented acts create liability
q_0467.rationale: Negligence is the failure to act in a reasonable and prudent manner, and nothing in that definition requires professional status. Malpractice is the narrower subset committed by "a professional and/or individual with specialized education and training."
q_0467.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item: harm alone does not convert a failure into malpractice, the actor's professional standing does. (C) substitutes the setting for the actor, which is the same mistake in different clothing.

q_0468.stem: A nurse fails to notice an infiltrated IV of a caustic drug, and a second nurse catches it before any tissue injury occurs. Which element of malpractice liability is missing?
options: Duty, because the second nurse took over responsibility
Breach of duty, because the error was corrected in time
Causation, because monitoring an IV site is not the nurse's duty
Damage, because no harm resulted
q_0468.rationale: The four elements are duty, breach of duty, causation, and damage, and all must be present. The chapter's own worked example runs duty as accurate assessment and monitoring of the IV site with timely reporting of changes, breach as not noticing that the site is swollen, red, painful, and warm, causation as failing to note extravasation that results in the need for skin grafting, and damage as extensive skin and nerve damage with limited use of the arm.
q_0468.trap: (B) treats an error that was caught as no breach at all. The breach happened; what is absent is the harm at the end of the chain, and without damage the set is incomplete.

q_0469.stem: A nurse charts that a scheduled dose was given, but the dose was never administered. Under the chapter's areas of potential liability, how is this classified?
options: A medication error, because a dose was omitted
Fraud, because documentation was falsified and care that was documented was not provided
Failure to assess, because the patient was not monitored afterward
Failure to ensure safety, because monitoring was inadequate
q_0469.rationale: Box 4.2 lists fraud as its own category, separate from medication errors, and gives as its examples "falsification of documentation on the medication profile or patient's record" and "failure to provide the nursing care that was documented."
q_0469.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because a missed dose is the textbook medication error. The falsified entry is what moves this into a different category with different consequences: an error is a failure of practice, fraud is a falsification of the record.

q_0470.stem: A hospital is preparing for accreditation and the staff nurses ask why this concerns them. Which statements match the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: The Joint Commission, the Healthcare Facilities Accreditation Program, and Det Norske Veritas all accredit health care facilities
The Joint Commission has for years been the number one choice for hospital accreditation, focusing on leadership standards and quality management
Det Norske Veritas emerged in 2008 and is seen as more facility friendly, with a more quality-management approach
Nurses should understand the credentialing process at their place of employment because of their priority of monitoring standard of patient care
These accrediting bodies issue the individual nurse's license and define her scope of practice
q_0470.rationale: The chapter names all three bodies, describes The Joint Commission as the number one choice with a focus on leadership standards and quality management, dates Det Norske Veritas to 2008 and calls it more "facility friendly," and says nurses need to understand both their own licensing and nurse practice acts and the credentialing of their employer because of their priority of monitoring standard of patient care.
q_0470.trap: (E) is the option from the wrong side of the state-versus-facility line, and it is the distinction worth holding: nurse practice acts are state law overseen by state boards of nursing, and they are what define scope of practice, while accreditation applies to the institution. Drug scheduling and approval, by contrast, are federal.

q_0471.topic: nursing ethical principles and placebo use
q_0471.stem: A nurse withholds an intervention that would cause a patient avoidable harm. Which ethical principle is she acting on?
options: Beneficence
Justice
Nonmaleficence
Veracity
q_0471.rationale: Nonmaleficence is "the duty to do no harm to a patient," and the ethical terms box gives its related nursing action as "avoiding doing any deliberate harm while rendering nursing care."
q_0471.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the two words sit one Latin element apart and appear in the same box. Nonmaleficence is the negative duty to refrain from harm; beneficence is the positive duty to actively promote good.

q_0472.topic: nursing ethical principles and placebo use
q_0472.stem: A nurse determines how a patient is best served and actively arranges that care. Which principle is this?
options: Nonmaleficence
Beneficence
Confidentiality
Autonomy
q_0472.rationale: Beneficence is "the ethical principle of doing or actively promoting good," with its related nursing action given as "determining how the patient is best served."
q_0472.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. Doing good and refraining from harm are separate duties, which is why the box lists them as two principles rather than one.

q_0473.topic: nursing ethical principles and placebo use
q_0473.stem: A patient with late-stage cancer says he wants to live to see his granddaughter's graduation but wants no extra treatments after that, and the nurse supports his decision. Which principle is being upheld?
options: Veracity
Beneficence
Maleficence
Autonomy
q_0473.rationale: Autonomy is "self-determination and the ability to act on one's own," and its related nursing actions include "promoting a patient's decision making," "supporting informed consent," and assisting in decisions or making a decision when a patient is posing harm to himself or herself.
q_0473.trap: (C) is not a principle in this chapter at all: the principle is nonmaleficence, and this distractor simply drops the negation. It appears among the options in the chapter's own review question on this scenario, which is why it is worth recognizing as a non-word rather than reasoning about it.

q_0474.topic: nursing ethical principles and placebo use
q_0474.stem: A patient enrolled in a drug study asks the nurse directly whether he is receiving a placebo. Which principle does the chapter attach most specifically to this situation?
options: Justice
Nonmaleficence
Confidentiality
Veracity
q_0474.rationale: Veracity is "the duty to tell the truth," and the box gives its related nursing action as "telling the truth with regard to placebos, investigational new drugs, and informed consent." All three of the chapter's truth-telling situations are gathered under this one principle.
q_0474.trap: (A) and (B) are principles from the same box, which is what makes them plausible, but neither is the one the chapter names by these exact words. Autonomy is also touched by this scenario, yet veracity is the principle the box ties to placebos.

q_0475.topic: nursing ethical principles and placebo use
q_0475.stem: A unit reviews the chapter's ethical terms box. Which pairings of principle and related nursing action are as the chapter gives them? Select all that apply.
options: Justice, with ensuring fairness in distributing resources for patient care and determining when to treat
Confidentiality, with not talking about a patient in public or outside the context of the health care setting
Autonomy, with assisting in decisions or making a decision when a patient is posing harm to himself or herself
Beneficence, with determining how the patient is best served
Veracity, with avoiding doing any deliberate harm while rendering nursing care
q_0475.rationale: The ethical terms box gives each of these four pairings, defining justice as "being fair or equal in one's actions" and confidentiality as "the duty to respect privileged information about a patient."
q_0475.trap: (E) attaches nonmaleficence's related action to veracity. Avoiding deliberate harm belongs to the do-no-harm principle; veracity's action is telling the truth about placebos, investigational new drugs, and informed consent.

q_0476.topic: nursing ethical principles and placebo use
q_0476.stem: A prescriber orders a placebo for a hospitalized patient who is not enrolled in any drug study. What is the nurse's appropriate action?
options: Administer it, since a placebo has no pharmacologic activity and therefore cannot harm the patient
Refuse to discuss the order with the prescriber and document the refusal
Inquire about the order and ask why a placebo is being prescribed, since this is within the legal purview of a professional nurse and the order must never be taken lightly
Administer it and tell the patient it is a strong new medication
q_0476.rationale: The chapter states that if an order is received for a placebo, "it is within the legal purview of a professional nurse to inquire about the order and to ask why a placebo is being prescribed; the order must never be taken lightly." Except in new drug studies, placebo use "is often considered to be unethical and deceitful, possibly creating mistrust" among nurse, prescriber, and patient, and the American Pain Society and the Agency for Health Care Policy and Research recommend avoiding placebos.
q_0476.trap: (A) reasons from the placebo's inertness straight to its harmlessness, which misses the objection entirely: the harm the chapter names is deception and mistrust, not pharmacologic injury. (D) is that deception carried out, and it violates veracity outright.

q_0477.topic: antiviral terminology and viral genome vocabulary
q_0477.stem: A nurse is charting for a patient whose medication list includes acyclovir for recurrent genital herpes and zidovudine for HIV infection. Which single term correctly describes both drugs?
options: Antiretroviral drugs, because both suppress viral replication
Antiviral drugs, the general term for drugs that destroy viruses either directly or indirectly by suppressing their replication
Antibiotics, because both act against an infectious organism
Immunoglobulins, because both attack a foreign antigen
q_0477.rationale: The key-terms box makes the relationship a general-to-specific one: antiviral drugs are "a general term for drugs that destroy viruses, either directly or indirectly by suppressing their replication," while antiretroviral drugs are "a specific term for antiviral drugs that work against retroviruses such as HIV." Every antiretroviral is an antiviral, so only the general term covers both drugs on this list.
q_0477.trap: (A) is the reflex pick the moment HIV appears anywhere in a stem, but acyclovir treats herpesviruses, not retroviruses, so it is not an antiretroviral. The chapter's own structure and its key points split the two halves the same way.

q_0478.topic: antiviral terminology and viral genome vocabulary
q_0478.stem: The same nurse must identify which of those two drugs belongs to the narrower category the chapter reserves for HIV therapy. Which statement is accurate?
options: Only zidovudine is an antiretroviral, because antiretroviral names drugs that work against retroviruses such as HIV
Only acyclovir is an antiretroviral, because herpesviruses replicate by reverse transcription
Both are antiretrovirals, because the two terms are interchangeable
Neither is an antiretroviral, because that term refers only to vaccines
q_0478.rationale: Retroviruses are the family Retroviridae, they carry RNA as their genome, and they replicate using reverse transcriptase; HIV is named as the currently most clinically significant retrovirus. Acyclovir's targets, HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, are herpesviruses and replicate without reverse transcriptase.
q_0478.trap: (C) is the mirror error of the previous item, collapsing the general term into the specific one so that everything antiviral gets called antiretroviral. (B) hands reverse transcription to the herpesviruses, which is the same confusion running the other way.

q_0479.topic: antiviral terminology and viral genome vocabulary
q_0479.stem: A patient's antiretroviral regimen lists tenofovir alafenamide as a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor and zidovudine as a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. What structural difference does that labeling describe?
options: A nucleotide is a nucleoside with an attached phosphate unit
A nucleoside is a nucleotide with an attached phosphate unit
A nucleotide is built from RNA and a nucleoside from DNA
A nucleoside is found only in host cells and a nucleotide only in viruses
q_0479.rationale: The chapter states it twice: "A nucleoside is a single unit consisting of a base and its attached sugar... A nucleotide is a nucleoside plus an attached phosphate." The key-terms box adds that the phosphate unit is what makes up the side chain backbone of a DNA or RNA molecule. The labeling is not cosmetic, since tenofovir alafenamide is the nucleotide agent while zidovudine, lamivudine, abacavir, emtricitabine, stavudine, and didanosine are nucleosides.
q_0479.trap: (B) is the inversion, and it is the common one because the two words differ by three letters and both appear in the same drug class. The cue is that nucleoTide equals phosphaTe.

q_0480.topic: antiviral terminology and viral genome vocabulary
q_0480.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with HIV asks why the virus is called a retrovirus. Which explanation is accurate?
options: It carries both DNA and RNA within the same virion
It carries RNA as its genome and uses reverse transcriptase to build DNA from that RNA, the reverse of the usual direction
It carries DNA as its genome and copies that DNA into RNA inside the nucleus
It replicates outside host cells and then enters them as mature virions
q_0480.rationale: Retroviruses "contain RNA (as opposed to DNA) as their genome and replicate using the enzyme reverse transcriptase," and reverse transcriptase is defined as "an RNA-directed DNA polymerase" that promotes "the synthesis of a DNA molecule from an RNA molecule, which is the reverse of the usual process."
q_0480.trap: (A) is chosen by students who remember that a viral genome may be either nucleic acid and conclude it can be both; the chapter states a virion's genome is DNA or RNA "but not both." (D) contradicts the definition of a virus as the smallest known class of microorganisms, which "can only replicate inside host cells."

q_0481.stem: A patient with laboratory-confirmed influenza B has a new order for amantadine. What should the nurse recognize about this order?
options: Amantadine is only effective against influenza A, so the drug does not match the diagnosis
Amantadine covers influenza A and B, so the order is appropriate
Amantadine is a neuraminidase inhibitor and is preferred for influenza B
Amantadine is appropriate here only if the patient is younger than 12 months
q_0481.rationale: Amantadine is "only effective against influenza A," and Table 40.1 sorts it and rimantadine under influenza A while listing zanamivir and oseltamivir under influenza A and B. A further problem sits behind the spectrum issue: CDC guidelines "do not recommend the use of amantadine or rimantadine to prevent or treat the flu."
q_0481.trap: (D) inverts the age rule, since being younger than 12 months is a printed contraindication for amantadine, not an indication. (C) borrows the neuraminidase inhibitor label that belongs to oseltamivir and zanamivir.

q_0482.stem: The prescriber asks which antiviral would actually cover this patient's influenza B. Which pair of drugs is effective against both influenza A and influenza B?
options: Amantadine and rimantadine
Oseltamivir and zanamivir
Acyclovir and valacyclovir
Entecavir and lamivudine
q_0482.rationale: Table 40.1 gives zanamivir and oseltamivir for influenza A and B. Both are neuraminidase inhibitors, and the chapter explains that this enzyme "enables budding virions to escape from infected cells," so blocking it traps new virions in the cell they were made in.
q_0482.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, since the two adamantanes are the influenza A only pair. (D) names two hepatitis B drugs, and (C) names two herpesvirus drugs, both of which read as plausible only if the drug is not sorted by the virus it treats.

q_0483.stem: A patient whose household member has active influenza asks for something to keep from getting sick. Which neuraminidase inhibitor fits, and why?
options: Zanamivir, because the inhaled route reaches the respiratory tract before infection takes hold
Oseltamivir, because it is oral and is indicated for both prophylaxis and treatment
Either drug, because both are approved for prophylaxis and for treatment
Neither drug, because neuraminidase inhibitors are approved only for hospitalized patients
q_0483.rationale: Oseltamivir is oral and is used for both prophylaxis and treatment, while zanamivir is inhaled by Diskhaler and is indicated for treatment of active illness only. Their adverse effects split the same way: oseltamivir causes nausea and vomiting, zanamivir causes diarrhea, nausea, and sinusitis.
q_0483.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because an inhaled drug sounds preventive at the site of viral entry, and the route is the very thing that makes the two drugs feel interchangeable. The indication, not the route, is the discriminator.

q_0484.topic: herpesvirus antiviral selection and look-alike names
q_0484.subtopic: matching the drug to the herpesvirus
q_0484.stem: A patient who received a kidney transplant 3 months ago develops cytomegalovirus retinitis. Which antiviral does the chapter identify for this infection?
options: Acyclovir
Ganciclovir
Oseltamivir
Ribavirin
q_0484.rationale: Ganciclovir is the nucleoside analogue for CMV, which is HHV-5, and it is also given prophylactically "in high-risk patients, such as those receiving organ transplants." Its ophthalmic form must be surgically inserted.
q_0484.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because acyclovir is the antiviral students know best and the two names differ by four letters, but acyclovir's spectrum is HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, not CMV. Review question 5 works this exact swap on a post-transplant patient.

q_0485.topic: herpesvirus antiviral selection and look-alike names
q_0485.subtopic: matching the drug to the herpesvirus
q_0485.stem: A patient presents with a recurrent episode of genital herpes caused by HSV-2. Which drug does the chapter name as the drug of choice?
options: Ganciclovir, because it covers all of the herpesviruses
Acyclovir, which is the drug of choice for both initial and recurrent episodes
Foscarnet, because it is the only injectable option
Trifluridine, which is used for herpes simplex infections at any site
q_0485.rationale: Acyclovir is a nucleoside analogue for HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, and the chapter calls it "the drug of choice" for both initial and recurrent episodes. Trifluridine's indication in Table 40.1 is herpes simplex keratitis specifically, not herpes simplex at any site.
q_0485.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, generalizing ganciclovir from CMV to the whole herpesvirus family. Note also that the chapter cautions "there can be anatomic overlap between the two types," so an option claiming HSV-1 can never cause genital lesions would be a distractor rather than a fact.

q_0486.topic: herpesvirus antiviral selection and look-alike names
q_0486.stem: A patient with severe disseminated herpes infection needs intravenous antiviral therapy, and a separate order calls for a topical antiviral ointment. Which drug can supply both of these forms?
options: Valacyclovir
Famciclovir
Acyclovir
Entecavir
q_0486.rationale: Acyclovir is the one drug in this group available in oral, topical, and injectable forms; valacyclovir and famciclovir are oral only. Valacyclovir is "a prodrug that is metabolized to acyclovir," dosed "three times daily versus five times daily."
q_0486.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because valacyclovir is the form most outpatients actually take, but it is oral only. The chapter warns twice that "acyclovir may be mistaken for valacyclovir and famciclovir" and to "note the slight inconsistencies in the spelling," so the working cue is that any stem naming an infusion, a finger cot, or an ointment is acyclovir, while the prefix val- signals a prodrug formulated for oral use, as in valacyclovir to acyclovir and valganciclovir to ganciclovir.

q_0487.topic: herpesvirus antiviral selection and look-alike names
q_0487.stem: A prescription written by trade name reads Zostrix for a patient being treated for genital herpes lesions. What should the nurse do?
options: Administer it, because Zostrix is the topical acyclovir product
Clarify the order, because Zostrix is capsaicin for arthritic pain while Zovirax 5% ointment is the topical acyclovir product
Administer it, but only once the lesions have crusted over
Clarify the order, because Zostrix is an oral drug and this patient needs a topical one
q_0487.rationale: The chapter's safety box, written up from a real reported error, contrasts Zostrix, capsaicin "derived from hot chili peppers" and used for arthritic pain, with Zovirax 5% ointment, topical acyclovir used for genital herpes. The fix the box names is using generic names.
q_0487.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the two trade names differ by three letters and both begin with the same syllable, and nothing in the trade name signals which drug is inside. (D) accepts the wrong drug and then argues about its route, which is the error that lets a look-alike order through.

q_0488.topic: herpesvirus antiviral selection and look-alike names
q_0488.stem: A patient telephones on the third day of a painful dermatomal rash diagnosed as herpes zoster and asks whether antiviral therapy is still worth starting. Within what window does the chapter say acyclovir should be started for herpes zoster?
options: Within 2 days of onset, the same window used for the influenza antivirals
Within 72 hours of onset, although the effect on recovery is usually not dramatic
Within 7 days of onset
At any point during the outbreak, because the window applies only to influenza
q_0488.rationale: Acyclovir in herpes zoster is started within 72 hours of onset and "may speed recovery, but this effect is usually not dramatic." The influenza figure is a different number: oseltamivir and zanamivir must be started within 2 days of symptom onset.
q_0488.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the 2-day influenza figure is repeated in both the assessment and the implementation sections and is the number that sticks. The cue is 2 days for influenza, 72 hours for zoster. A third figure, 24 to 48 hours, appears only in patient teaching and is keyed to the patient noticing a recurrence, not to a clinician's clock.

q_0489.topic: hepatitis b and c antiviral therapy
q_0489.subtopic: sorting the drug to the hepatitis type
q_0489.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis B is started on entecavir. Which instruction and expectation match the chapter's description of this drug?
options: Take it with a full meal, and expect a 4-week course
Take it on an empty stomach, and expect a course of at least 12 months
Take it with ribavirin, and expect a 12-week course
Take it on an empty stomach, and expect a single dose
q_0489.rationale: Entecavir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for hepatitis B, given for a minimum of 12 months and on an empty stomach. Its black box warning covers acute exacerbations of hepatitis B, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, and resistance developing in unrecognized HIV infection, which is why HIV status matters before it is started.
q_0489.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the chapter's general rule really is to take oral antivirals with meals; entecavir and indinavir are the two printed empty-stomach exceptions. Ribavirin in (C) belongs to the hepatitis C regimens, not to hepatitis B, whose drugs are entecavir, lamivudine, and tenofovir.

q_0490.topic: hepatitis b and c antiviral therapy
q_0490.subtopic: sorting the drug to the hepatitis type
q_0490.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis C is prescribed sofosbuvir. Which statement about this drug is accurate?
options: It is the first-in-class RNA polymerase inhibitor and is not to be used as monotherapy
It is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor used for hepatitis B
It is given as monotherapy, because it was the first regimen that does not require interferon
It is a neuraminidase inhibitor active against RNA viruses generally
q_0490.rationale: Sofosbuvir is "the first-in-class RNA polymerase inhibitor" for chronic hepatitis C and the first treatment "that can be given without interferon," but it is used with ribavirin and is "not to be used as monotherapy." Harvoni, sofosbuvir with ledipasvir, was the separate milestone: "the first treatment for hepatitis C that does not require the combined use of ribavirin," one pill once a day.
q_0490.trap: (C) is the reflex pick because "without interferon" and "as monotherapy" sound like the same claim, and they are two different claims about two different drugs. (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, sorting a hepatitis C drug into the hepatitis B group; the cue is that hepatitis B gets entecavir, lamivudine, and tenofovir while hepatitis C gets the -buvir, -asvir, and -previr combinations headed by sofosbuvir.

q_0491.topic: hepatitis b and c antiviral therapy
q_0491.stem: An infant is hospitalized with severe respiratory syncytial virus infection and ribavirin is ordered. Which route matches this indication, and what does that route change for staff?
options: Oral, and no special staff precaution applies
Inhaled aerosol, and pregnant health care providers must stay out of the room during administration
Intravenous, and the drug must be infused over 1 hour
Inhaled aerosol, and staff need only wear gloves
q_0491.rationale: Inhaled ribavirin by small-particle aerosol generator is for hospitalized infants with severe RSV, while the oral form is used for hepatitis C, so the route names both the disease and the population. Ribavirin carries a black box warning for significant teratogenic and embryocidal effects, and the chapter states that "pregnant health care providers, or those wishing to become pregnant, must stay out of the patient rooms when the aerosol form is being administered."
q_0491.trap: (D) is the reflex pick because personal protective equipment is the usual answer to an exposure hazard; here the rule removes the at-risk staff member from the room instead. The same exposure logic extends to the patient's household, since ribavirin is contraindicated in pregnant women and their male sexual partners, may be present in the body for up to 6 months after exposure, and requires at least two reliable forms of contraception during treatment and for 6 months after.

q_0492.subtopic: the three viral enzymes and the class suffixes
q_0492.stem: A patient's regimen includes raltegravir. Which viral enzyme does this drug inhibit, and what does that enzyme normally do?
options: Protease, which chemically separates new viral RNA from viral protein molecules
Integrase, which splices the newly made viral DNA into the host cell DNA to form a provirus
Reverse transcriptase, which builds DNA from the viral RNA genome
Neuraminidase, which lets budding virions escape the infected cell
q_0492.rationale: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors work by "inhibiting the catalytic activity of the enzyme integrase," and integrase "promotes the integration of this viral DNA into the host cell DNA. This hybrid DNA complex is known as a provirus." The chapter says the naming is deliberate: "the name of each class... provides a reminder of its role," and the suffix -tegravir marks this class, as in raltegravir, dolutegravir, and cabotegravir.
q_0492.trap: (C) is the reflex pick because reverse transcriptase is the HIV enzyme students meet first and it acts immediately before integrase in the replication sequence, so the wrong step feels like the right one. (D) names an influenza enzyme rather than an HIV one.

q_0493.subtopic: the three viral enzymes and the class suffixes
q_0493.stem: A different patient is taking indinavir. Which enzyme does this drug inhibit?
options: Integrase, and the suffix -navir marks that class
Protease, which chemically separates the new viral RNA from viral protein molecules
Reverse transcriptase, an RNA-directed DNA polymerase
Protease, which splices the viral DNA into the host chromosome
q_0493.rationale: Protease inhibitors work by "inhibiting the protease retroviral enzyme," and protease "serves to chemically separate the new viral RNA from viral protein molecules"; the key-terms box adds that a protease cleaves the peptide bonds linking amino acids. The suffix -navir marks this class, as -tegravir marks the integrase inhibitors.
q_0493.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, attaching the -navir suffix to the integrase class. (D) is the half-right pick that catches more students: it names the correct class but gives integrase's job, so the enzyme name alone is not enough to answer on.

q_0494.subtopic: reverse transcriptase inhibitors and the entry blockers
q_0494.stem: A regimen contains both zidovudine and nevirapine, and the patient asks why two drugs that hit the same enzyme are both needed. What distinguishes an NRTI from an NNRTI?
options: NRTIs block reverse transcriptase and NNRTIs block integrase
Both block reverse transcriptase; the NRTIs are nucleoside or nucleotide analogues and the NNRTIs are not
Both block protease; the NRTIs are analogues and the NNRTIs are not
NRTIs are used only in pregnancy and NNRTIs only in treatment-experienced patients
q_0494.rationale: Both classes block reverse transcriptase, so membership is the reliable discriminator: zidovudine, abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, and the tenofovirs are the NRTIs, while nevirapine, delavirdine, doravirine, efavirenz, etravirine, and rilpivirine are the NNRTIs. The chapter also notes a clinical use for the distinction, that switching a patient from a protease inhibitor to an NNRTI may help reduce lipodystrophy.
q_0494.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the extra N looks as though it must signal a different target; it signals a different chemical structure instead, since the two classes are one letter apart, hit the same enzyme, and appear in the same HAART recipes.

q_0495.subtopic: reverse transcriptase inhibitors and the entry blockers
q_0495.stem: A treatment-experienced patient with HIV is being taught to give an antiretroviral by subcutaneous injection. Which drug and class is this?
options: Enfuvirtide, the only fusion inhibitor and the only injected antiretroviral named in this chapter
Maraviroc, the only entry inhibitor, given subcutaneously
Raltegravir, an integrase inhibitor available only by injection
Tenofovir, a nucleotide analogue given subcutaneously
q_0495.rationale: Enfuvirtide works by "inhibiting viral fusion" and is the only drug in its class as well as the only subcutaneously injected antiretroviral the chapter names. Fusion is defined as "the process by which viruses attach themselves to, or fuse with, the cell membranes of host cells."
q_0495.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because enfuvirtide and maraviroc are twinned in every other respect: both block HIV before it gets inside, both are the sole member of their class, and both are indicated for treatment-experienced patients. Maraviroc is oral, so route is what separates them.

q_0496.subtopic: reverse transcriptase inhibitors and the entry blockers
q_0496.stem: A patient is starting maraviroc and the pharmacy sends an FDA-approved medication guide along with it. Which description of this drug is accurate?
options: It is a fusion inhibitor that binds the viral envelope before attachment
It is an entry inhibitor and CCR5 antagonist that binds the type 5 chemokine coreceptors on the CD4 cells, and it carries a risk of hepatotoxicity with allergic-type features
It is an integrase inhibitor, and it does not interact with CYP3A4 inducers or inhibitors
It is a protease inhibitor associated with nephrolithiasis
q_0496.rationale: Maraviroc works by "selectively and reversibly binding to the type 5 chemokine coreceptors located on the CD4 cells," is the only drug in its class, requires an FDA-approved medication guide before dispensing, and carries "hepatotoxicity with allergic-type features."
q_0496.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, since fusion inhibition is enfuvirtide's mechanism and maraviroc binds the host cell's coreceptor rather than the virus. (C) states raltegravir's CYP3A4 exemption and (D) states indinavir's signature toxicity, both real facts moved onto the wrong drug.

q_0497.stem: A patient with HIV has a CD4 count that has fallen to 180 cells/mm3. What does this number most directly signal?
options: The viral load is now undetectable
This is the level at which prophylaxis for opportunistic infections is most frequently given
The patient has reached the primary goal of antiretroviral therapy
The patient no longer requires antiretroviral therapy
q_0497.rationale: A CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 is the point at which prophylaxis for opportunistic infections "is most frequently given." Opportunistic infections are defined by the host rather than the organism: infections caused by "any type of microorganism that occur in an immunocompromised host but normally would not occur in an immunocompetent host."
q_0497.trap: (C) is the reflex pick because CD4 count and viral load are both numbers a patient tracks and the two merge in memory. The cue is that CD4 200 is a floor you fall below and act on, while viral load below 50 copies/mL is a target you drive down to.

q_0498.stem: The same patient's viral load report reads fewer than 50 copies/mL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: It represents an undetectable viral load and a primary goal of antiretroviral therapy
It is the threshold for beginning prophylaxis against opportunistic infections
It is evidence of drug resistance
It means the virus has been eliminated from the body
q_0498.rationale: A viral load below 50 copies/mL is "an undetectable" viral load and "a primary goal of antiretroviral therapy." Evidence of drug resistance is a different pattern entirely, a falling CD4 count and a rising viral load moving in opposite directions at the same time.
q_0498.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, swapping the two numbers so that the therapy target becomes the prophylaxis trigger. (D) is the eradication distractor the chapter plants throughout, since these drugs suppress but do not cure the infection and undetectable is not the same as eliminated.

q_0499.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a device used on a patient with HIV. Which regimen does the chapter give for occupational exposure prophylaxis?
options: Emtricitabine and tenofovir alone, taken daily
Raltegravir plus emtricitabine and tenofovir, started after the exposure
Acyclovir, started within 72 hours
Didanosine alone
q_0499.rationale: Table 40.5 gives raltegravir plus Truvada, which is emtricitabine and tenofovir, following exposure to "blood; fluid containing visible blood or other potentially infectious fluid or tissue." The transmission risk from a percutaneous injury is 0.3%.
q_0499.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because Truvada appears in both prophylaxis regimens, which is precisely what makes them swappable; Truvada alone and daily is the preexposure regimen, not the postexposure one. (C) imports a herpes zoster drug and its window into an HIV exposure.

q_0500.stem: The HIV-negative partner of a patient with HIV asks about a daily pill that would keep them from becoming infected. What should the nurse describe?
options: Raltegravir plus Truvada, taken daily for life
Preexposure prophylaxis with tenofovir and emtricitabine, up to 90% effective if it is used as prescribed
An HIV vaccine, now available to high-risk partners
Zidovudine monotherapy, begun after any exposure
q_0500.rationale: PrEP is tenofovir and emtricitabine taken daily before exposure by people at "very high risk," and it is "up to 90%" effective "if it is used as prescribed."
q_0500.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, applying the postexposure regimen to a preexposure situation because Truvada sits inside both. (C) is wrong for a mechanistic reason worth holding onto: reverse transcriptase "has a high rate of errors," which allows frequent genetic mutations and hampers the development of an effective vaccine.

q_0501.stem: A patient asks why HIV is treated with a combination of at least three drugs rather than with one. Which statements support the use of combination therapy? Select all that apply.
options: The combination is more effective against resistant strains, because drugs that work by different mechanisms reduce the likelihood of viral resistance
The combination reduces viral load, which is a primary goal of therapy
The combination carries fewer toxicities than single-drug therapy
The combination reduces T-cell counts
The combination increases the incidence of opportunistic infections
q_0501.rationale: HAART uses "combinations of antiretroviral drugs" that work by different mechanisms, "reducing the likelihood of viral resistance," and driving the viral load below 50 copies/mL is a primary goal of therapy. Therapy is "normally begun immediately on confirmation of HIV infection" and usually uses "at least three medications."
q_0501.trap: (C), (D), and (E) are each a true statement with its direction reversed, so check direction before content. Antiretrovirals "carry significant toxicities," treatment "significantly increases T-cell counts," and treatment produces "a significant reduction in mortality and incidence of opportunistic infections."

q_0502.subtopic: matching toxicity to the organ already compromised
q_0502.stem: A heart transplant recipient taking cyclosporine develops a CMV infection. Why does the chapter prefer ganciclovir over foscarnet for this patient?
options: Cyclosporine is nephrotoxic, and the dose-limiting toxicity of foscarnet and cidofovir is renal toxicity
Cyclosporine suppresses the bone marrow, and ganciclovir spares the marrow
Foscarnet has no activity against CMV
Ganciclovir is the only one of the two available in an oral form
q_0502.rationale: The chapter reasons it out as a decision: cyclosporine "is nephrotoxic. Therefore using foscarnet in this patient may be more dangerous than using ganciclovir." Ganciclovir's dose-limiting toxicity is bone marrow suppression, while "that of foscarnet and cidofovir is renal toxicity."
q_0502.trap: (B) inverts the toxicity assignment, since marrow suppression is ganciclovir's own dose-limiting problem and cannot be the reason to choose it. The cue that survives the exam is to match the drug to the organ the patient has not already compromised.

q_0503.subtopic: matching toxicity to the organ already compromised
q_0503.stem: A patient immunocompromised after a bone marrow transplant develops a CMV infection. Which drug does the chapter suggest may be the better choice here, and why?
options: Ganciclovir, because its dose-limiting toxicity is renal
Foscarnet, because ganciclovir's dose-limiting toxicity is bone marrow suppression
Acyclovir, because it spares both the marrow and the kidney
Zidovudine, because it treats CMV in immunocompromised hosts
q_0503.rationale: The chapter states that "a patient... immunocompromised because of a bone marrow transplant might be better treated using foscarnet," because ganciclovir's dose-limiting toxicity is bone marrow suppression and this patient's marrow is already the compromised organ.
q_0503.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, swapping the two organ toxicities so the same drug is chosen for the opposite reason. (D) is wrong twice over: zidovudine is an HIV drug, and its major dose-limiting adverse effect is also bone marrow suppression, which is the reason a patient is often switched off it.

q_0504.subtopic: matching toxicity to the organ already compromised
q_0504.stem: A patient with HIV is starting zidovudine. Which of the following are adverse effects of the drug itself? Select all that apply.
options: Nausea
Headache
Bone marrow suppression
Retinitis
Kaposi's sarcoma
q_0504.rationale: Table 40.2 lists nausea, headaches, and bone marrow suppression for zidovudine, and the chapter singles out bone marrow suppression as "the major dose-limiting adverse effect... often the reason a patient... must be switched to another anti-HIV drug."
q_0504.trap: (D) and (E) are manifestations of HIV disease rather than adverse effects of any drug, and that separation is the axis this item sorts on. Retinitis belongs to CMV disease, which is HHV-5, and Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV-8, an oncogenic herpesvirus treated with antineoplastics, radiation, and surgery rather than with an antiviral.

q_0505.subtopic: what to teach and when to escalate
q_0505.stem: A patient starting acyclovir for recurrent genital herpes says, "So this will get rid of the virus for good." Which response is accurate?
options: "Yes, a full course will eradicate the virus."
"No. These drugs suppress the infection but do not cure it. What you should see is that lesions crust over and recurrences become less frequent."
"Yes, as long as your partner is treated at the same time."
"No, but taking it every day will keep you from passing the virus to a partner."
q_0505.rationale: The patient teaching section states that these drugs "suppress but do not cure the viral infection," and what the patient can realistically expect is that "herpetic lesions will crust over, and the frequency of recurrence will decrease."
q_0505.trap: (A) is the eradication distractor the chapter plants in more than one review question, once worded as "these drugs will eventually eliminate the virus from my body," and it pulls because a completed antibiotic course really does clear a bacterial infection. (D) sounds responsible but credits the drug with preventing transmission, which abstinence and condoms do.

q_0506.subtopic: what to teach and when to escalate
q_0506.stem: A patient taking nevirapine calls to report a rash that now includes blistering, oral lesions, fever, and myalgias. What is the priority nursing response?
options: Reassure the patient that rash is a listed adverse effect of nevirapine and continue the drug
Tell the patient to contact the prescriber immediately or seek prompt emergency medical attention
Advise an antihistamine and reassess at the next scheduled visit
Hold the next dose and call back in 24 to 48 hours
q_0506.rationale: Rash is a listed adverse effect of nevirapine along with fever, nausea, headache, and abnormal liver function test results, but the chapter directs that blistering, fever, malaise, myalgias, oral lesions, swelling or edema, or conjunctivitis calls for contacting the prescriber immediately or seeking prompt emergency medical attention.
q_0506.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because rash genuinely is on nevirapine's adverse effect list, so the drug name appears to settle the question; it is the accompanying findings that set the priority. The cue is that an isolated rash is monitored, while a rash plus mucous membrane or systemic signs is an emergency. (D) borrows the 24-to-48-hour figure from the teaching about recurrent herpes episodes, where it has nothing to do with an adverse reaction.

q_0507.stem: A microbiology report on a wound describes the organism as a single-celled fungus that reproduces by budding, with a daughter cell pouching out of and breaking off from a mother cell. Which term names this organism?
options: A yeast
A mold
A dermatophyte
A mycelium
q_0507.rationale: Yeasts are single-celled fungi that reproduce by budding, a process in which "a daughter cell forms by pouching out of and breaking off from a mother cell." Fungi as a group are a very large, diverse group of eukaryotic microorganisms consisting of yeasts and molds.
q_0507.trap: (B) pulls because the two words are learned as a pair and both name fungi. Molds are multicellular, built of long branching filaments called hyphae that entwine into a mycelium — the structural opposite of a single cell that buds.

q_0508.stem: A second report describes a fungus made of long, branching filaments that entwine to form a complex branched structure. What is that structure called, and what type of fungus is this?
options: A mycelium, and the fungus is a mold
A mycelium, and the fungus is a yeast
A hypha, and the fungus is a yeast
A sterol, and the fungus is a mold
q_0508.rationale: Molds are multicellular fungi characterized by long, branching filaments called hyphae, which entwine to form a complex branched structure known as a mycelium. The key points restate the yeast and mold contrast verbatim and add that yeasts may be harmful, causing infections, or helpful, aiding in baking or brewing beer.
q_0508.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, keeping the right structure but attaching it to the single-celled fungus.
