q_0587.rationale: The contraindication is printed inside the black box itself: NSAIDs are contraindicated for the treatment of perioperative pain in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft surgery.
q_0587.trap: (B) treats a flat contraindication as a caution to be managed, which is the reflex whenever a warning appears in the same box as a graded risk. This line is not graded; it is a contraindication.

q_0588.stem: A patient on aspirin 81 mg daily for cardioprotection begins taking ibuprofen several times a day for arthritis. What is the concern?
options: All NSAIDs except aspirin carry a black box warning for cardiovascular thrombotic events, and NSAIDs may counteract the cardioprotective effects of aspirin
Ibuprofen and aspirin together produce excessive antiplatelet effect and a high bleeding risk from the aspirin
Ibuprofen will increase aspirin's cardioprotective effect, so the aspirin dose must be reduced
There is no concern, since both drugs are NSAIDs and their effects are the same
q_0588.rationale: All NSAIDs except aspirin share a black box warning regarding increased risk for adverse cardiovascular thrombotic events, including fatal MI and stroke, and NSAIDs may counteract the cardioprotective effects of aspirin. Aspirin is the NSAID that protects the heart; the rest carry a warning for threatening it.
q_0588.trap: (D) is chosen by anyone who reasons from class membership alone, and it is the answer most students give before they meet the aspirin exemption. Same class, opposite cardiovascular labeling.

q_0589.stem: Which statements appear in the FDA-required gastrointestinal warning on all NSAIDs? (Select all that apply.)
options: NSAIDs increase the risk for serious gastrointestinal events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines
These events can be fatal
These events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms
Older adult patients are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events
Warning symptoms such as dyspepsia reliably precede serious events
q_0589.rationale: Box 44.3 states that NSAIDs cause an increased risk for serious gastrointestinal adverse events, including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal, that these events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms, and that older adult patients are at greater risk.
q_0589.trap: (E) directly contradicts the box's own wording and is the option that feels clinically sensible, since dyspepsia and heartburn genuinely are common on NSAIDs. Common early symptoms do not mean the serious events announce themselves.

q_0590.stem: A patient has taken high-dose aspirin daily for months for rheumatoid arthritis and now has symptoms of salicylate toxicity. Which term names this, and what causes it?
options: Salicylism, which results from short-term administration of high dosages or prolonged therapy with high or even low dosages
Salicylism, which results only from a single ingestion of more than 150 mg/kg
Acute salicylate intoxication, since any toxicity from aspirin is acute by definition
Salicylism, which occurs only when the patient has renal impairment
q_0590.rationale: Chronic salicylate intoxication is also known as salicylism and results from either short-term administration of high dosages or prolonged therapy with high or even low dosages.
q_0590.trap: (B) imports the acute overdose grading into the chronic definition. The mg/kg thresholds describe a single toxic dose, and salicylism can develop on doses that were never single or large.

q_0591.stem: An adult taking aspirin long term for arthritis reports ringing in the ears and difficulty hearing conversation. Which interpretation is correct?
options: These are the most common manifestations of chronic salicylate intoxication in adults
These findings occur only in acute overdose and rule out chronic toxicity
These findings are unrelated to salicylates and suggest a middle ear infection
These are expected effects of therapeutic aspirin and need no action
q_0591.rationale: In adults the most common manifestations of chronic salicylate intoxication are tinnitus and hearing loss. Tinnitus, hearing loss, increased heart rate, and dizziness are the salicylate toxicity signs patients are taught to report.
q_0591.trap: (D) treats a toxicity marker as a nuisance effect, which is easy to do because tinnitus also appears in Table 44.2 as a general NSAID adverse effect. On aspirin specifically, tinnitus points at salicylism.

q_0592.stem: A 7-year-old on long-term salicylate therapy is brought in drowsy, dizzy, breathing rapidly, and behaving unlike herself, with no complaint of ringing in the ears. Which interpretation is correct?
options: This is the pediatric presentation of chronic salicylate intoxication, which features hyperventilation and CNS effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, and behavioral changes
Chronic salicylate toxicity is ruled out, because tinnitus is required for the diagnosis
This presentation indicates acute overdose rather than chronic toxicity
These findings reflect the respiratory acidosis typical of salicylate toxicity
q_0592.rationale: In children the most common manifestations are hyperventilation and central nervous system effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, and behavioral changes. Metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis often occur to varying degrees in chronic salicylate intoxication, and hypoglycemia may also arise and can be life threatening.
q_0592.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item. Adults ring, children breathe and change behavior, so requiring the adult finding in a child throws the diagnosis away.

q_0593.stem: Which findings are consistent with chronic salicylate intoxication? (Select all that apply.)
options: Tinnitus
Headache
Constipation
Nausea
Bradycardia
q_0593.rationale: Table 44.3 lists tinnitus, hearing loss, dimness of vision, headache, dizziness, mental confusion, lassitude, and drowsiness under the central nervous system; nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea under gastrointestinal; increased heart rate under cardiovascular; and sweating, thirst, hyperventilation, hypoglycemia, or hyperglycemia under metabolic.
q_0593.trap: (E) is a direction reversal of a real table entry, since the cardiovascular row reads increased heart rate. (C) is the same trick on the gastrointestinal row, which reads diarrhea. Both distractors are the opposite of something genuinely listed, which is why they read as familiar.

q_0594.stem: A teenager is brought in 7 hours after swallowing an unknown quantity of aspirin, and a serum salicylate level has been drawn. How will the Done nomogram be used?
options: It plots the serum salicylate level against time since ingestion to estimate the severity of this acute intoxication, and a level drawn 6 hours or longer after ingestion is usable
It estimates the severity of both acute and chronic salicylate intoxication
It should not be used, since a level drawn after 6 hours is too late to interpret
It is unnecessary here, because an estimated dose below 150 mg/kg means toxicity is not possible
q_0594.rationale: A serum salicylate concentration measured 6 hours or longer after ingestion may be used with the Done nomogram, a graphic plot of serum salicylate level as a function of time since ingestion, first published in a 1960 issue of Pediatrics. The nomogram is intended for estimating only the severity of acute intoxications and not the severity of chronic salicylate intoxication.
q_0594.trap: (D) treats the mg/kg severity table as absolute when the text immediately qualifies it: doses lower than 150 mg/kg have resulted in fatal toxicity. (B) extends the nomogram to chronic cases, which its own definition excludes.

q_0595.stem: Two patients present with large single-drug ingestions, one of aspirin and one of naproxen. Which statement about their management is accurate?
options: Hemodialysis is written into the severe-treatment protocol for salicylates but appears to be of no value for other NSAIDs because of their high protein binding
Hemodialysis clears both drugs equally well, since both are salicylate derivatives
Hemodialysis is useless for salicylates and is the treatment of choice for other NSAIDs
Neither ingestion is treated with hemodialysis; activated charcoal is the only option for both
q_0595.rationale: For severe acute salicylate intoxication, treatment includes discontinuation, intensive symptomatic and supportive therapy, and dialysis for high salicylate levels, unresponsive acidosis with pH below 7.1, impaired renal function or renal failure, pulmonary edema, persistent CNS symptoms, or progressive deterioration. Unlike in the case of salicylates, hemodialysis appears to be of no value in enhancing the elimination of NSAIDs because of their high protein binding, and nonsalicylate NSAID overdose is treated with activated charcoal plus supportive and symptomatic care.
q_0595.trap: (C) is the exact inversion, and it is the one to guard against, because the same overdose question with a different drug has a different answer. High protein binding is what keeps the nonsalicylate NSAIDs out of the dialysate.

q_0596.stem: Which finding in a patient's history is a contraindication to NSAID therapy?
options: Peptic ulcer disease
Osteoarthritis of the knee
A history of primary dysmenorrhea
A prior episode of gouty arthritis
q_0596.rationale: Contraindications include known drug allergy and conditions that place the patient at risk for bleeding, including vitamin K deficiency and peptic ulcer disease. The key points add gastrointestinal tract lesions, peptic ulcers, and bleeding disorders.
q_0596.trap: (D) is the option most likely to be read as a contraindication because gout has its own drug class later in the chapter. Acute gout and acute gouty arthritis are the first two FDA-approved indications in Box 44.2, and the NSAIDs are first-line therapy for most patients with gout.

q_0597.stem: A patient in her third trimester of pregnancy asks whether she may keep taking the ibuprofen she used earlier in the pregnancy. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: NSAIDs are pregnancy category D and not recommended in the third trimester, because of excessive maternal bleeding, decreased amniotic fluid, and neonatal toxicity
NSAIDs are safest in the third trimester and are restricted only in the first
NSAIDs are unrestricted throughout pregnancy but not during breastfeeding
NSAIDs are contraindicated in all trimesters and in all patients of childbearing age
q_0597.rationale: NSAIDs are generally categorized as pregnancy category C drugs for use during the first two trimesters but as pregnancy category D, not recommended, for use during the third trimester, because NSAID use has been associated with excessive maternal bleeding, decreased amniotic fluid, and neonatal toxicity during the perinatal period. They are also not recommended for nursing mothers, since they are known to be excreted into human milk.
q_0597.trap: (B) reverses the two categories, and the split is easy to reverse because the chapter prints it as a single hybrid label whose footnote reads first trimester for one letter and third trimester for the other.

q_0598.stem: A patient taking ibuprofen for arthritis is scheduled for a diagnostic laparoscopy in 2 weeks and says it is only a minor procedure. What should the nurse advise?
options: Stop the NSAID at least 1 week before surgery, because of the potential to increase bleeding
Continue the NSAID, since only major surgery requires stopping it
Switch to aspirin for the 2 weeks, since aspirin is gentler on the platelets
Stop the NSAID the morning of the procedure
q_0598.rationale: Because of the potential of NSAIDs to increase bleeding, patients undergoing elective surgery need to stop taking NSAIDs at least 1 week before surgery.
q_0598.trap: (C) is worse than doing nothing, and it is chosen because aspirin feels like the milder over-the-counter option. Aspirin's COX-1 inhibition inside the platelet is irreversible, so switching to it makes the bleeding risk larger, not smaller. The "only a minor procedure" framing in the stem is the bait.

q_0599.stem: A patient taking aspirin 325 mg daily adds over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain, reasoning that two mild drugs are safer than one strong one. What is the problem?
options: The combination produces increased gastrointestinal toxicity with no therapeutic advantage
The combination produces a therapeutic advantage but requires monitoring of liver enzymes
Ibuprofen blocks aspirin's absorption entirely, so the aspirin is simply wasted
The combination is safe as long as the doses are taken 4 hours apart
q_0599.rationale: Table 44.5 lists aspirin and other salicylates taken with other NSAIDs as producing reduction of NSAID absorption and additive gastrointestinal toxicities, with the result stated as increased gastrointestinal toxicity with no therapeutic advantage. The combination also undercuts aspirin's cardioprotection.
q_0599.trap: (C) takes the "reduction of NSAID absorption" half of the mechanism and turns it into a complete block, which makes the combination sound merely pointless rather than harmful. The table names doubled risk alongside the absent benefit.

q_0600.stem: A patient whose hypertension has been well controlled on a thiazide diuretic and an ACE inhibitor begins daily naproxen, and the blood pressure rises over the next 2 weeks. What is the most likely explanation?
options: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which reduces the hypotensive and diuretic effects of these drugs
The antihypertensive regimen has stopped working and needs to be replaced
Naproxen has caused fluid retention through direct renal tubular damage
The rise is unrelated to the naproxen, since NSAIDs lower blood pressure
q_0600.rationale: Table 44.5 lists diuretics and ACE inhibitors with NSAIDs as producing inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis with the result of reduced hypotensive and diuretic effects.
q_0600.trap: (B) reads the situation as treatment failure and would lead to changing the wrong drug. This is a drug-interaction item, and the second layer is that hypertension also appears in Table 44.1 as a comorbidity with its own suggested NSAIDs, which are sulindac, nonacetylated salicylate, ibuprofen, and etodolac.

q_0601.stem: Which combinations with an NSAID increase the patient's bleeding risk? (Select all that apply.)
options: Alcohol
Warfarin
Feverfew, garlic, ginger, and ginkgo
Bisphosphonates
Misoprostol
q_0601.rationale: Table 44.5 lists alcohol as additive for increased gastrointestinal bleeding, anticoagulants as producing increased bleeding tendencies through platelet inhibition and hypoprothrombinemia, the herbals feverfew, garlic, ginger, and ginkgo as interfering with platelet function for increased bleeding risk, and bisphosphonates as additive gastrointestinal toxicities with increased gastrointestinal bleeding risk.
q_0601.trap: (E) is the drug given to prevent the bleed rather than one that causes it, and it draws students who assume every drug in a long interaction list belongs on the same side of the ledger. Note that the herbal row exists at all, which is why the medication history must include herbals and supplements.

q_0602.stem: A patient is discharged on an oral NSAID for chronic arthritis. Which instruction is correct?
options: Take the drug with food, milk, or antacids to minimize gastrointestinal upset
Take the drug on an empty stomach to speed absorption
Take the drug at bedtime with nothing by mouth afterward
Take the drug with alcohol only if the dose is small
q_0602.rationale: Most oral NSAIDs are better tolerated if taken with food to minimize gastrointestinal upset, and the teaching instruction is to take NSAIDs with food, milk, or antacids. The Clinical Pearl pairs this with hydration: NSAIDs can cause GI bleed and renal failure, so take with food and stay well hydrated.
q_0602.trap: (D) reads alcohol as dose-dependent rather than as an interaction. Alcohol is listed in Table 44.5 as additive with NSAIDs for increased gastrointestinal bleeding.

q_0603.stem: A patient with difficulty swallowing asks whether her enteric-coated aspirin and her sustained-release NSAID can be crushed and mixed into applesauce. Which response is correct?
options: These forms are not to be crushed or chewed, and the prescriber should be asked for an alternative dosage form
They may be crushed as long as they are taken with food
Only the enteric-coated form may be crushed, since the coating is for taste
They may be chewed but not crushed
q_0603.rationale: These drugs, if in sustained-release or enteric-coated dosage forms, are not to be crushed or chewed. Enteric-coated aspirin is designed to protect the stomach mucosa by dissolving in the duodenum, and sustained-release formulations exist to allow once- or twice-daily dosing, which is known to improve adherence.
q_0603.trap: (C) misreads the purpose of the enteric coating as cosmetic. The coating is what keeps the aspirin out of the stomach, so destroying it removes the only gastric protection that dosage form provides.

q_0604.stem: Which findings should a patient on long-term NSAID therapy be taught to report? (Select all that apply.)
options: Ringing in the ears
Black or tarry stools
Bleeding around the gums
Petechiae or easy bruising
Relief of joint stiffness within the first week
q_0604.rationale: The teaching list names ringing in the ears, persistent gastrointestinal problems, black or tarry stools, bleeding around the gums, petechiae, ecchymosis, and purpura, along with unusual bleeding and blood in the stool or vomitus.
q_0604.trap: (E) is the therapeutic response rather than an adverse one: the expected outcome is a decrease in acute pain and a decrease in swelling, pain, stiffness, and tenderness of a joint or muscle area. It gets selected because it appears in the same teaching section as the warnings.

q_0605.stem: A patient will begin long-term NSAID therapy for rheumatoid arthritis. Which baseline laboratory work does the chapter indicate?
options: RBC count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, WBC count, platelet count, BUN, and liver enzymes such as ALP, AST, and LDH
No laboratory work, since NSAIDs are available over the counter
Serum uric acid and a Done nomogram plot
Coagulation studies only, since bleeding is the sole concern
q_0605.rationale: If long-term use is indicated, the chapter lists RBC count, hemoglobin level, hematocrit, WBC count, platelet count, BUN level, and liver enzyme levels such as ALP, AST, and LDH.
q_0605.trap: (B) states the chapter's own exception and applies it to the wrong patient. Laboratory studies are usually not indicated when NSAIDs are used short-term for fever or acute pain, because those drugs are available over the counter and often self-administered; this patient is on long-term therapy.

q_0606.stem: A nurse is planning NSAID therapy for an 80-year-old patient. Which consideration applies?
options: Use these drugs very cautiously because of decreased liver and renal functioning, and note that older adults are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events
Older adults tolerate NSAIDs better than younger adults because of reduced inflammation
Age has no bearing on NSAID selection, only on dosing intervals
Older adults require doubled doses because of reduced absorption
q_0606.rationale: The chapter states that these drugs are to be used very cautiously in older adult patients because of their decreased liver and renal functioning, and Box 44.3 states that older adult patients are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events. Ketorolac makes the point numerically, with an intravenous or intramuscular maximum of 120 mg/day under age 65 and 60 mg/day at 65 or older.
q_0606.trap: (D) moves the dose in the wrong direction, which is the reflex whenever a stem mentions reduced organ function without specifying which process is reduced. Reduced clearance calls for less drug, and ketorolac's age-split maximum is the chapter's own example.

q_0607.stem: A patient with recurrent gout attacks says he takes his allopurinol every day without fail, drinks three or four beers most evenings, and starts each morning with several cups of coffee. Which teaching is indicated?
options: Alcohol and caffeine must be avoided because they will increase uric acid levels, and fluid intake should be increased to 3 L/day unless contraindicated
Adherence is the only issue, and the beverage habits are unrelated to the attacks
Fluid intake should be restricted to 1 L/day to concentrate the drug at the renal tubule
Coffee is acceptable because caffeine is a diuretic and increases uric acid excretion
q_0607.rationale: The gout teaching directs the patient to increase fluid intake to 3 L/day unless contraindicated and to avoid alcohol and caffeine because these will increase uric acid levels. Antigout assessment includes hydration status and baseline serum uric acid levels.
q_0607.trap: (B) addresses only medication adherence, which is where the stem's own wording points by emphasizing perfect dosing. The chapter names a dietary half to this problem, and skipping it leaves the attacks unexplained. Note that this chapter pushes fluids for two different reasons: on an NSAID, hydration protects the kidney; in gout, it helps clear uric acid.

q_0608.stem: A parent asks for something to bring down the fever of a 5-year-old with chickenpox. Which recommendation is correct?
options: Give acetaminophen or ibuprofen, because aspirin and other salicylates are contraindicated in children with flulike symptoms
Give a children's aspirin, and switch to acetaminophen only if the fever does not break
Give aspirin, since the risk applies only to teenagers
Give nothing and allow the fever to break on its own
q_0608.rationale: Aspirin and other salicylates have one very specific contraindication: the class is contraindicated in children with flulike symptoms, because their use has been strongly associated with Reye's syndrome. The lifespan box names acetaminophen and ibuprofen as the drugs that may be used instead.
q_0608.trap: (B) is the most attractive wrong answer because it sounds cautious, using aspirin only as a fallback. There is no fallback here; the contraindication does not relax if the first drug underperforms.

q_0609.stem: A parent asks how long aspirin must be avoided after a child receives a varicella vaccine. Which response reflects the chapter's teaching?
options: Avoid aspirin for several weeks after a child or teenager has received a varicella vaccine
Aspirin may be resumed as soon as the injection site heals
The precaution applies only to the live influenza vaccine
There is no precaution, since vaccines do not cause viral illness
q_0609.rationale: The prevention teaching states that aspirin or medications that contain aspirin must not be given to children or teenagers to treat viral illnesses or fever, and to avoid aspirin for several weeks after a child or teenager has received a varicella vaccine.
q_0609.trap: (D) reasons from the vaccine rather than from the teaching, and it is the option that sounds most scientific. The chapter's instruction is stated as a flat interval, not as a judgment about whether the vaccine produces an illness.

q_0610.stem: A parent is taught to keep all salicylates away from a child recovering from influenza. Which products and label terms should the parent be taught to check for? (Select all that apply.)
options: Acetylsalicylic acid, acetylsalicylate, salicylic acid, or salicylate on the ingredient list
Alka-Seltzer
Pepto-Bismol
Products containing oil of wintergreen
Children's acetaminophen suspension
q_0610.rationale: Other names for aspirin include acetylsalicylic acid, acetylsalicylate, salicylic acid, and salicylate. Aspirin is contained in many over-the-counter drugs, including Alka-Seltzer, some Excedrin products, and Pepto-Bismol, and substances with oil of wintergreen may also contain salicylates.
q_0610.trap: (E) is one of the two drugs named as the substitute for aspirin in this situation, so selecting it inverts the teaching entirely. This is the same trade-name trap Ch 38 builds around drugs whose names do not announce their class.

q_0611.stem: A 12-year-old who is recovering from influenza and received aspirin at home is brought in quiet, lethargic, and vomiting persistently. Which action is the priority?
options: Report the findings and anticipate emergency AST, ALT, and serum ammonia levels, because this presentation suggests Reye's syndrome
Treat the vomiting as gastroenteritis and offer oral rehydration
Give another dose of aspirin for the residual fever
Reassure the parent, since Reye's syndrome does not occur after the illness has resolved
q_0611.rationale: Reye's syndrome is suspected with unexpected vomiting after any viral illness or with signs of disturbed brain function. Emergency aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and serum ammonia levels need to be drawn. Signs and symptoms typically develop within 12 hours to 3 weeks after recovery from a viral illness, upper respiratory tract infection, or gastroenteritis, and hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly may be present.
q_0611.trap: (D) uses recovery from the viral illness as reassurance, which is exactly backwards: the syndrome characteristically appears in the window after recovery, and more commonly in children and teenagers recovering from chickenpox or flu.

q_0612.stem: A child with Reye's syndrome who was obtunded with decorticate posturing and intact pupillary light reflexes now has dilated pupils with minimal light reflexes and decerebrate posturing. What does this change represent?
options: Progression from stage 3 to stage 4
Progression from stage 1 to stage 2
Improvement from stage 4 to stage 3
No change in stage, since posturing is not part of the staging
q_0612.rationale: The staging box gives stage 3 as obtunded with possible seizures and decorticate posturing with intact pupillary light reflexes, and stage 4 as pupil dilation with minimal light reflexes, seizures, deepening coma, and decerebrate posturing. Stage 1 is quiet, lethargic, and sleepy with persistent copious vomiting, and stage 2 is stupor, disorientation, and combativeness with hyperventilation and hyperreflexia.
q_0612.trap: (C) reads the change as improvement because the posturing terms sound interchangeable. Decorticate comes before decerebrate, and the pupillary response is the discriminator the box supplies.

q_0613.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with gout asks what went wrong in the body. Which explanation is correct?
options: Gout is caused by overproduction of uric acid, decreased uric acid excretion, or both, resulting in hyperuricemia and deposits of urate crystals in tissues and joints
Gout is caused by an autoimmune attack on the joint synovium
Gout is caused by excessive purine excretion, which strips the joints of protective crystals
Gout is caused by calcium deposits in the joints from excess dietary calcium
q_0613.rationale: Gout is caused by the overproduction of uric acid, decreased uric acid excretion, or both, and persons with gout either overproduce or underexcrete uric acid, which is the end product of purine metabolism. Deposits of uric acid crystals collect in tissues and joints, causing an inflammatory response and extreme pain, because the crystals are like small needles that jab and stick into sensitive tissues and joints.
q_0613.trap: (C) reverses the direction of the excretion defect and inverts the role of the crystals, and it is chosen by anyone who registers "purine" and "excretion" without noting which way each one runs.

q_0614.stem: A patient's gout is attributed to excess production of uric acid. Which drug targets that defect, and how?
options: Allopurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase and thereby prevents uric acid production
Probenecid, which inhibits xanthine oxidase and thereby prevents uric acid production
Allopurinol, which inhibits reabsorption of uric acid in the kidney
Colchicine, which blocks the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine
q_0614.rationale: Allopurinol is used for patients whose gout is caused by the excess production of uric acid, and it inhibits the enzyme xanthine oxidase, which thereby prevents uric acid production. Fig. 44.2 shows allopurinol and its metabolite oxypurinol blocking both xanthine oxidase steps, hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. The same upstream action is why allopurinol is also used to prevent acute tumor lysis syndrome during chemotherapy that causes cell death.
q_0614.trap: (C) keeps the right drug and gives it the wrong site of action, which is the more dangerous half of this confusion because the drug name still looks correct. Cue: allopurinol works upstream at the enzyme, not downstream at the tubule.

q_0615.stem: A different patient's gout is attributed to underexcretion of uric acid, and probenecid is prescribed. How does it work, and what limits its use?
options: It binds the transporter in the proximal convoluted renal tubule that returns uric acid to the blood, so uric acid stays in the urine; it is ineffective and not to be used in renal impairment
It inhibits xanthine oxidase, so less uric acid is made; it is ineffective in hepatic impairment
It dissolves urate crystals already deposited in the joint; it is ineffective once tophi have formed
It reduces the inflammatory response to urate crystals; it is ineffective for lowering uric acid
q_0615.rationale: Probenecid inhibits the reabsorption of uric acid in the kidney and thus increases its excretion, binding the special transporter protein in the proximal convoluted renal tubule that takes uric acid from the urine and places it back into the blood. The probenecid is then reabsorbed while the uric acid remains in the urine and is excreted. It is ineffective and is not to be used in patients with renal impairment.
q_0615.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, swapping the uricosuric and the xanthine oxidase inhibitor. The contraindication follows from the mechanism: a drug that works in the kidney needs a working kidney, which is why the limiting organ is renal, not hepatic.

q_0616.stem: A patient in an acute gout attack is given colchicine. What does it do to the serum uric acid level?
options: Nothing directly; it reduces the inflammatory response to the deposits of urate crystals by inhibiting the metabolism, mobility, and chemotaxis of polymorphonuclear leukocytes
It lowers the level by inhibiting xanthine oxidase
It lowers the level by increasing renal excretion of uric acid
It raises the level temporarily by dissolving joint deposits into the blood
q_0616.rationale: Colchicine's mechanism is not clearly defined but is thought to inhibit the metabolism, mobility, and chemotaxis of polymorphonuclear leukocytes, reducing the inflammatory response to the deposits of urate crystals. Chemotaxis is the chemical attraction of leukocytes to the site of inflammation, which worsens an inflammatory response.
q_0616.trap: (B) assigns colchicine the mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, and it is the reflex answer to any class-level question phrased as "antigout drugs work by decreasing serum uric acid levels." Colchicine, strictly, does not satisfy that description.

q_0617.stem: Which drugs act on uric acid levels themselves rather than on the inflammation? (Select all that apply.)
options: Allopurinol
Febuxostat
Probenecid
Lesinurad
Colchicine
q_0617.rationale: Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase and block production, while probenecid and lesinurad act at the renal tubule to increase excretion. Febuxostat is a nonpurine selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase that is more selective for the enzyme than allopurinol is, and lesinurad is a uric acid transporter inhibitor that blocks renal uric acid reabsorption.
q_0617.trap: (E) is the drug every student associates with gout, and it is the one that does nothing to uric acid. Colchicine reduces the inflammatory response to urate crystals and leaves the underlying defect untouched.

q_0618.stem: A patient has a first acute attack of gouty arthritis. Which therapy does the chapter identify as first-line?
options: An NSAID such as indomethacin, naproxen, or sulindac
Colchicine, because it is the oldest available therapy for acute gout
Allopurinol, to stop uric acid production immediately
Probenecid, to increase uric acid excretion immediately
q_0618.rationale: Although specific antigout drugs are available, the NSAIDs are considered first-line therapy for most patients with gout, and colchicine is considered second-line therapy, after the NSAIDs. Table 44.1 names indomethacin, naproxen, and sulindac as the suggested NSAIDs for gout, and acute gout and acute gouty arthritis head the FDA-approved indications in Box 44.2.
q_0618.trap: (B) is the trap this whole section sets, because colchicine is the drug students associate with gout and the chapter itself calls it the oldest available therapy for acute gout. Oldest is not first-line; it is explicitly second-line.

q_0619.stem: A patient is in the middle of an acute gout attack, and a new order reads allopurinol to relieve the pain. What is the problem?
options: Allopurinol's onset is 1 to 2 weeks, so it will not relieve an attack in progress
Allopurinol's onset is 12 hours, so a faster agent is needed
Allopurinol is contraindicated in gout caused by overproduction of uric acid
Allopurinol should be given only after the serum uric acid has normalized
q_0619.rationale: The pharmacokinetics table gives allopurinol an onset of 1 to 2 weeks and colchicine an onset of 12 hours. Neither is the rescue drug for an attack in progress in the way an NSAID is, and the goals of treatment are to decrease the symptoms of an acute attack and to prevent recurrent attacks. Allopurinol is dosed 200 to 600 mg/day to a maximum of 800 mg/day, and its serious adverse effects are agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and potentially fatal skin conditions including exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
q_0619.trap: (B) attaches colchicine's 12-hour onset to allopurinol. The two numbers sit next to each other in the same table and differ by more than an order of magnitude.

q_0620.stem: A patient is taking colchicine 0.6 mg hourly for an acute attack and develops severe nausea and diarrhea after a cumulative dose of 3.6 mg. What does this indicate?
options: A stopping endpoint has been reached, and the drug should be stopped even though the 6-mg maximum has not been reached
An expected effect to be managed with an antiemetic while the dosing continues to 6 mg
An allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
Underdosing, since gastrointestinal symptoms indicate poor absorption
q_0620.rationale: Acute dosing is an initial dose of 0.6 to 1.2 mg followed by 0.6 mg/hr until pain is relieved, the patient develops severe nausea and diarrhea, or a total of 6 mg has been administered, and some practitioners limit the cumulative dose to 3 mg. Three days must pass before a second course of therapy is initiated, and there is no specific antidote for colchicine poisoning.
q_0620.trap: (B) treats the gastrointestinal symptoms as a side effect to be managed rather than as one of the three stated stopping endpoints, and the presence of an unreached numeric maximum makes continuing feel defensible. Any one endpoint stops the drug.

q_0621.stem: A patient on colchicine reports blood in the urine, and the chart shows a creatinine clearance that has fallen since admission. Which actions does the chapter support?
options: Stop the drug for the bleeding and expect the dose to be adjusted for decreased renal function
Continue the drug, since urinary bleeding is an expected effect of urate crystals
Continue the drug at the same dose, since colchicine is not renally handled
Give the specific colchicine antidote and continue therapy
q_0621.rationale: Severe adverse effects include bleeding into the gastrointestinal or urinary tracts, and the drug needs to be stopped if such effects appear. The Clinical Pearl states that the colchicine dose must be adjusted for decreased renal function, and there is no specific antidote for colchicine poisoning.
q_0621.trap: (D) invents a rescue that does not exist, which is the assumption most drugs in a nursing course encourage. The chapter states flatly that there is no specific antidote for colchicine poisoning, which is part of why the injectable form was withdrawn in 2008.

q_0622.stem: A prescriber is weighing febuxostat against allopurinol for a patient with coronary artery disease. Which fact is the discriminator?
options: In 2017 the FDA issued a warning regarding an increased risk for cardiac death with febuxostat compared with allopurinol
Febuxostat has no cardiovascular risk, while allopurinol carries a black box warning for cardiac death
Febuxostat acts on the renal tubule, so it is safer in cardiac disease
Febuxostat is contraindicated in gout caused by overproduction of uric acid
q_0622.rationale: Febuxostat is a nonpurine selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase and the first new drug approved for gout since the 1960s. Clinical trials suggest it may pose a greater risk for cardiovascular events than allopurinol does, and in 2017 the FDA issued a warning regarding an increased risk for cardiac death when compared with allopurinol.
q_0622.trap: (B) reverses which drug carries the cardiac warning, and the reversal is easy because newer usually reads as safer in this chapter's other comparisons. Same mechanism and same target enzyme, so the cardiac risk is the discriminator.

q_0623.stem: An order reads lesinurad 200 mg daily as the sole drug for a patient's gout. What should the nurse do?
options: Question the order, because lesinurad must be given in combination with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, and its black box names the risk for acute renal failure
Administer it and monitor liver enzymes, since the black box concerns hepatotoxicity
Administer it and hold all fluids, since lesinurad causes fluid overload
Administer it only if the patient is also taking probenecid
q_0623.rationale: Lesinurad must be given in combination with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, and its black box warning covers both the risk for acute renal failure and the requirement that it be taken in conjunction with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. It is dosed 200 mg/day with food, and patients are advised to stay well hydrated with at least 2 L of fluid per day.
q_0623.trap: (C) inverts the hydration instruction that the drug's own labeling requires, and (D) pairs it with another uricosuric rather than with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, which leaves the black box requirement unmet while looking like a combination.

q_0624.stem: A patient taking probenecid for gout is prescribed an NSAID for the pain of an acute attack. What is the concern?
options: NSAIDs antagonize uricosurics, which decreases uric acid excretion
Probenecid delays the renal excretion of the NSAID, which raises NSAID levels to toxic range
The combination has no interaction, since the two drugs act at different sites
NSAIDs potentiate uricosurics, which risks precipitating hypouricemia
q_0624.rationale: Table 44.5 lists uricosurics with NSAIDs under the mechanism of antagonism and the result of decreased uric acid excretion. Two drugs aimed at the same disease work against each other.
q_0624.trap: (B) borrows probenecid's real and famous property and points it at the wrong drug. Probenecid delays the renal excretion of penicillin, which increases serum penicillin levels and prolongs its effect, and Ch 38 and Ch 39 carry the same effect for cephalosporins, quinolones, and nitrofurantoin. That is an antibiotic interaction, not an NSAID one.

q_0625.topic: cell cycle specificity in cancer chemotherapy
q_0625.stem: A combination regimen pairs a drug that is cytotoxic only while DNA is being synthesized with a second drug that kills cells at any point in the cycle. How should the nurse classify the first drug?
options: A cell cycle–specific drug, because it is cytotoxic during a specific phase of the cellular growth cycle
A cell cycle–nonspecific drug, because it is cytotoxic in any phase of the cellular growth cycle
A cell cycle–specific drug, because it is the more potent of the two agents
A cell cycle–nonspecific drug, because anything acting on DNA acts throughout the cycle
q_0625.rationale: Cell cycle–specific denotes antineoplastic drugs that are cytotoxic during a specific phase of the cellular growth cycle; the antimetabolites are the example, working primarily in the S phase during which DNA synthesis is most active. Chapter 45 covers the cell cycle–specific drugs and Chapter 46 the nonspecific ones, and the chapter states that split outright on p. 706.
q_0625.trap: (C) reaches the right label by the wrong reasoning and will carry a learner to the wrong answer on the mirror item. The book defeats potency reasoning itself: regardless of the cell cycle characteristics of a drug, it is more effective on rapidly growing tumors. Specific and nonspecific describe when a drug kills, not how hard.

q_0626.topic: cell cycle specificity in cancer chemotherapy
q_0626.stem: The second drug in that regimen is described as cytotoxic in any phase of the cellular growth cycle. What does that tell the nurse?
options: It is cell cycle–nonspecific, and being phase-indifferent does not make it the stronger of the two drugs
It is cell cycle–specific, since acting in every phase means it must be targeted to each one
It is cell cycle–nonspecific and therefore more effective than the phase-limited drug
It is cell cycle–nonspecific and is therefore reserved for slowly growing tumors
q_0626.rationale: Antineoplastic drugs that are cytotoxic in any phase of the cycle are cell cycle–nonspecific. The chapter adds that drugs may have actions falling into both categories, and that regardless of the cell cycle characteristics of a drug, it is more effective on rapidly growing tumors (p. 706).
q_0626.trap: (C) is the mirror error of the previous item, now attaching potency to the other label. (D) inverts the chapter's one comparative claim, which is that rapid growth predicts response for both categories alike.

q_0627.topic: cell cycle specificity in cancer chemotherapy
q_0627.subtopic: phases of the cell growth cycle
q_0627.stem: A patient asks why chemotherapy must be repeated in cycles rather than given once until every cancer cell is dead. Which explanation is grounded in the cell growth cycle?
options: Cancer cells sitting in the resting phase are not susceptible to cell cycle–specific drugs, so any single dose misses them
Cancer cells develop resistance to the drug within hours of the first dose
The drugs are cleared from the body too quickly to reach all of the cells at once
Repeated dosing is required to keep the tumor's doubling time from shortening
q_0627.rationale: Table 45.5 states that cancer cells in the G0 resting phase are not susceptible to the toxic effects of cell cycle–specific drugs, and p. 704 describes G0 cells as considered out of the cell cycle. That escape hatch is the rationale for combination regimens and for the existence of a separate cell cycle–nonspecific class in Chapter 46.
q_0627.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because acquired resistance is the familiar explanation for an incomplete kill. The chapter's stated reason is phase location, not resistance. When a stem asks why chemotherapy fails to eradicate every cell, the resting phase is the answer.

q_0628.topic: cell cycle specificity in cancer chemotherapy
q_0628.subtopic: phases of the cell growth cycle
q_0628.stem: A student lists the phases of the cell growth cycle as G1, S, G2, prophase, and metaphase. Which correction should the nurse make?
options: The five phases are G0, G1, S, G2, and M; prophase and metaphase are subphases within M
The five phases are correct, but prophase and metaphase come before G1 rather than after G2
The list is accurate as given, since mitosis is subdivided rather than named as a phase
The five phases are G0, G1, S, G2, and telophase
q_0628.rationale: Table 45.5 gives five phases: G0 resting, G1 first gap or postmitotic, S DNA synthesis, G2 second gap or premitotic, and M mitosis. M is divided into four subphases — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase — after which the cell divides into two daughter cells.
q_0628.trap: (D) is the same level swap with a different subphase promoted, which is why it survives a quick scan. Any option that lists a mitotic subphase alongside G1 and S has collapsed two levels of the outline into one.

q_0629.topic: cell cycle specificity in cancer chemotherapy
q_0629.subtopic: phases of the cell growth cycle
q_0629.stem: A pathology report describes a tumor with a high percentage of its cells in mitosis at any given time and a short doubling time. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The tumor has a high growth fraction, and its short doubling time makes it difficult to cure because of rapid regrowth
The tumor has a high mitotic index, which is another name for the same measurement as growth fraction
The short doubling time predicts a better cure rate, since rapidly dividing tumors respond to chemotherapy
The tumor is largely in the resting phase and will respond poorly to any chemotherapy
q_0629.rationale: Growth fraction is the percentage of cells in mitosis at any given time, and p. 704 states that tumors with shorter doubling times are often difficult to cure because of rapid regrowth. Chemotherapy is most effective in a rapidly dividing or highly proliferative tumor, so rapid proliferation cuts both ways.
q_0629.trap: (B) treats growth fraction and mitotic index as synonyms because both count dividing cells. Growth fraction is a percentage; the mitotic index is the actual number of cells per unit, usually 1000 cells, undergoing mitosis. Doubling time is neither of those — it is a clock.

q_0630.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0630.subtopic: which classes belong to this chapter
q_0630.stem: A nurse is reviewing which antineoplastic drug classes are cell cycle–specific. Select all that apply.
options: Antimetabolites
Mitotic inhibitors
Alkylating drugs
Alkaloid topoisomerase II inhibitors
Topoisomerase I inhibitors
Antineoplastic enzymes
Cytotoxic antibiotics
Hormonal and antihormonal drugs
q_0630.rationale: The chapter's key points name exactly five cell cycle–specific classes: antimetabolites, mitotic inhibitors, alkaloid topoisomerase II inhibitors, topoisomerase I inhibitors, and antineoplastic enzymes (p. 724). Alkylating drugs, cytotoxic antibiotics, and hormonal and antihormonal drugs are cell cycle–nonspecific and belong to Chapter 46.
q_0630.trap: (C) is the strongest pull, because alkylating drugs are the most familiar chemotherapy class and the name sounds mechanism-directed; they are in fact the flagship nonspecific class. (G) and (H) pull for the same reason. Scoring is all-or-nothing, so the five are learned as a set rather than judged one at a time.

q_0631.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0631.stem: Methotrexate is started, and the nurse explains that it belongs to the antimetabolites. Which statement describes how this class works?
options: It is an antagonist analogue that interferes with DNA synthesis, working primarily in the S phase
It is an agonist analogue that supplies the folic acid a rapidly dividing tumor demands
It acts in any phase of the cycle by cross-linking DNA strands directly
It halts mitosis during metaphase by producing nonfunctional microtubules
q_0631.rationale: Antimetabolites are cell cycle–specific analogues that antagonize folic acid, purines, or pyrimidines, and they work primarily in the S phase during which DNA synthesis is most active (p. 709). An analogue may have agonist or antagonist activity, and an antagonist analogue is also known as an antimetabolite.
q_0631.trap: (B) collapses analogue and antimetabolite into synonyms and then picks the wrong half. Every antimetabolite is an analogue, but not every analogue is an antimetabolite — the antimetabolite is specifically the antagonist kind. (D) is the taxane mechanism borrowed from a class two pages later.

q_0632.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0632.stem: A patient receives vincristine. By which mechanism do the vinca alkaloids kill dividing cells?
options: They bind to tubulin and prevent the assembly of microtubules, so the mitotic spindle dissolves
They cause the formation of nonfunctional microtubules, which halts mitosis during metaphase
They inhibit topoisomerase II, which causes breaks in DNA strands
They convert asparagine to aspartic acid so the cell cannot synthesize protein
q_0632.rationale: The vinca alkaloids are plant-derived mitotic inhibitors that bind tubulin and prevent the assembly of microtubules, dissolving the mitotic spindle. The mitotic inhibitors as a group all work shortly before or during mitosis (p. 712).
q_0632.trap: (B) is the taxane mechanism, and the two classes swap constantly because both are plant-derived drugs acting on microtubules around mitosis. The cue is that vincas prevent microtubules from being built while taxanes build them wrong.

q_0633.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0633.stem: The same patient is later switched to paclitaxel. How does its action on microtubules differ from vincristine's?
options: Paclitaxel causes the formation of nonfunctional microtubules, which halts mitosis during metaphase
Paclitaxel binds tubulin and prevents microtubules from assembling at all
Paclitaxel leaves microtubules intact and instead binds the DNA–topoisomerase I complex
Paclitaxel acts in the S phase rather than around mitosis
q_0633.rationale: The taxanes cause the formation of nonfunctional microtubules, which halts mitosis during metaphase (p. 712). Both taxanes and vincas are mitotic inhibitors reaching the same endpoint — a cell that cannot complete mitosis — by opposite routes.
q_0633.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item. Prevented assembly is the vinca mechanism; a built but nonfunctional spindle is the taxane one. The name cue is that vincas come from periwinkle and taxanes carry the "-taxel" stem from the yew.

q_0634.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0634.stem: A patient with metastatic colorectal cancer is to receive irinotecan. Which description of this drug's class is accurate?
options: It is a camptothecin that binds the DNA–topoisomerase I complex in the S phase, retarding religation and producing a DNA strand break
It is a derivative of epipodophyllotoxin that inhibits topoisomerase II in late S and G2
It is a vinca alkaloid that dissolves the mitotic spindle during metaphase
It is an antineoplastic enzyme approved exclusively for acute lymphocytic leukemia
q_0634.rationale: The camptothecins — topotecan and irinotecan — inhibit proper DNA function in the S phase by binding to the DNA–topoisomerase I complex, retarding religation and producing a DNA strand break (p. 714).
q_0634.trap: (B) names the other topoisomerase, and a single numeral is the whole distinction between the two classes. Topoisomerase I means the camptothecins in S phase; topoisomerase II means the epipodophyllotoxins in late S and G2.

q_0635.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0635.stem: A patient with testicular cancer receives etoposide. Which statement about this drug is accurate?
options: It is a derivative of epipodophyllotoxin that inhibits topoisomerase II, causing breaks in DNA strands, and acts in late S and G2
It is a camptothecin that binds the DNA–topoisomerase I complex during the S phase
It is an alkylating drug and therefore cell cycle–nonspecific
It depletes circulating asparagine so that leukemic cells cannot synthesize protein
q_0635.rationale: Etoposide and teniposide are derivatives of epipodophyllotoxin and act by inhibiting the enzyme topoisomerase II, which causes breaks in DNA strands (p. 712).
q_0635.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, with the numeral flipped. Note also that the book files the topoisomerase II inhibitors under the mitotic-inhibitor heading on p. 712 while listing them separately in its key points, so an option that calls etoposide a mitotic inhibitor is not thereby wrong.

q_0636.topic: cell cycle–specific drug classes and mechanisms
q_0636.stem: A child with acute lymphocytic leukemia is receiving pegaspargase. Beyond the usual chemotherapy toxicities, which assessment is specific to this drug class?
options: Monitor blood glucose and for abdominal pain, because impaired pancreatic function can produce hyperglycemia and severe or fatal pancreatitis
Monitor for peripheral neuropathy, because this class is the most significant neurotoxin among the cytotoxic drugs
Monitor for delayed diarrhea beginning 2 to 10 days after the infusion
Monitor the palms and soles for hand-foot syndrome
q_0636.rationale: The antineoplastic enzymes asparaginase and pegaspargase are approved exclusively for the treatment of acute lymphocytic leukemia. They convert asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia, so leukemic cells are then unable to synthesize the asparagine required. Their distinguishing toxicity is impaired pancreatic function, with hyperglycemia and severe or fatal pancreatitis (p. 715).
q_0636.trap: (B) is vincristine's signature toxicity and (C) is irinotecan's. Both pull because they are the chapter's other two drug-specific assessments, and a learner who has memorized "chemotherapy has drug-specific toxicities" without pairing each to its drug picks whichever sounds most serious.

q_0637.subtopic: naming the condition and the moment
q_0637.stem: A patient who received chemotherapy 14 days ago calls the clinic. Applying the concept of the nadir, when is this patient at greatest risk for infection?
options: Now, because the nadir normally occurs approximately 10 to 28 days after dosing
Within the first 24 hours after the infusion, when drug levels peak
Not until the next cycle begins and the doses accumulate
Only once a fever has actually developed
q_0637.rationale: The nadir is the lowest point in any fluctuating value over time — for example, the lowest white blood cell count measured after the count has been depressed by chemotherapy. It normally occurs approximately 10 to 28 days after dosing, and anticipating it guides the timing of prophylactic antibiotics and hematopoietic growth factors (p. 707).
q_0637.trap: (B) assumes toxicity tracks the infusion, which is true for acute reactions and false for marrow toxicity. The chapter puts the window at 10 to 28 days, so the patient feels best at the point of greatest danger.

q_0638.subtopic: naming the condition and the moment
q_0638.stem: The same patient's counts return with a low white blood cell count, a low hemoglobin, and a low platelet count all at once. Which term names the condition producing all three?
options: Myelosuppression, the suppression of bone marrow function
Nadir, since the nadir is what makes all three counts fall
Tumor lysis syndrome
A paraneoplastic syndrome
q_0638.rationale: Myelosuppression, also known as bone marrow suppression, results from destruction of the rapidly dividing cellular precursors of white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets, and leads to leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia (p. 707).
q_0638.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item. Myelosuppression is the condition and the nadir is the moment, which is why the key-terms box prints them side by side. "Why are all three cell lines low" wants myelosuppression; "when is the risk greatest" wants nadir.

q_0639.stem: A patient is thrombocytopenic after chemotherapy. Which findings should the nurse attribute specifically to the low platelet count? Select all that apply.
options: Petechiae
Gingival bleeding
Fatigue and pallor of the conjunctiva
Prolonged bleeding from puncture sites
Ecchymosis
Fever and chills
q_0639.rationale: Thrombocytopenia makes the patient more susceptible to bleeding, and the chapter lists petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis, gingival bleeding, and prolonged bleeding from puncture sites. Fatigue and pallor sort to anemia, which often leads to hypoxia and fatigue; fever and chills sort to neutropenia.
q_0639.trap: (C) is the reliable decoy because fatigue feels universal in a chemotherapy patient, but this chapter files it under anemia. (F) sorts into the neutropenia bucket, and an option offering an elevated white blood cell count would be wrong on its face, since that count is the value that has fallen.

q_0640.stem: A patient with severe bone marrow suppression has documented fatigue, altered body image from alopecia, impaired mobility, and a white blood cell count near its nadir. Which problem takes priority?
options: Risk for infection
Fatigue
Altered body image
Impaired physical mobility
q_0640.rationale: All four are documented in this chapter, which is what makes the distractors strong, but the physiologic threat to life wins. Here that is infection, because myelosuppression has cost the patient the ability to mount a defense. Because fever is a principal early sign of infection, an oral or axillary temperature is taken at least every 4 hours (p. 720).
q_0640.trap: (B) pulls because fatigue is the most commonly reported chemotherapy symptom and the chapter names it directly as an effect of anemia. Priority items in this chapter resolve to the physiologic threat unless the scenario supplies active bleeding or an airway or circulation problem.

q_0641.stem: A patient's absolute neutrophil count returns at 420 cells/mm3 on the morning the next chemotherapy cycle is due. What does the nurse anticipate?
options: The dose will be held, because an ANC below 500 is severe neutropenia and carries a high risk for infection
The dose will proceed as scheduled, since 420 falls within the normal range of 1500 to 8000 cells/mm3
The dose will proceed with an added antibiotic, since the count only reflects marrow recovery
A platelet transfusion will be given first, since this value reflects the bleeding risk
q_0641.rationale: A normal absolute neutrophil count is 1500 to 8000 cells/mm3, severe neutropenia is less than 500, and Box 45.2 places an ANC of 500 or lower at high risk for infection. Chemotherapy is held below 500 (p. 708).
q_0641.trap: (D) reads any low chemotherapy value as a platelet problem, which is a common reflex because bleeding precautions are the most visible nursing intervention in this chapter. The ANC reports neutrophils; the separate bleeding threshold is a platelet count under 100,000/mm3, with some guidelines using 50,000.

q_0642.topic: vesicant extravasation and chemotherapy route safety
q_0642.stem: During an infusion of a chemotherapy drug with vesicant potential, the nurse notes swelling and blanching at the intravenous site. What is the first action?
options: Stop the infusion and leave the intravenous cannula in place
Apply cold compresses and elevate the extremity
Inject the prescribed antidote through the catheter
Give subcutaneous epinephrine at the site
q_0642.rationale: The drug is usually discontinued immediately and the intravenous cannula is left in place for possible use of antidotes through the cannula (p. 721). Extravasation is the leakage of an intravenously administered medication into the tissue space surrounding the vein, and it is a serious complication of chemotherapy.
q_0642.trap: (C) is the strong distractor because it is eventually correct — just not first, and it depends on the cannula still being there. Stop the exposure before treating it.

q_0643.topic: vesicant extravasation and chemotherapy route safety
q_0643.stem: Two chemotherapy drugs infiltrate on the same unit. One is classified as an irritant and the other as a vesicant. What distinguishes the vesicant?
options: It causes cell death with extravasation, producing necrosis with ulcerations
It irritates the intravenous site and vein without causing tissue death
It produces a mild local reaction such as erythema or bruising
It causes a systemic hypersensitivity reaction rather than a local injury
q_0643.rationale: These drugs may be irritants, irritating the intravenous site and vein, or vesicants, causing cell death with extravasation and necrosis with ulcerations (p. 718). Only vesicant extravasation carries emergency status.
q_0643.trap: (C) describes what topotecan extravasation produces, a mild local reaction such as erythema or bruising, which sits at the irritant end of the spectrum and reads as reassuring rather than wrong.

q_0644.topic: vesicant extravasation and chemotherapy route safety
q_0644.stem: Vincristine has extravasated, and the protocol directs hyaluronidase 150 units/mL by multiple subcutaneous injections into the site. What else does Table 45.8 specify?
options: Warm compresses, since corticosteroids and topical cooling appear to worsen toxicity
Cold compresses, since cooling limits the spread of the drug through the tissue
A topical corticosteroid cream applied over the affected area
Elevation with an ice pack for the first 24 hours
q_0644.rationale: Table 45.8 covers etoposide, teniposide, vinblastine, and vincristine, and specifies hyaluronidase 1 to 6 mL by multiple subcutaneous injections into the site, repeated over the next few hours, plus warm compresses. Its footnote states that administration of corticosteroids and topical cooling appear to worsen toxicity (p. 712).
q_0644.trap: (B) is right elsewhere and wrong here. The chapter lists hot or cold packs among possible protocol measures on p. 721, which is exactly what makes cold read as safe. Compress temperature is drug-specific, and the instruction is to follow the hospital or infusion protocol without exception.

q_0645.topic: vesicant extravasation and chemotherapy route safety
q_0645.stem: A pharmacy technician asks whether vincristine can be sent up for intrathecal administration, since cytarabine on the same unit is given by that route. What is the nurse's response?
options: Vincristine is for intravenous use only and is fatal if given by other routes; several deaths have been reported after inadvertent intrathecal administration
Vincristine may be given intrathecally provided it is diluted in 25 to 50 mL first
Either drug may be given intrathecally as long as it is dispensed in a syringe
Intrathecal vincristine is acceptable when the goal is to treat central nervous system disease
q_0645.rationale: Every vincristine product carries the warning that it is for intravenous use only and fatal if given by other routes. The safeguards are to dilute the dose in 25 to 50 mL and never dispense it in a syringe. Intrathecal is a legitimate route in this same chapter for cytarabine, which may be given intravenously, subcutaneously, or intrathecally (pp. 712 and 713).
q_0645.trap: (D) pulls because the intrathecal route exists precisely to deliver chemotherapy to the central nervous system and is correct for other drugs on the same unit. The axis of this question is route, not indication. (B) inverts the safeguard: intrathecal drugs are not normally dispensed in a minibag, so the 25 to 50 mL dilution is what makes the fatal error harder to commit.

q_0646.topic: vesicant extravasation and chemotherapy route safety
q_0646.stem: A patient receiving vincristine reports numbness and tingling in the fingertips and difficulty buttoning a shirt. Which assessment priority does this reflect?
options: Peripheral neuropathy, because vincristine is the most significant neurotoxin of the cytotoxic drug class
Early myelosuppression, so the complete blood count becomes the priority assessment
Hand-foot syndrome developing at the infusion site
Cytarabine syndrome, which appears 6 to 12 hours after administration
q_0646.rationale: Vincristine is described as the most significant neurotoxin of the cytotoxic drug class, and it continues to be used in part because of its relative lack of bone marrow suppression (p. 713). Assessment for peripheral neuropathy is the stated priority for this drug (p. 718).
q_0646.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because "monitor the complete blood count" is the right answer for nearly every other drug in the chapter. Vincristine is the exception whose whole selling point is relative marrow sparing, so the reflex answer is the wrong assessment here.

q_0647.topic: tumor lysis syndrome and uric acid prophylaxis
q_0647.stem: A patient begins induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia. Which pattern of laboratory changes is consistent with tumor lysis syndrome?
options: Elevated potassium, elevated phosphate, elevated uric acid, and reduced calcium
Elevated potassium, phosphate, uric acid, and calcium
Reduced potassium, phosphate, and uric acid with elevated calcium
Elevated calcium and uric acid with a normal potassium
q_0647.rationale: The key term defines tumor lysis syndrome by excessive cellular waste products and electrolytes including uric acid, phosphate, and potassium, and by reduced serum calcium levels. The chapter names hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia, and hypocalcemia, and calls it a common postchemotherapy condition often associated with induction chemotherapy for rapidly growing hematologic malignancies (pp. 701 and 710).
q_0647.trap: (B) flips calcium, and it is the intuitive reading because cells bursting suggests everything spills upward at once. Calcium is the single value that falls, and the key term prints it as the discriminator. Note also the stage cue in the stem: this is an induction-phase event in a rapidly growing hematologic malignancy, not a maintenance-phase event in a slow-growing solid tumor.

q_0648.topic: tumor lysis syndrome and uric acid prophylaxis
q_0648.subtopic: the two rescues and what each rescues from
q_0648.stem: Allopurinol is ordered before induction chemotherapy begins. A student asks whether it is an antineoplastic drug. What is the nurse's response?
options: No; it inhibits xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid levels, and although it is chemically similar to purines it does not disrupt DNA synthesis
Yes; it is a purine antimetabolite that antagonizes DNA synthesis in the S phase
No; it is an enzyme that degrades the uric acid already circulating in the blood
Yes; it slows the rate of cell kill so that waste products are released gradually
q_0648.rationale: Allopurinol and rasburicase are both indicated for the hyperuricemia associated with tumor lysis syndrome and are usually given in anticipation of the condition rather than in response to it. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which reduces serum and urinary levels of uric acid, and it is also used commonly in oral form to treat gout (p. 709).
q_0648.trap: (B) is exactly the distractor the chapter pre-empts. Allopurinol looks like a purine, so it reads as a purine antagonist and therefore an antimetabolite. The text states plainly that it does not disrupt DNA synthesis, which means it has no direct antineoplastic action at all.

q_0649.topic: tumor lysis syndrome and uric acid prophylaxis
q_0649.subtopic: the two rescues and what each rescues from
q_0649.stem: The same patient's uric acid is already markedly elevated. Which drug acts on uric acid that has already formed?
options: Rasburicase, an enzyme that degrades uric acid to more soluble end products
Allopurinol, which degrades the uric acid already present in the circulation
Leucovorin, which rescues the patient from hyperuricemia
Filgrastim, which lowers uric acid as it raises the neutrophil count
q_0649.rationale: Rasburicase is an enzyme that degrades uric acid to more soluble end products, while allopurinol prevents uric acid from being formed by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. Both are indicated for the hyperuricemia associated with tumor lysis syndrome (p. 709).
q_0649.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item. The two drugs address the same problem from opposite ends: allopurinol stops uric acid from being made, rasburicase destroys what is already there.

q_0650.topic: tumor lysis syndrome and uric acid prophylaxis
q_0650.subtopic: the two rescues and what each rescues from
q_0650.stem: A patient is to receive high-dose methotrexate. Which drug is given with it, and for what purpose?
options: Leucovorin, an antidote for folic acid antagonists, always given with high-dose methotrexate as a rescue
Allopurinol, which is the rescue drug for methotrexate toxicity
Rasburicase, which reverses the binding of methotrexate at its target
Hyaluronidase, which rescues the bone marrow from methotrexate
q_0650.rationale: High-dose methotrexate is always given in conjunction with the rescue drug leucovorin, and leucovorin is an antidote for folic acid antagonists (p. 710). Allopurinol and rasburicase rescue a different problem entirely, the hyperuricemia of tumor lysis syndrome.
q_0650.trap: (B) trades one rescue for the other, and the pull is real because both rescues appear within a page of each other in this chapter. Leucovorin also appears as a component of an irinotecan and fluorouracil regimen on p. 714, which is the adjacent-fact decoy that makes it look like a companion drug rather than an antidote.

q_0651.topic: chemotherapy emetic potential and antiemetic timing
q_0651.stem: A patient scheduled for chemotherapy asks that the antiemetic be held until nausea actually starts. What is the nurse's best response?
options: Antiemetics are given 30 to 60 minutes before chemotherapy, because preventing nausea works better than treating it once it has begun
That is reasonable, since antiemetics are most effective when given only on request
Distraction with light activity is preferred over routine antiemetic dosing
Holding fluids before the infusion will control the nausea without medication
q_0651.rationale: Antiemetics are given before chemotherapy (p. 706). Anticancer drugs cause nausea and vomiting by stimulating the cells of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and the chapter's own review question places the antiemetic 30 to 60 minutes before the dose.
q_0651.trap: (B) is the trap that sounds patient-centered, deferring to the patient's stated preference. (D) is the trap that sounds preventive while actually risking dehydration in a patient who may already be vomiting. The principle is prevent, do not rescue.

q_0652.topic: chemotherapy emetic potential and antiemetic timing
q_0652.stem: A nurse is told a patient will receive methotrexate and asks what level of antiemetic coverage to plan for. Why can that not be answered from the drug name alone?
options: Methotrexate crosses all three emetic tiers depending on dose, at thresholds of 250 and 1000 mg/m2
Methotrexate has essentially no emetic potential at any dose
Emetic potential is determined by the patient's prior history rather than by the drug
Methotrexate always sits in the high tier, so maximum coverage is assumed
q_0652.rationale: Box 45.1 lists methotrexate under 250 mg/m2 in the low tier, 250 to 1000 mg/m2 in the moderate tier, and over 1000 mg/m2 in the high tier (p. 707).
q_0652.trap: (D) assigns a flat tier to the drug name, which is the swap Box 45.1 is built to catch. Emetic potential is dose-tiered rather than drug-tiered for methotrexate, cytarabine, and fluorouracil, each of which appears in more than one tier with a dose threshold printed beside it.

q_0653.topic: chemotherapy emetic potential and antiemetic timing
q_0653.stem: Cytarabine is ordered at 1500 mg/m2. Which emetic tier applies, and what should the nurse plan for?
options: High, because cytarabine crosses from low to high above 1000 mg/m2, so aggressive prophylactic antiemetic coverage is planned
Low, because cytarabine is listed in the low tier
Moderate, because the antimetabolites as a class are moderately emetogenic
No tier applies, because cytarabine is not listed in Box 45.1
q_0653.rationale: Box 45.1 lists cytarabine under 1000 mg/m2 in the low tier and cytarabine over 1000 mg/m2 in the high tier. Most of this chapter's cell cycle–specific drugs cluster in the low tier; the high tier is dominated by the alkylating and platinum drugs covered in Chapter 46 (p. 707).
q_0653.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, reading the drug's most common listing and stopping before the dose qualifier. The threshold is printed next to the drug name for exactly this reason.

q_0654.stem: A patient starting cyclophosphamide says her sister's chemotherapy was described as working only while the cancer cells were in one particular part of their growth cycle, and asks how her own drug differs. Which explanation is accurate?
options: It has antineoplastic activity regardless of the phase of the cell cycle
It is active only during specific phases of the cell growth cycle
It is effective against any type of cancer rather than against one tumor type
It damages cancer cells while sparing normal cells
q_0654.rationale: Chapter 45 describes the antineoplastic drugs effective against cancer cells during specific phases in the cell growth cycle; in contrast, this chapter focuses on drugs that have antineoplastic activity regardless of the phase of the cell cycle (p. 726). Cyclophosphamide is one of the classic alkylating drugs in that second group.
q_0654.trap: (C) and (D) are the axis swaps that make "nonspecific" sound like breadth or safety, and they pull because both are things a patient would want to hear. The word describes the phase of the cell cycle only - not the tumor type, and not any selectivity for cancer cells over normal cells.

q_0655.stem: The same patient's sister is receiving a drug her oncologist called cell cycle-specific. What does that label establish about the sister's drug?
options: It acts only while cells are in particular phases of the cell growth cycle
It acts on cancer cells no matter which phase of the cycle they are in
It is specific to her tumor type and would not be used for a different cancer
It targets only cancer cells and leaves normal dividing cells untouched
q_0655.rationale: The specific/nonspecific split is what divides these two chapters: Chapter 45's drugs are effective during specific phases in the cell growth cycle, while this chapter's drugs work regardless of phase (p. 726).
q_0655.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, and it is easy to slide into right after "nonspecific" has just been explained. (C) repeats the tumor-type swap in the opposite direction.

q_0656.stem: A student concludes that every drug discussed in the chapter on cell cycle-nonspecific drugs must itself be cell cycle-nonspecific. Which drug shows that conclusion to be wrong?
options: Bleomycin, which the chapter flags as actually being a cell cycle-specific drug
Doxorubicin, which acts by intercalating into DNA
Cisplatin, which is a bifunctional alkylating drug
Busulfan, which is grouped with the miscellaneous alkylating drugs
q_0656.rationale: The chapter names "bleomycin (which is actually a cell cycle-specific drug)" (p. 729), and hydroxyurea likewise works in the S and G1 phases and appears here only because it is included as a miscellaneous drug. Chapter membership is not classification.
q_0656.trap: (D) is the reflex pick, because "miscellaneous" reads as "the exception" - but busulfan is an alkylating drug and nonspecific like the rest of its group; miscellaneous is only a subcategory heading. The chapter marks its real exception in a parenthesis around bleomycin.

q_0657.stem: A nurse is grouping the drug classes covered in the chapter on cell cycle-nonspecific antineoplastics. Which classes does the chapter name as the two broad classes of cell cycle-nonspecific cancer drugs? (Select all that apply.)
options: Alkylating drugs
Cytotoxic antibiotics
Antimetabolites
Mitotic inhibitors
Topoisomerase inhibitors
q_0657.rationale: "There are two broad classes of cell cycle-nonspecific cancer drugs: alkylating drugs and cytotoxic antibiotics" (p. 726). The chapter's two other groupings, miscellaneous and hormonal drugs, are not cell-cycle-based classifications at all.
q_0657.trap: (E) is the strongest pull, because cytotoxic antibiotics genuinely do inhibit topoisomerase II - but "topoisomerase inhibitors" is a class heading from the cell cycle-specific chapter and appears nowhere here. (C) and (D) are the same borrowing from the previous chapter.

q_0658.stem: A patient receiving mechlorethamine asks how the drug actually kills the cancer cells. Which description matches the mechanism of an alkylating drug?
options: It alters the chemical structure of the cell's DNA so that abnormal chemical bonds form between adjacent DNA strands
It is inserted between the two strands of the DNA molecule and blocks DNA synthesis
It inhibits topoisomerase II and generates free radicals
It is inactive until enzymes in the liver convert it to an active form
q_0658.rationale: Alkylating drugs alter the chemical structure of the cells' DNA, so abnormal chemical bonds form between adjacent DNA strands, yielding defective nucleic acids and cell death (p. 727); alkylation itself is a chemical reaction in which an alkyl group is transferred from one molecule to another.
q_0658.trap: (B) and (C) both describe the cytotoxic antibiotics, and they pull because the two classes are cell cycle-nonspecific and are presented side by side. (D) is the prodrug fact, which is true of cyclophosphamide but is not a mechanism of cell kill.

q_0659.stem: The same patient is later switched to doxorubicin and asks whether the new drug works the same way. Which mechanism belongs to the cytotoxic antibiotics?
options: Intercalation, in which the drug is inserted between the two strands of a DNA molecule and ultimately blocks DNA synthesis
Alkylation, in which alkyl groups are transferred to DNA so that abnormal bonds form between adjacent strands
Transfer of two reactive alkyl groups to two separate sites on the DNA molecule
Inhibition of the bcr-abl tyrosine kinase
q_0659.rationale: Cytotoxic antibiotics work by intercalation, "inserted between the two strands of a DNA molecule, ultimately blocking DNA synthesis"; they also inhibit the enzyme topoisomerase II, and many generate free radicals (p. 729).
q_0659.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item and (C) restates it in bifunctional terms. The word "antibiotic" is the other pull here: these are natural substances produced by the mold Streptomyces that kill cancer cells, not anti-infectives, and inhibiting topoisomerase II does not make them topoisomerase inhibitors.

q_0660.stem: A drug reference describes mechlorethamine as a bifunctional alkylating drug. What does the nurse understand about the molecule?
options: It has two reactive alkyl groups and can therefore alkylate at two sites on the DNA molecule
It can engage in several alkylation reactions per single molecule of drug
It must be activated in the body before it can alkylate anything
It is active during two different phases of the cell cycle
q_0660.rationale: Bifunctional refers to alkylating drugs composed of molecules that have two reactive alkyl groups and that are therefore able to alkylate at two sites on the DNA molecule (p. 726). Mechlorethamine and cisplatin are the chapter's bifunctional examples.
q_0660.trap: (B) is the polyfunctional definition, one prefix away. (D) is the level swap that reads "functional" as a cell-cycle claim; neither bifunctional nor polyfunctional says anything about phase, and these drugs are nonspecific.

q_0661.stem: Cyclophosphamide is ordered, and the reference describes it as a polyfunctional alkylating drug and a prodrug. Which statement reflects both of those descriptions?
options: It can engage in several alkylation reactions per single molecule of drug, and it requires in vivo activation before it acts
