The drug acts on the vestibular apparatus, which then signals the chemoreceptor trigger zone
q_0732.rationale: The chapter states that neurotransmitter signals are sent to the vomiting center from the chemoreceptor trigger zone. The CTZ is the area of the brain involved in the sensation of nausea and the action of vomiting, and Fig. 52.1 shows the labyrinth, GI tract, and cerebral cortex feeding the CTZ, with the CTZ feeding the vomiting center in the medulla.
q_0732.trap: (B) reverses the direction of the signal, and it is the reflex pick because the key terms box defines both structures with the same opening words, "the area of the brain that is involved in." The signal runs CTZ to VC, never the reverse.

q_0733.subtopic: chemoreceptor trigger zone versus vomiting center
q_0733.stem: A patient asks which part of the brain actually sets off the retching and vomiting once the signal has arrived. Which structure should the nurse name?
options: The chemoreceptor trigger zone, because it senses emetogenic substances in the blood
The vomiting center in the medulla, because it initiates the physiologic events that lead to nausea and vomiting
The vestibular nuclei, because they receive input from the inner ear
The reticular formation, because it is where the tetrahydrocannabinoids act
q_0733.rationale: The vomiting center is defined as the area of the brain involved in stimulating the physiologic events that lead to nausea and vomiting, and the body text says it is responsible for initiating those events. Fig. 52.1 places it in the medulla.
q_0733.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. The CTZ senses and signals; the VC initiates. Because both key-term definitions begin identically, the discriminator has to come from the verbs.

q_0734.stem: A postoperative patient reports feeling queasy and says the urge to vomit keeps coming and going, but nothing has come up. How should the nurse document this?
options: Emesis, because the urge to vomit is itself the defining feature of emesis
Nausea, because nausea is the sensation that often leads to the urge to vomit
Neither term applies until gastric contents are actually expelled
Either term is correct, because the chapter uses nausea and emesis interchangeably
q_0734.rationale: Nausea is the sensation often leading to the urge to vomit, described elsewhere in the chapter as an unpleasant feeling that often precedes vomiting. Emesis is the forcible emptying or expulsion of gastric and occasionally intestinal contents through the mouth, which has not occurred here.
q_0734.trap: (A) is the reflex pick for students who treat the two words as interchangeable. Nausea is the feeling; emesis is the event, and only emesis requires forcible expulsion. An antiemetic is defined against both, as a drug given to relieve nausea and vomiting, not vomiting alone.

q_0735.stem: A nurse is reviewing the neurotransmitters involved in nausea and vomiting alongside the drug classes that act on them. Which of these neurotransmitters listed by the chapter are blocked by one of the seven antiemetic categories? Select all that apply.
options: Acetylcholine
Dopamine
Histamine
Prostaglandins
Serotonin
Substance P
q_0735.rationale: Table 52.1 lists six neurotransmitters in the vomiting pathway, but only five map to a blocking class in Tables 52.2 and 52.3: acetylcholine to the anticholinergics, histamine to the antihistamines, dopamine to the antidopaminergics and the prokinetics, serotonin to the serotonin blockers, and substance P or neurokinin 1 to the neurokinin antagonists.
q_0735.trap: (D) is the option the whole item turns on. Prostaglandins act in the GI tract and are printed right in Table 52.1, so they look as though they belong, but no antiemetic category in this chapter blocks them. The tetrahydrocannabinoids are the opposite case: one of the seven categories, but described only by anatomic site, with no receptor in Table 52.1 at all.

q_0736.stem: A patient taking scopolamine for motion sickness and a patient taking meclizine for motion sickness both report dry mouth and blurred vision. How should the nurse explain the difference in mechanism?
options: Scopolamine blocks acetylcholine receptors directly, while meclizine blocks histamine 1 receptors and thereby prevents acetylcholine from binding
Scopolamine blocks histamine 1 receptors, while meclizine blocks acetylcholine receptors directly
Scopolamine acts at the chemoreceptor trigger zone, while meclizine acts at the vestibular nuclei
Only scopolamine has anticholinergic activity; meclizine's effects have nothing to do with acetylcholine
q_0736.rationale: Table 52.3 says anticholinergics block ACh receptors in the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation, while antihistamines block histamine 1 receptors, thereby preventing ACh from binding to receptors in the vestibular nuclei. The chapter adds that antihistamines also have potent anticholinergic activity, which is why the dry mouth and blurred vision set appears under both classes in Table 52.4.
q_0736.trap: (D) is the reflex pick because the class name antihistamine says nothing about acetylcholine. Table 52.1 gives acetylcholine and histamine 1 the identical site entry and the shared adverse effect profile cannot discriminate these two classes, so only the receptor actually bound can.

q_0737.stem: A patient is started on dimenhydrinate and the nurse anticipates dry mouth and urinary retention. Which explanation is correct?
options: Dimenhydrinate blocks acetylcholine receptors directly in the vestibular nuclei
Dimenhydrinate blocks histamine 1 receptors and also has potent anticholinergic activity
Dimenhydrinate blocks dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Dimenhydrinate blocks serotonin receptors in the GI tract
q_0737.rationale: Dimenhydrinate is one of the antihistamine antiemetics along with meclizine and diphenhydramine. Table 52.3 says antihistamines block histamine 1 receptors, thereby preventing ACh from binding in the vestibular nuclei, and these drugs also have potent anticholinergic activity. Table 52.4 gives this class dizziness, drowsiness, and confusion plus blurred vision, dilated pupils, dry mouth, and urinary retention.
q_0737.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, handing the anticholinergic's direct receptor blockade to the antihistamine. Same destination, different door: anticholinergics block acetylcholine directly, antihistamines get there through histamine 1.

q_0738.stem: A patient says a friend told her that "a histamine blocker" will prevent her motion sickness, and she already has a histamine 2 receptor blocker at home for gastric acid control. What should the nurse explain?
options: The histamine 2 blocker will work, because all histamine blockers act on the vestibular pathways
Only histamine 1 blockers are antiemetics; histamine 2 blockers act at the parietal cell for gastric acid control and are a different drug group
The histamine 2 blocker will work, but only if it is taken 1 hour before travel
Neither histamine 1 nor histamine 2 blockers are used for motion sickness
q_0738.rationale: The chapter warns directly that the antihistamine antiemetics are not to be confused with histamine 2 receptor blockers, used for gastric acid control, which are covered in Chapter 50. Histamine 1 blockers act on the vestibular and labyrinthine pathways of the inner ear; histamine 2 blockers control gastric acid.
q_0738.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because both drug groups are called histamine blockers in ordinary speech. The subscript is the entire distinction, and this is a confusion the chapter flags itself rather than one a test writer invented.

q_0739.stem: A patient with delayed gastric emptying reports nausea after every meal. Which antiemetic class is aimed at that problem?
options: Antidopaminergics, because they block dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Prokinetics, because along with blocking dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone their primary action is to stimulate peristalsis and empty stomach contents into the duodenum
Serotonin blockers, because they act at the GI tract, chemoreceptor trigger zone, and vomiting center
Anticholinergics, because they reduce gastrointestinal secretions
q_0739.rationale: Both antidopaminergics and prokinetics block dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and the key points say so outright. What separates the prokinetics is that their primary action is to stimulate peristalsis in the GI tract, promoting emptying of stomach contents into the duodenum. Table 52.2 gives prokinetics the indications delayed gastric emptying, gastroesophageal reflux, and nausea and vomiting.
q_0739.trap: (A) is the reflex pick precisely because it is true as far as it goes; both classes do block dopamine at the CTZ, so a partially correct mechanism feels like the answer. The prokinetic row of Table 52.3 is the only line in the chapter where a class stimulates a receptor rather than blocking one, and motility is the discriminator.

q_0740.stem: A hospitalized patient has intractable hiccups and also needs an injectable antiemetic. Which class and drug fit both needs?
options: Prokinetics, such as metoclopramide, because they empty the stomach
Antidopaminergics, such as prochlorperazine, because the class also treats psychotic disorders and intractable hiccups
Serotonin blockers, such as ondansetron, because the class has very few adverse effects
Neurokinin antagonists, such as aprepitant, because the class covers acute and delayed vomiting
q_0740.rationale: Table 52.2 gives the antidopaminergics the indications psychotic disorders including mania, schizophrenia, and anxiety, intractable hiccups, and nausea and vomiting. Prochlorperazine, especially in the injectable form, is used frequently in the hospital setting.
q_0740.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. Since both classes block dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, the stem's cue decides: gastric emptying, reflux, or motility points to the prokinetic, while psychosis, hiccups, or an injectable hospital antiemetic points to the antidopaminergic.

q_0741.subtopic: sites of action across the pathway
q_0741.stem: A prescriber wants an antiemetic that acts at every level of the vomiting pathway for a patient starting chemotherapy. Which class does the chapter describe as acting at all three sites?
options: Anticholinergics
Antihistamines
Serotonin blockers
Neurokinin antagonists
q_0741.rationale: Table 52.3 says serotonin blockers block serotonin receptors in the GI tract, the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and the vomiting center, and Fig. 52.2 places only the serotonin blockers at the vomiting center. Prokinetics reach two sites; every other class reaches one.
q_0741.trap: (A) pulls because Table 52.1 lists acetylcholine as acting at the vomiting center in the brain. That entry names where the neurotransmitter acts, not where the drug was placed, and Fig. 52.2 does not put anticholinergics at the vomiting center. (D) reaches the brain stem only.

q_0742.subtopic: sites of action across the pathway
q_0742.stem: A prescriber asks the nurse which conditions the prokinetic class is indicated for. Which does the chapter list? Select all that apply.
options: Motion sickness
Vertigo
Gastroesophageal reflux
Delayed gastric emptying
Gastrointestinal obstruction
Nausea and vomiting
q_0742.rationale: Table 52.2 gives the prokinetics exactly three indications: delayed gastric emptying, gastroesophageal reflux, and nausea and vomiting. Motion sickness and vertigo belong to the anticholinergics and the antihistamines, and metoclopramide is contraindicated in gastrointestinal obstruction.
q_0742.trap: (E) is the sharpest distractor in the set because it inverts a contraindication into an indication, which is the most damaging form this tactic takes: stimulating peristalsis against a mechanical blockage is exactly what the contraindication forbids. (A) and (B) borrow the indications of the two motion-sickness classes.

q_0743.stem: A patient is leaving on a 5-day cruise and wants something for motion sickness that will not have to be taken over and over. Which drug fits?
options: meclizine, taken 1 hour before departure and repeated daily during travel
scopolamine transdermal patch, applied behind one ear every 3 days
prochlorperazine by injection each morning
ondansetron 30 minutes before each meal
q_0743.rationale: Scopolamine is the primary anticholinergic drug used as an antiemetic, and its transdermal patch is applied to a hairless area behind one ear every 3 days, releasing a total of 1 mg over 72 hours. That 72-hour duration is what makes it the travel option.
q_0743.trap: (A) is a genuine motion-sickness option and not a throwaway, which is what makes it pull: meclizine is dosed 25 to 50 mg 1 hour before travel and repeated daily during travel. The cue in the stem is the patch and the multi-day duration, and that points to scopolamine.

q_0744.stem: A patient with dizziness and vertigo asks for a drug that treats vertigo specifically. Which drug carries that separate indication?
options: scopolamine, because it corrects an imbalance between acetylcholine and norepinephrine
meclizine, because it treats the dizziness, vertigo, and nausea and vomiting associated with motion sickness
metoclopramide, because it stimulates peristalsis in the GI tract
dronabinol, because it acts on the reticular formation and cerebral cortex
q_0744.rationale: The meclizine profile states that it treats the dizziness, vertigo, and nausea and vomiting associated with motion sickness, and it is the only drug in the chapter's dosage table carrying a separate treatment-of-vertigo indication.
q_0744.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. Both drugs treat motion sickness, both are contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma, and both sedate, so the stem's cue decides: a patch or travel points to scopolamine, while the word vertigo points to meclizine.

q_0745.stem: A patient with narrow-angle glaucoma asks for something for motion sickness before a long car trip. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: A scopolamine patch will be ordered, because the transdermal route avoids systemic anticholinergic effects
Meclizine will be ordered, because the glaucoma concern applies only to scopolamine
Another antiemetic or antinausea drug must be prescribed, because the glaucoma concern applies to both scopolamine and the antihistamines
Either drug may be used as long as intraocular pressure is checked afterward
q_0745.rationale: Scopolamine is contraindicated in patients with glaucoma, and the nursing process section extends the point explicitly: the same concern regarding use in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma applies to antihistamines such as meclizine. The taught action is that another antiemetic or antinausea drug must be prescribed.
q_0745.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because the contraindication is printed inside the scopolamine profile and not inside the meclizine profile. Glaucoma rules out both of the motion-sickness options, which makes this stem a dead end rather than a choice between two drugs.

q_0746.stem: A patient is admitted for a first cycle of highly emetogenic chemotherapy and has orders for both ondansetron and dronabinol. Which should the nurse expect to give?
options: dronabinol, because it also stimulates appetite in patients with cancer
ondansetron, because dronabinol is generally used as a second-line drug after treatment with other antiemetics has failed
dronabinol, because tetrahydrocannabinoids act on the cortex where anticipatory nausea begins
Neither, until the patient actually reports nausea
q_0746.rationale: Dronabinol is generally used as a second-line drug after treatment with other antiemetics has failed, and the chapter's case study models exactly that sequence, adding dronabinol only after 2 weeks of failed ondansetron. The key points name granisetron and ondansetron as most commonly used for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
q_0746.trap: (D) fails the chapter's core principle, since antiemetics for chemotherapy are prophylactic and given 30 to 60 minutes before the drug rather than held for symptoms. (A) attaches a true fact about dronabinol to a decision that fact does not govern; a first round of chemotherapy points to the serotonin blocker.

q_0747.stem: A patient has had nausea and vomiting through 2 weeks of chemotherapy despite scheduled ondansetron. Which drug does the chapter support adding, and on what grounds?
options: dronabinol, because it is generally used as a second-line drug after treatment with other antiemetics has failed
dronabinol, because it is the first-line drug for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
phosphorated carbohydrate solution, because it acts directly on the walls of the GI tract
meclizine, because it treats dizziness and vertigo
q_0747.rationale: Dronabinol is the only commercially available tetrahydrocannabinoid, a synthetic derivative approved in 1985, and is generally used as a second-line drug after treatment with other antiemetics has failed. It also stimulates appetite and promotes weight gain in patients with AIDS and cancer.
q_0747.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, and it is unusually seductive because it names the same drug with only the sequence inverted. (C) names the phosphorated carbohydrate solution, which is explicitly not sufficient for nausea as severe as that associated with cancer chemotherapy.

q_0748.stem: A patient asks whether the over-the-counter phosphorated carbohydrate solution in her medicine cabinet can be used for her chemotherapy-related vomiting. What is the nurse's best response?
options: It is appropriate, because it acts directly on the walls of the GI tract and reduces cramping
It is not sufficient for treatment of nausea as severe as that associated with cancer chemotherapy
It may be used, but only after other antiemetics have not worked
It should be reserved for severe chemotherapy-induced nausea
q_0748.rationale: Phosphorated carbohydrate solution has a direct local action on the walls of the GI tract, where it reduces cramping, but the chapter states twice that it is not sufficient for treatment of more severe nausea symptoms such as those associated with cancer chemotherapy. Its unlabeled use is for morning sickness.
q_0748.trap: (C) describes dronabinol, the second-line drug, and is the answer a student reaches for after drilling that sequence. (D) inverts the fact outright. This drug's local GI action with no central receptor blockade at all is what confines it to mild nausea.

q_0749.stem: A nurse is reviewing dronabinol before administering it. Which statements about this drug are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It is indicated for nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy
It is the drug named for treatment of hyperemesis gravidarum
It stimulates appetite and promotes weight gain in patients with AIDS and cancer
It can cause extrapyramidal symptoms
It can cause drowsiness, dizziness, and euphoria
q_0749.rationale: Dronabinol is a synthetic tetrahydrocannabinoid indicated for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and for anorexia associated with weight loss in patients with AIDS and cancer. Table 52.4 gives its central nervous system effects as drowsiness, dizziness, anxiety, confusion, and euphoria, along with visual disturbances and dry mouth.
q_0749.trap: (B) borrows ondansetron's profile, which is where hyperemesis gravidarum appears. (D) borrows the antidopaminergic and prokinetic rows of Table 52.4. Both false options are lifted from a neighboring drug's profile rather than invented, which is what makes an all-or-nothing item hard.

q_0750.stem: A serotonin blocker is ordered to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting. When should it be given?
options: Approximately 30 minutes before the beginning of the surgical procedure
Approximately 30 minutes before the end of the surgical procedure
30 to 60 minutes after the patient arrives in the recovery area
When the patient first reports nausea after surgery
q_0750.rationale: For postoperative nausea and vomiting the chapter directs that serotonin blockers be given approximately 30 minutes before the end of the surgical procedure, so the drug is already on board as the patient wakes.
q_0750.trap: (A) is the distractor form this fact always takes: same class, same 30 minutes, opposite anchor, and the two phrases differ by one word. Surgical nausea is prevented at the back end of the procedure; chemotherapy nausea is prevented at the front end.

q_0751.stem: The same serotonin blocker is ordered for a patient about to receive chemotherapy. When should it be given?
options: 30 to 60 minutes before the start of chemotherapy
30 minutes before the end of the chemotherapy infusion
4 hours before the start of chemotherapy
At the first sign of nausea
q_0751.rationale: For chemotherapy the chapter gives 30 to 60 minutes before the start of chemotherapy, and states more generally that antiemetics are given 30 to 60 minutes before a chemotherapy drug is administered and may also be given during the treatment.
q_0751.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, dragging the surgical anchor onto a chemotherapy stem. (D) fails the chapter's default of prophylaxis rather than rescue.

q_0752.stem: A patient receiving a highly emetogenic chemotherapy drug says he would rather wait and take the antiemetic only if he actually gets sick. What is the nurse's best response?
options: That is reasonable, because antiemetics work equally well once nausea has started
Antiemetics for chemotherapy are given beforehand so the trigger zone is blocked before it fires, though a dose may also be given during the treatment
Antiemetics must never be given once nausea has already begun
He should take it 4 hours before the infusion instead
q_0752.rationale: The chapter's default is prophylaxis rather than rescue: antiemetics are given 30 to 60 minutes before a chemotherapy drug is administered, and they may also be given during the chemotherapy treatment. Chapter 45 calls premedication 30 to 60 minutes before the preferred approach.
q_0752.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because it matches how patients use antiemetics at home, but by the time nausea is reported the chemoreceptor trigger zone has already fired. (C) overcorrects into an absolute the chapter does not make, since a breakthrough dose during treatment is supported.

q_0753.stem: A patient's chemotherapy regimen produces vomiting both on the day of treatment and for several days afterward. Which antiemetic class does the chapter describe as inhibiting both the acute and the delayed phases?
options: Anticholinergics
Antihistamines
Neurokinin antagonists
Tetrahydrocannabinoids
q_0753.rationale: Table 52.2 gives the neurokinin antagonists the indication acute and delayed vomiting associated with chemotherapy, and the body text says these drugs inhibit the acute and delayed phases of chemotherapy-induced emesis. Aprepitant, fosaprepitant, and rolapitant are the drugs in this class.
q_0753.trap: (D) pulls because dronabinol is also a chemotherapy antiemetic and students sort chemotherapy stems by drug rather than by phase. The acute-and-delayed phrasing is printed only for the neurokinin antagonists, so when a stem names the delayed phase that class is in the answer.

q_0754.stem: A nurse is preparing to give intravenous promethazine to a patient with a peripheral line. Which action is correct?
options: Give it undiluted as a rapid intravenous push through the port closest to the patient's vein
Dilute it in at least 10 mL of fluid and give it in a running intravenous line at the port farthest from the patient's vein, using a large-bore vein
Give it subcutaneously if intravenous access cannot be obtained
Give it into a hand or wrist vein so that any reaction is easy to see
q_0754.rationale: Promethazine is the chapter's only high-alert drug. The intravenous route is not the preferred route but is commonly used, and when it is used the drug is best diluted in at least 10 mL of fluid, the more dilute the better, and given in a running intravenous line at the port farthest from the patient's vein or through a large-bore vein, not a hand or wrist vein. Therapy must be discontinued immediately if burning or pain occurs.
q_0754.trap: (D) names the exact vein the chapter forbids, and it pulls because a small visible vein feels easier to monitor. (C) is forbidden outright: promethazine is not to be given subcutaneously. If promethazine is inadvertently given intraarterially instead of intravenously, severe tissue damage often requiring amputation can occur.

q_0755.stem: A patient has an order for intramuscular hydroxyzine for nausea, and the intramuscular site is bruised. The nurse considers giving the dose intravenously instead. What is correct?
options: Hydroxyzine may be given intravenously if it is diluted in at least 10 mL of fluid
Hydroxyzine must never be given by the intravenous route, and intravenous, intraarterial, or subcutaneous administration can cause tissue damage, thrombosis, and gangrene
Hydroxyzine may be given intravenously but never intraarterially
Hydroxyzine may be given subcutaneously as the alternative route
q_0755.rationale: The Safety and Quality Improvement box titled Right Route Is Essential states that hydroxyzine is given orally or intramuscularly only, and that intravenous, intraarterial, or subcutaneous administration of hydroxyzine can result in significant tissue damage, thrombosis, and gangrene.
q_0755.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, carrying promethazine's dilution rule across to hydroxyzine. These two drugs are the safety box's two examples and they sit one word apart: for promethazine the intravenous route is allowed but not preferred, while for hydroxyzine it is never allowed.

q_0756.stem: A patient is being taught to use a scopolamine patch before travel. Which instruction is correct?
options: Apply the patch to the shoulder at least 4 hours before travel and leave it in place for 72 hours
Apply the patch to a hairless, cleansed, dried, nonirritated area behind one ear at least 4 hours before travel, rotating sites and washing hands before and after
Apply the patch to the temple the day before travel and replace it every day
If the patch becomes dislodged, press it back into place right away
q_0756.rationale: The dosage table directs applying 1 patch to a hairless area behind 1 ear every 3 days, starting at least 4 hours before travel, and the patient teaching section adds cleansed, dried, nonirritated skin, rotation of sites, and handwashing before and after. If the patch is dislodged, the residual drug must be washed off and a fresh patch put in place.
q_0756.trap: (D) is the reflex action a patient would take on their own and it is wrong twice over, since the residual drug has to be washed off and a fresh patch applied. (A) and (C) move the site off the area behind the ear, which is the only site the chapter teaches.

q_0757.stem: A patient has been taking metoclopramide for several months. Which finding reflects the problem named in the FDA advisory that specifically concerns long-term use of this drug?
options: Acute dystonia within hours of the first dose
Tardive dyskinesia, an involuntary neurologic movement
Orthostatic hypotension on standing
Prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram
q_0757.rationale: In 2009 the FDA issued a public health advisory regarding the potential for development of tardive dyskinesia with long-term use of metoclopramide. Tardive dyskinesia is described as an involuntary neurologic movement, and it is the long-term-use problem, whereas extrapyramidal symptoms are what the nurse assesses at baseline, monitors throughout therapy, and reports immediately.
q_0757.trap: (A) names dystonia, which Table 52.4 genuinely does list for the prokinetics, so it is a real adverse effect placed in the wrong time frame. Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia sit in the same cell of that table, which is what makes the pair invertible. (D) belongs to the serotonin blockers and to droperidol.

q_0758.stem: A patient is starting aprepitant with a chemotherapy regimen. Which of the patient's current drugs or drug groups does this chapter identify as interacting with aprepitant? Select all that apply.
options: digoxin
warfarin
oral contraceptives
nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs
corticosteroids
q_0758.rationale: Neurokinin antagonists may induce the metabolism of warfarin, so the INR must be checked before each cycle, and they may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives. Aprepitant may also increase the bioavailability of corticosteroids including dexamethasone and methylprednisolone, whose dosages may need to be adjusted by 25% to 50%. The chapter names these three separately on three different pages.
q_0758.trap: (A) and (D) appear nowhere in this chapter's interaction text, and in an all-or-nothing item the two absent options are the whole question. Aprepitant is a major inhibitor of cytochrome P-450, so the real caution list is CYP3A4 substrates such as azole antifungals, clarithromycin, diltiazem, nicardipine, protease inhibitors, and verapamil.

q_0759.stem: A prescriber asks whether aprepitant can simply replace ondansetron for a patient on highly emetogenic chemotherapy. What should the nurse know about aprepitant?
options: It blocks the same serotonin receptors as ondansetron, so it is a direct substitute
In contrast to other antiemetics it has little affinity for serotonin and dopamine receptors, and it is used in conjunction with serotonin blockers and glucocorticoids to augment them
It blocks dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, so it also treats intractable hiccups
It has no significant drug interactions, so it is the safer of the two drugs
q_0759.rationale: The aprepitant profile states that in contrast to other antiemetics this drug has little affinity for serotonin and dopamine receptors; it inhibits the substance P and neurokinin receptors in the brain stem. Neurokinin blockers are used in conjunction with serotonin blockers and glucocorticoids, and their use augments those drugs, because combining categories blocks more than one pathway.
q_0759.trap: (D) is exactly backwards, and it is the reflex pick because the two drugs are given together and their profiles blur. Aprepitant is the most interaction-heavy drug in the chapter; the serotonin blockers are the class with no significant drug interactions. Aprepitant adds a pathway rather than replacing one.

q_0760.subtopic: the classes that stay clean, and one that loses effect
q_0760.stem: A patient taking ondansetron is worried about interactions because he takes several other medications. What does the chapter say about this class?
options: Serotonin blockers are major inhibitors of cytochrome P-450 and interact with many drugs
Serotonin blockers have no significant known drug interactions, and the tetrahydrocannabinoids are the only other class the chapter describes the same way
Serotonin blockers may induce the metabolism of warfarin and reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives
Serotonin blockers must not be combined with any other antiemetic class
q_0760.rationale: The chapter states that serotonin blockers and tetrahydrocannabinoids have no significant drug interactions, and the ondansetron profile repeats it: very specific actions, very few adverse effects, and no significant drug interactions known to occur. Ondansetron's only listed contraindication is known drug allergy.
q_0760.trap: (A) and (C) both borrow aprepitant's paragraph, which sits directly beside this one on the page. The class that revolutionized chemotherapy antiemesis is the cleanest; the class that augments it is the dirtiest. (D) contradicts the chapter's own point that combining categories works because more than one pathway becomes blocked.

q_0761.subtopic: the classes that stay clean, and one that loses effect
q_0761.stem: A postoperative patient receiving opioids has metoclopramide ordered for delayed gastric emptying, and the nurse notes that an anticholinergic is also on the medication list. What effect should the nurse anticipate?
options: Additive central nervous system depression
The motility effects of metoclopramide will be blocked, decreasing its action
An increased risk of extrapyramidal reactions
Prolongation of the QT interval
q_0761.rationale: The chapter states that anticholinergics and analgesics can block the motility effects of metoclopramide, and that its action is decreased when it is taken with anticholinergics or opiates. This is the only interaction in the chapter that reduces an antiemetic's effect rather than compounding a toxicity, and it is clinically likely, because opioid patients are exactly the ones receiving antiemetics.
q_0761.trap: (A) substitutes the far more common interaction type, and it pulls because metoclopramide with alcohol genuinely does produce additive central nervous system depression. (C) names a real metoclopramide danger with the wrong partner: it is the phenothiazines, prochlorperazine and promethazine, that would lead to exacerbation of extrapyramidal reactions.

q_0762.stem: A patient three days after an ischemic stroke has an intact and fully functioning gastrointestinal tract but fails a swallow screen and cannot safely take food by mouth. Which form of nutritional support does the chapter identify as preferred for this patient?
options: Enteral nutrition delivered through a feeding tube
Peripheral parenteral nutrition, because it avoids the risk of aspiration
Central total parenteral nutrition through a subclavian catheter
No nutritional support until the swallow study is repeated
q_0762.rationale: Enteral nutrition is "the preferred route of administration of nutritional supplements" and is used "when the patient has a functioning gastrointestinal tract"; tube delivery exists precisely for patients with depressed consciousness, altered anatomy, or abnormal peristalsis who cannot eat. A working gut plus an inability to eat is the definition case for tube feeding.
q_0762.trap: (B) pulls because the stem names a swallowing problem and a vein seems to route around it, but parenteral nutrition is reserved for when oral or enteral support is impossible or when absorptive capacity is insufficient. Neither is true here.

q_0763.stem: A patient with short bowel syndrome has been on an elemental formula for two weeks and continues to lose weight, and the team documents that the remaining absorptive capacity is not sufficient to meet nutrient needs. Which form of support is now indicated?
options: Add a modular protein product to the elemental formula
Change to a polymeric formula to reduce osmolarity
Parenteral nutrition, which bypasses the gastrointestinal system entirely
Continue enteral feeding, because enteral is always preferred
q_0763.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is used "only when oral or enteral support is impossible or when the gastrointestinal absorptive or functional capacity is not sufficient," and it "bypasses the entire gastrointestinal system, which eliminates the need for absorption, metabolism, and excretion." Documented insufficient absorptive capacity is the stated trigger.
q_0763.trap: (D) is the mirror error of the previous item — the enteral preference is conditional on a gut that can absorb, not absolute, and treating it as absolute is what keeps a malabsorbing patient undernourished.

q_0764.stem: A nursing student charts that a patient on total parenteral nutrition "developed hyperalimentation" after two days of therapy. Which correction should the nurse make?
options: Hyperalimentation is an older term for parenteral nutrition itself, not a complication of it
Hyperalimentation means overfeeding and should be documented as a caloric excess
Hyperalimentation refers to enteral feeding delivered faster than the ordered rate
Hyperalimentation is the correct term for the metabolic response to a high dextrose load
q_0764.rationale: The key terms box defines hyperalimentation as "an older term for parenteral nutrition; its use is now discouraged because it may be misinterpreted to mean overfeeding," and states that the process is now referred to as total parenteral nutrition.
q_0764.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because the prefix hyper- reads as excess, which is exactly the misreading the book says caused the term to be retired. The word never named a complication; it named the therapy.

q_0765.stem: A patient who eats poorly is started on an oral polymeric supplement between meals, and a student concludes that the patient is now on enteral nutrition and therefore no longer needs to be assessed for oral intake. Which statement corrects the student?
options: Oral supplements are not enteral nutrition, because no feeding tube is involved
Enteral nutrition may supplement an oral diet or be used alone to meet all nutrient needs, so how much of the need it covers is a separate question from the route
Any enteral formulation by definition supplies the patient's total nutrient requirement
Once a supplement is ordered, oral intake no longer contributes to the nutritional plan
q_0765.rationale: Enteral nutrition can "supplement an oral diet ... or be used alone to meet all of the patient's nutrient needs," and the oral route is itself one of the six enteral routes and the most common and least invasive. Route and completeness are independent axes.
q_0765.trap: (C) is the swap distractors are built on — students trade where the nutrition goes for how much of the need it covers. The same swap runs through Table 55.2, where peripheral parenteral nutrition is supplemental and central is total, even though both are parenteral.

q_0766.stem: A nurse is reviewing the complications the chapter attributes to enteral feeding. Which of the following belong to enteral nutrition rather than to parenteral nutrition? Select all that apply.
options: Gastrointestinal intolerance manifesting as diarrhea
Aspiration
Air embolism
Dumping syndrome
Rebound hypoglycemia
q_0766.rationale: The key points list the enteral complications as "hyperglycemia, dumping syndrome, and aspiration," and diarrhea is named as the most common adverse effect of enteral feeding. Air embolism and rebound hypoglycemia appear on the parenteral list.
q_0766.trap: (E) is the option that trips people, because hypoglycemia sounds like a feeding problem in general; the chapter attaches it specifically to abrupt discontinuation of parenteral nutrition. (C) is the giveaway parenteral option, since an air embolism requires a vascular line.

q_0767.topic: enteral tube routes and formula selection
q_0767.stem: An order reads "insert nasogastric tube for feeding." A new nurse asks whether the surgical team needs to be notified. Which description of the tube is accurate?
options: A feeding tube placed from the nose to the stomach, requiring no surgery
A feeding tube surgically inserted directly into the stomach
A feeding tube placed from the nose to the duodenum
A feeding tube surgically inserted into the esophagus
q_0767.rationale: Table 55.1 defines the nasogastric route as a "feeding tube placed from the nose to the stomach," and a feeding tube is used in five of the six enteral routes. Only the ostomy routes are surgically created.
q_0767.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because both names end in the same organ and the word "gastric" carries all the attention; the prefix is what decides whether a surgeon is involved. Naso- means through the nose with no surgery, and -ostomy means a surgically created opening.

q_0768.topic: enteral tube routes and formula selection
q_0768.stem: A patient with a history of gastric outlet obstruction is scheduled for placement of a feeding tube that will require an operative procedure and will deliver formula directly into the jejunum. Which route is being described?
options: Nasojejunal
Jejunostomy
Nasoduodenal
Esophagostomy
q_0768.rationale: Table 55.1 defines jejunostomy as a "feeding tube surgically inserted into the jejunum," while the nasojejunal route reaches the same organ from the nose without surgery. The second half of each name gives the destination organ and the first half gives the method.
q_0768.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — it names the right organ by the wrong method. Reading only the organ half of these words is what makes all four cells of Table 55.1 interchangeable to a student.

q_0769.topic: enteral tube routes and formula selection
q_0769.stem: A postoperative patient with a fully functional gastrointestinal tract and no specialized nutrient requirements needs tube feeding for a few weeks. Which formulation does the chapter state is preferred, and why?
options: An elemental formula, because predigested nutrients are gentler on the gut
A polymeric formula, because it most closely resembles normal dietary intake and is less hyperosmolar than elemental formulas
A modular formula, because single nutrients can be titrated individually
An altered amino acid formula, because surgery raises amino acid requirements
q_0769.rationale: Polymeric formulations contain complex nutrients — proteins, carbohydrates, and fat — and are "preferred over elemental formulations for patients with a fully functional gastrointestinal tract and few specialized nutrient requirements" because they most closely resemble normal dietary intake and are "less hyperosmolar than elemental formulations and therefore cause fewer gastrointestinal problems."
q_0769.trap: (A) is the intuitive inversion: predigested sounds gentler, so students reach for elemental whenever the gut is mentioned at all. The chapter puts elemental where digestion is impaired and polymeric where it is intact, and the hyperosmolarity runs the other way from the intuition.

q_0770.topic: enteral tube routes and formula selection
q_0770.stem: A patient with radiation enteritis and documented malabsorption cannot tolerate a standard tube feeding. Which formulation matches this patient's problem?
options: Polymeric, containing complex proteins, carbohydrates, and fat
Impaired glucose tolerance formula, containing protein, carbohydrate, fat, sodium, and potassium
Elemental, containing dipeptides, tripeptides, or crystalline amino acids and requiring minimal digestion with minimal residue
Infant formulation used as sole or supplemental intake
q_0770.rationale: Box 55.1 lists elemental formulations as requiring "minimal digestion" and leaving "minimal residue," indicated for malabsorption, partial bowel obstruction, irritable bowel disease, radiation enteritis, bowel fistula, and short bowel syndrome.
q_0770.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — polymeric is correct only when digestion is intact, and a stem naming malabsorption has already ruled that out. Matching the formula to the gut's remaining capacity is the whole decision.

q_0771.topic: enteral tube routes and formula selection
q_0771.stem: A family member asks whether the patient could be maintained entirely on the protein supplement listed on the plan of care as a modular product. Which response is accurate?
options: Modular products are single-nutrient formulas added to an elemental or polymeric formulation, not a complete feeding
Modular products contain all required macronutrients and can serve as sole nutrition
Modular products are indicated only for genetic metabolic enzyme deficiencies
Modular products must be given intravenously to be complete
q_0771.rationale: Box 55.1 describes modular formulations as "single-nutrient formulas" of protein, carbohydrate, or fat that are "added to a monomeric or polymeric formulation to provide a more individualized nutrient formulation." Carbohydrate, fat, and protein modulars are all named as additives.
q_0771.trap: (B) is a true statement about complete formulations attached to the wrong product. A modular is real nutrition, which is what makes the option feel defensible, but by itself it supplies one macronutrient and leaves the rest of the requirement unmet.

q_0772.subtopic: matching the patient to the vein
q_0772.stem: A patient is expected to need parenteral support for about 10 days after abdominal surgery, has modest nutritional needs of roughly 1600 kcal per day, and tolerates large fluid volumes without difficulty. Which form of parenteral nutrition fits the chapter's criteria?
options: Peripheral parenteral nutrition, using a dextrose concentration below 10%
Central total parenteral nutrition, using a dextrose concentration of 25%
Peripheral parenteral nutrition, using a dextrose concentration of 20%
Central total parenteral nutrition, because any therapy beyond 7 days must be central
q_0772.rationale: Table 55.2 sets peripheral parenteral nutrition at fewer than 14 days, dextrose less than 10%, and fewer than 2000 kcal per day, and requires that fluid tolerance "must be high." The chapter also describes it as "a temporary means (less than 2 weeks)" for patients without large nutritional needs.
q_0772.trap: (C) pairs the right vein with a central-line dextrose concentration, and it pulls because the stem's duration and calories both fit peripherally, so students stop reading before the concentration. Dextrose above 10% in a peripheral vein scleroses the vein and is the setup for phlebitis.

q_0773.subtopic: matching the patient to the vein
q_0773.stem: A patient with severe burns requires about 3000 kcal per day, a dextrose concentration of 25%, and support expected to last several weeks, possibly continuing at home. Which route is indicated?
options: Peripheral parenteral nutrition, because the therapy can be started immediately
Central total parenteral nutrition through a large central vein such as the subclavian or internal jugular
Peripheral parenteral nutrition, because burns raise fluid tolerance
Enteral feeding by nasogastric tube regardless of gastrointestinal status
q_0773.rationale: Central total parenteral nutrition uses "a large central vein ... usually the subclavian or internal jugular" for a "prolonged period, usually longer than 7 to 10 days," carries dextrose of 10% to 35% and more than 2000 kcal per day, and can be continued at home. Large nutritional requirements from metabolic stress or hypermetabolism are a stated indication.
q_0773.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — every one of the three numbers in this stem violates a peripheral limit, and picking the peripheral route because it is quicker to start is the reflex when a patient looks unstable.

q_0774.subtopic: matching the patient to the vein
q_0774.stem: A student states that the way to tell peripheral parenteral nutrition from central total parenteral nutrition is that only the central solution is hyperosmolar. Which correction is accurate?
options: Only the peripheral solution is hyperosmolar, which is why it causes phlebitis
Both are hyperosmolar at 600 to 900 mOsm/L, so osmolarity does not distinguish them
Neither solution is hyperosmolar once lipids are added
Osmolarity is not reported for parenteral solutions
q_0774.rationale: Table 55.2 gives the identical osmolarity range, hyperosmolar at 600 to 900 mOsm/L, in both columns. The chapter also notes that the components of the two solutions "are the same. The difference lies in the concentrations and amounts." The reason central access is used is "the hyperosmolarity of the substances used and the need for dilution provided by a larger-diameter vein."
q_0774.trap: (A) inverts a row that is not a difference at all, and it pulls because phlebitis really is a peripheral problem, so students reason backwards from the complication to a difference the table does not state. Osmolarity is the one row of Table 55.2 that cannot discriminate.

q_0775.subtopic: matching the patient to the vein
q_0775.stem: A patient with heart failure who cannot tolerate large fluid volumes needs parenteral nutrition. A new nurse suggests the peripheral route because it is less invasive. Which reasoning should the nurse apply instead?
options: Peripheral is correct, because peripheral solutions are given in smaller volumes
Peripheral is correct, because a central line would worsen fluid overload
Central is correct, because peripheral dextrose is capped below 10% to avoid sclerosing the vein, so large fluid volumes are required to deliver the calories
Either route is acceptable, because fluid volume is determined only by the prescriber's order
q_0775.rationale: Table 55.2 states that peripheral fluid tolerance "must be high" while central "can be fluid-restricted," and the chapter explains why: peripheral dextrose is "generally less than 10%, to avoid sclerosing the vein. Thus large volumes are needed," and patients "with renal failure or heart failure, cannot tolerate large fluid volumes."
q_0775.trap: (A) is the classic miss, because the smaller vein suggests smaller volumes and the fluid rule actually runs the opposite way. Heart failure and renal failure push a patient toward central access, not away from it.

q_0776.subtopic: matching the patient to the vein
q_0776.stem: A patient receiving peripheral parenteral nutrition reports increasing pain at the infusion site. The site looks unremarkable, vital signs are stable, and the hanging bag reads 20% dextrose. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Stop the infusion
Apply a warm compress and continue the infusion at a slower rate
Document the finding and reassess at the end of the shift
Draw a blood glucose level before taking any other action
q_0776.rationale: The chapter states that "the most devastating adverse effect of PPN is phlebitis," which "can lead to the loss of a limb, although this is rare," and peripheral dextrose is held below 10% precisely to prevent it. A 20% concentration is a central-line strength running in a peripheral vein, so the solution is causing the injury and comes off first.
q_0776.trap: (B) pulls because a stable patient with a normal-looking site does not feel like an emergency, and slowing an infusion feels like a reasonable middle step. When the infusing solution is itself the cause, slowing it continues the injury; the only situation that outranks stopping the line is hemodynamic instability, which this stem rules out.

q_0777.topic: parenteral nutrition components and amino acid classes
q_0777.stem: A parenteral formulation for an infant is being reviewed, and the pharmacist notes that arginine and histidine must be supplied even though an adult would not require them from the diet. How should the nurse classify these two amino acids?
options: Essential, because the body cannot manufacture them at all
Semiessential, because the body produces them but not in sufficient amounts during rapid growth in infancy and childhood
Nonessential, because the body produces them without dietary help at every age
Conditionally toxic, because they accumulate in infants
q_0777.rationale: Box 55.3 lists arginine and histidine as the two semiessential amino acids, and the chapter states they "are not manufactured by the body in large enough quantities during rapid growth periods such as infancy or childhood." Semiessential amino acids are defined as those the body can produce but that infants and children cannot produce in sufficient amounts.
q_0777.trap: (A) is the promotion error, and it pulls because the stem says the infant must be supplied with them, which sounds like the definition of essential. The distinction is that the body makes these two at all, just not fast enough during growth.

q_0778.topic: parenteral nutrition components and amino acid classes
q_0778.stem: A nurse is teaching about the eight amino acids listed as essential, including leucine and tryptophan. Which statement correctly explains what makes them essential?
options: They cannot be manufactured by the body and must come from intake
They are produced by the body but not in sufficient amounts during infancy
They are the amino acids the body produces without extracting them from dietary intake
They are the only amino acids that participate in protein synthesis
q_0778.rationale: Essential amino acids are defined as "those amino acids that cannot be manufactured by the body," and Box 55.3 lists eight of them: isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. The body is able to manufacture "all but eight."
q_0778.trap: (C) is the mirror error of the previous item, stating the nonessential definition under the essential label; the two definitions differ only in whether the body can make the compound. Nonessential also does not mean unnecessary, only that it is not dietarily required.

q_0779.topic: parenteral nutrition components and amino acid classes
q_0779.stem: A patient with severe trauma is receiving amino acids as part of total parenteral nutrition. Which statement describes the intended metabolic effect?
options: They promote catabolism, liberating energy by breaking down complex substances
They promote anabolism, supporting protein synthesis and reducing the breakdown of proteins
They replace dextrose as the greatest source of calories in the solution
They eliminate the need for lipid emulsion in the solution
q_0779.rationale: The chapter states that the primary role of amino acids is "protein synthesis, or anabolism," and that they "reduce the breakdown of proteins (catabolism)." Anabolism is defined as the conversion of simple substances into more complex compounds, or tissue building.
q_0779.trap: (A) inverts the pair, and it pulls because an "accelerated catabolic status" is one of the chapter's own indications for supplementation, so the word appears in the same context. Catabolism is the problem being treated, not the goal of the therapy; ana- builds up and cata- tears down.

q_0780.topic: parenteral nutrition components and amino acid classes
q_0780.stem: A nurse is explaining the purpose of the intravenous fat emulsion hanging alongside a patient's total parenteral nutrition. Which functions does the chapter assign to lipid emulsions? Select all that apply.
options: Supplying essential fatty acids the body cannot synthesize
Serving as a source of energy or calories
Supplying the amino acids needed for protein synthesis
Supplying trace minerals such as zinc and selenium
Supplying immunoglobulins for infection resistance
q_0780.rationale: Lipid emulsions "serve two functions: they supply essential fatty acids and are a source of energy or calories." Linoleic acid cannot be synthesized by the body and is needed to produce linolenic and arachidonic acid. Covering part of the caloric load with fat prevents hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and hyperosmolarity that occur when the entire caloric need is met by dextrose alone.
q_0780.trap: (C) and (D) are each true of a different component of the same bag — amino acid solutions and trace element additives — which is what makes them feel correct when the question is read as "what is in parenteral nutrition" instead of "what do the lipids do." (E) is not a component of parenteral nutrition at all.

q_0781.stem: A total parenteral nutrition infusion has fallen behind schedule, and a nurse considers increasing the rate to deliver the ordered volume by the end of the shift. What is the concern with this action?
options: Accelerating the rate risks hyperglycemia, and the chapter directs that these infusion rates never be accelerated
Accelerating the rate risks rebound hypoglycemia from pancreatic overshoot
Accelerating the rate risks air embolism from turbulent flow
There is no concern, because the total daily volume is what matters
q_0781.rationale: The chapter instructs, "Never accelerate these infusion rates to increase plasma volume," and lists a high dextrose load and an accelerated rate as the causes of hyperglycemia. Because dextrose is a sugar, supplemental insulin may be given simultaneously with the infusion.
q_0781.trap: (B) names the right chapter and the wrong direction, and it pulls because both glucose complications belong to parenteral nutrition and students memorize the pair without the causes. Sort by cause first: too much sugar too fast raises glucose, and stopping abruptly drops it.

q_0782.stem: A patient's total parenteral nutrition bag runs dry and the replacement bag will not arrive from pharmacy for two hours. What is the nurse's priority concern and action?
options: Hyperglycemia; hold all glucose sources until the new bag arrives
Rebound hypoglycemia; check the blood glucose and infuse 5% to 10% glucose in the interim
Fluid volume overload; restrict oral intake until the infusion resumes
Phlebitis; discontinue the line and restart it at a new site
q_0782.rationale: If parenteral nutrition "is discontinued abruptly, rebound hypoglycemia may result." The chapter's prevention rules are a gradual reduction of the intravenous feeding rate to allow the pancreas time to adapt, and, when the feeding must stop immediately, "providing infusions of 5% to 10% glucose."
q_0782.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — a bag that has stopped is the opposite problem from a bag running too fast, yet hyperglycemia is the complication students associate with the therapy. Hanging plain saline or simply waiting for pharmacy is the same error in a different form: neither bridges the glucose.

q_0783.stem: Shortly after a total parenteral nutrition infusion is interrupted, a patient becomes symptomatic. Which findings does the chapter attribute to hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.
options: Cold clammy skin
Dizziness
Tachycardia
Polyuria
Polydipsia
q_0783.rationale: The chapter lists hypoglycemia as "cold clammy skin, dizziness, tachycardia, and tingling of the extremities," with the patient teaching section adding restlessness, nervousness, and fainting. Polyuria and polydipsia appear on the hyperglycemia list.
q_0783.trap: (D) and (E) are the directional inversions this pair generates — both are glucose symptoms in this chapter, just from the opposite complication, and the shared "poly-" prefix makes them read as generic glucose findings rather than as hyperglycemia findings.

q_0784.stem: A patient receiving total parenteral nutrition with a high dextrose concentration reports headache and excessive thirst, is voiding large volumes, and appears dehydrated. Which complication do these findings indicate?
options: Rebound hypoglycemia from a slowed infusion
Hyperglycemia from the dextrose load
Fluid volume overload from the infusion volume
Essential fatty acid deficiency
q_0784.rationale: Hyperglycemia in parenteral nutrition presents as "polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, headache, dehydration, nausea, vomiting, and weakness," and its causes in this chapter are a high dextrose concentration and an accelerated infusion rate.
q_0784.trap: (C) pulls because a large-volume infusion is running and the patient's fluid status is abnormal, but fluid overload presents as weak pulse, tachycardia, confusion, decreased urine output, and pitting edema. Urine output is the discriminator: it rises with hyperglycemia and falls with overload.

q_0785.topic: tube feeding administration and nutrient-drug interactions
q_0785.stem: Before administering a scheduled tube feeding, a nurse aspirates gastric contents and tests the pH, which reads 5.0. What does this finding indicate?
options: The tube is correctly positioned within the stomach
The tube has migrated into the respiratory tract
The tube tip has advanced into the jejunum
The reading is inconclusive and the feeding may proceed regardless
q_0785.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to test the pH of the aspirate: "With a pH of 5.5 or lower, the tube is in the correct position (within the stomach)." Placement may also be confirmed by x-ray. Newer small-bore tubes of 5 to 10 French make checking for gastric aspiration more difficult.
q_0785.trap: (D) pulls when a student remembers only that x-ray is the definitive check and treats every bedside method as unusable. The chapter gives an explicit numeric threshold, and a reading below it is an actionable confirmation, not a guess.

q_0786.topic: tube feeding administration and nutrient-drug interactions
q_0786.stem: A patient is receiving continuous tube feedings at 50 mL per hour. The nurse checks the gastric residual and obtains 140 mL. What is the correct action?
options: Discard the aspirate and continue the feeding at the ordered rate
Return the aspirate, hold the feeding, contact the prescriber, and keep the head of the bed elevated
Return the aspirate and increase the rate to compensate for the delay
Discard the aspirate and lower the head of the bed to promote gastric emptying
q_0786.rationale: For continuous feedings, a residual of "more than the volume delivered over the previous 2 hours" calls for returning the aspirate, holding the feeding, contacting the prescriber, and keeping the head of the bed elevated at least 30 to 45 degrees. At 50 mL per hour the two-hour volume is 100 mL, so 140 mL exceeds the threshold. For intermittent bolus feedings the threshold is instead more than 50% of the volume previously infused.
q_0786.trap: (D) inverts the positioning rule, and it pulls because lying flat sounds like it would help a stomach empty; head-of-bed elevation is what protects against aspiration and it matters more with nasogastric than with gastrostomy feedings. Discarding the aspirate also discards the patient's own electrolytes and feeding.

q_0787.topic: tube feeding administration and nutrient-drug interactions
q_0787.stem: A patient on continuous nasogastric feedings of a polymeric formula is ordered phenytoin. Which action reflects the chapter's interaction rule?
options: Hold the tube feeding for at least 2 hours before and after the phenytoin dose
Give the phenytoin 2 hours before or after the feeding, but do not interrupt the feeding
Mix the phenytoin directly into the feeding bag for even delivery
No separation is needed, because feedings affect only antibiotic absorption
q_0787.rationale: Tube feedings "can also reduce the absorption of phenytoin ... which may result in seizures," and the chapter recommends that "tube feedings be held for at least 2 hours before and after" the dose. The chapter also notes that the interaction is considered "more theoretical than actual" by some, so some institutions ignore it while others continue to hold the feedings, and intravenous phenytoin is often required when continuous feedings are necessary.
q_0787.trap: (B) uses the right interval on the wrong object. Two separation rules in this chapter share the same two hours, and the thing being moved is what differs: for phenytoin, the feeding is held around the dose.

q_0788.topic: tube feeding administration and nutrient-drug interactions
q_0788.stem: A patient receiving intermittent tube feedings is ordered oral ciprofloxacin and doxycycline. How should these doses be timed relative to the feedings?
options: Hold the feeding for 2 hours before and after each dose, as with phenytoin
Give each drug at least 2 hours before or after the tube feedings
Give each drug with the feeding to reduce gastric irritation
No separation is needed, because chemical inactivation affects only intravenous drugs
q_0788.rationale: The absorption of "tetracyclines and quinolones is decreased, as a result of chemical inactivation," and these drugs "must be given at least 2 hours before or after tube feedings." The Clinical Pearl states that enteral feedings interact with quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics and phenytoin and need to be separated by 2 hours.
q_0788.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — same interval, wrong object moved. For these antibiotics the drug is scheduled around the feeding, while for phenytoin the feeding is held around the drug.

q_0789.topic: tube feeding administration and nutrient-drug interactions
q_0789.stem: A patient receiving intermittent bolus gastric feedings develops nausea, sweating, palpitations, and diarrhea shortly after a bolus is delivered quickly. Which complication does this presentation indicate, and what change is needed?
options: Aspiration; raise the head of the bed and suction the airway
Dumping syndrome; slow the rate of delivery
Hypoglycemia; infuse 5% to 10% glucose
Fluid volume overload; restrict fluids and notify the prescriber
q_0789.rationale: Dumping syndrome is "a complex reaction to the rapid entry of concentrated nutrients into the jejunum," producing "nausea, weakness, sweating, palpitations, syncope, sensations of warmth, and diarrhea," and it occurs with enteral feedings administered too rapidly as well as after partial gastrectomy. The chapter states that rapid feeding or bolus doses can result in dumping syndrome.
q_0789.trap: (A) pulls because both complications come from how the feeding is delivered rather than what is in it, so students pick the more feared one. Sort by the trigger: too fast produces dumping, while a high residual, a flat bed, or a compromised gag reflex produces aspiration.

q_0790.topic: otc, legend, and complementary medicine terms
q_0790.subtopic: legend drugs versus otc drugs versus dietary supplements
q_0790.stem: A patient empties a bag onto the bedside table during a medication history: acetaminophen (Tylenol), warfarin (Coumadin), ginkgo biloba, morphine sulfate, and diphenhydramine (Benadryl). Which of these are legend drugs? Select all that apply.
options: acetaminophen (Tylenol)
warfarin (Coumadin)
ginkgo biloba
morphine sulfate
diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
q_0790.rationale: Legend drugs are "medications that are not legally available without a prescription from a prescriber; also called prescription drugs." Acetaminophen and diphenhydramine both appear in Table 7.1 as OTC products, and ginkgo biloba is a dietary supplement — a third legal category that is not a drug at all.
q_0790.trap: (C) pulls because an herb is the least ordinary item in the bag and feels like it needs special classification, but "legend" means prescription-only and has nothing to do with folklore or herbal tradition; ginkgo is sold freely under DSHEA. (A) and (E) pull because both are real drugs with real toxicity, and students slide from how dangerous a product is to how it is legally obtained.

q_0791.topic: otc, legend, and complementary medicine terms
q_0791.subtopic: legend drugs versus otc drugs versus dietary supplements
q_0791.stem: A patient tells the nurse, "The pharmacist keeps my pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) behind the counter now, so it must have become a prescription drug." Which response is accurate?
options: Correct — it was reclassified as a legend drug because of its abuse potential
It is still an OTC drug; it is kept behind the counter because it can be used to manufacture methamphetamine
It is now classified as a dietary supplement, so DSHEA governs where it is shelved
It became prescription-only in 2009, when the FDA began requiring special labeling
q_0791.rationale: Table 7.1 still lists pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) among the OTC antihistamines and decongestants. The chapter explains that pseudoephedrine is "used to manufacture the widely abused street drug methamphetamine" and that "because of the potential for abuse, products containing pseudoephedrine must be sold from behind the pharmacy counter."
q_0791.trap: (A) confuses where a drug is stored with what it legally is; counter placement is an abuse-diversion control, not reclassification to legend status. (D) borrows a real 2009 event — the FDA labeling requirement for acetaminophen, aspirin, and NSAIDs — and attaches it to the wrong drug.

q_0792.topic: otc, legend, and complementary medicine terms
q_0792.stem: A patient receiving scheduled chemotherapy also attends weekly acupuncture and massage sessions and intends to complete the full chemotherapy course. Which term names what this patient is doing?
options: Alternative medicine
Complementary medicine
Conventional medicine
Iatrogenic therapy
q_0792.rationale: Complementary medicine is "alternative medicine when used simultaneously with, rather than instead of, standard Western medicine," and the chapter adds that this practice "is also referred to as integrative medicine."
q_0792.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because acupuncture and massage are themselves alternative therapies, and the option matches the therapy rather than the pattern. The axis this term names is not what the therapy is but what it is used with, and this patient is still receiving chemotherapy.

q_0793.topic: otc, legend, and complementary medicine terms
q_0793.stem: A second patient declines the recommended chemotherapy entirely and treats the diagnosis with herbal preparations alone. Which term names what this patient is doing?
options: Complementary medicine
Integrative medicine
Alternative medicine
Conventional medicine
q_0793.rationale: Alternative medicine is "herbal medicine, chiropractic, acupuncture, massage, reflexology, and any other therapies traditionally not emphasized in Western medical schools." It becomes complementary only when used simultaneously with, rather than instead of, standard Western medicine.
q_0793.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item — this patient stopped the conventional therapy, so nothing is being complemented. (B) fails a second way: integrative is simply the chapter's other name for complementary, so whenever both appear as options the discriminator lies elsewhere in the stem.

q_0794.topic: otc, legend, and complementary medicine terms
q_0794.stem: A patient holding a ginkgo capsule asks the nurse what part of it actually produces an effect in the body. Which answer is accurate?
options: The herbs — the bark, root, leaf, seed, flower, and fruit components of the plant
The phytochemicals — the pharmacologically active ingredients in the remedy
The herbal medicine — the practice of using herbs to heal
The standardized legend ingredients the FDA verified before marketing
q_0794.rationale: Phytochemicals are "the pharmacologically active ingredients in herbal remedies," and the chapter describes herbal products as containing "a wide variety of active phytochemicals (plant compounds)." Herbs are the plant parts themselves, and herbal medicine is the practice of using them.
q_0794.trap: (A) names the level immediately below the answer and pulls hard because the capsule literally contains plant material; the stem asks what produces the effect, not what the capsule is made of. (C) swaps a practice for a substance, which is the same nesting error one step further out.

q_0795.topic: otc, legend, and complementary medicine terms
q_0795.stem: A nursing student asks why interest in "natural health" surged in the United States beginning in the 1960s. Which answer reflects the chapter?
options: Clinical trials had begun to show that herbs outperform conventional drugs
Concern over the iatrogenic effects of conventional medicine, together with a desire for more self-reliance
The FDA had begun approving herbal products as drugs, which reassured consumers
Herbal products had become substantially cheaper than prescription drugs
q_0795.rationale: The chapter states that "in the 1960s, concerns were expressed over the iatrogenic effects of conventional medicine. These concerns, along with a desire for more self-reliance, led to a renewed interest in 'natural health.'" Iatrogenic effects are "unintentional adverse effects that are caused by the actions of a prescriber or other health care professional, or by a specific treatment."
q_0795.trap: (A) pulls because evidence of benefit feels like the natural driver of a health trend, but the chapter attributes the shift to distrust of conventional care — and it says elsewhere that "there are few published scientific data regarding the safety of dietary supplements." (C) inverts the regulatory picture entirely.

q_0796.subtopic: what dshea does and does not require
q_0796.stem: A patient asks what the FDA actually requires of the company that makes her supplement. Which requirements currently apply to dietary supplement manufacturers? Select all that apply.
options: Comply with quality-control standards set by the DSHEA of 1994
Prove the product's efficacy before it is sold
Identify the active ingredients on the label
Obtain FDA approval before the product is marketed
Demonstrate that the product is free from contaminants such as microbes, pesticides, and heavy metals
q_0796.rationale: "The DSHEA requires no proof of efficacy and sets no standards for quality control for supplements," and "dietary supplements do not need approval from the FDA before they are marketed." Since June 2007, however, manufacturers "must provide data that demonstrate product identity, composition, quality, purity, and strength of active ingredients" and "must also demonstrate that products are free from contaminants such as microbes, pesticides, and heavy metals."
q_0796.trap: (A), (B), and (D) are each a genuine FDA requirement moved to the wrong category — all three apply to legend drugs, for which "the FDA has specific and stringent requirements." (D) is the strongest pull, because a product sitting on a pharmacy shelf looks approved.

q_0797.subtopic: what dshea does and does not require
q_0797.stem: A patient states flatly that the FDA has no authority whatsoever over herbal products. Which response is accurate?
options: That is correct; when DSHEA passed in 1994 the FDA lost all jurisdiction over supplements
The FDA banned ephedra, posts warnings on its website, and has set manufacturing standards since 2007, but it does not approve supplements before they are marketed
The FDA approves each supplement for safety, though not for effectiveness
The FDA reviews every supplement label for accuracy before the product reaches the shelf
q_0797.rationale: The chapter's operative rule is that these products "are not regulated by the FDA unless there is sufficient data to support a recall of the product. Companies are not required to provide evidence of safety and/or effectiveness." The FDA nonetheless banned ephedra in April 2004, sent a consumer-warning letter about kava in 2002, "posts warnings on herbal products on its website," and imposed good manufacturing practice requirements in June 2007.
q_0797.trap: (A) overshoots in one direction while (C) and (D) undershoot in the other, and the chapter's position is the modest middle one. (C) pulls hardest because "approved for safety but not effectiveness" sounds like a sensible regulatory compromise and describes no real category here.

q_0798.subtopic: what dshea does and does not require
q_0798.stem: A patient asks how dietary supplements came to have a law of their own. Which sequence is accurate?
options: The FDA threatened to remove supplements from the market in 1993, the public mounted a letter-writing campaign, and the 103rd Congress passed the DSHEA in 1994
Congress passed the DSHEA in 1972 as part of the FDA's OTC Drug Review
The German Commission E monographs of 1978 were adopted into United States law as the DSHEA
The US Pharmacopeia drafted the DSHEA in 2002 as part of its verification program
q_0798.rationale: "In 1993, the FDA threatened to remove dietary supplements from the market. The American public reacted with a massive letter-writing campaign to Congress, and the 103rd Congress responded by passing the Dietary Supplement and Health Education Act (DSHEA) of 1994." Before that, "neither federal legislation nor the FDA provided any safeguards," and "manufacturers were responsible only for ensuring product safety."
q_0798.trap: (B) moves the 1972 date, which belongs to the FDA's OTC Drug Review, onto the supplement law. (C) and (D) move the act to the wrong actor entirely: the 1978 Commission E monographs are German, and the 2002 US Pharmacopeia program is independent certification, not legislation.

q_0799.subtopic: what dshea does and does not require
q_0799.stem: A patient wants some assurance that a supplement bottle actually contains what its label claims. Which resource does the chapter offer?
options: The FDA preapproval seal, required on every supplement since 1994
The US Pharmacopeia's Dietary Supplement Verification Program, which certifies products it has independently tested
The Commission E monographs, which certify United States supplement manufacturers
The DSHEA registry of verified supplement ingredients
q_0799.rationale: In 2002 the US Pharmacopeia, "an independent organization that is the government's official standard-setting authority for dietary supplements, began certifying products that it had independently tested as part of its Dietary Supplement Verification Program."
q_0799.trap: (C) pulls because Commission E is the one herbal-quality body most students can name, but it is the German equivalent of the FDA, and its 1978 monographs "focus on herbs whose effectiveness for specific indications is supported by the research literature" rather than certifying United States products. (A) describes a seal that does not exist.

q_0800.subtopic: what dshea does and does not require
q_0800.stem: A supplement label reads "supports joint comfort," and the patient asks whether the manufacturer is allowed to print that. Which statement is accurate?
options: Manufacturers may claim an effect but cannot promise a specific cure on the product label
Manufacturers may make any claim, including a cure, because DSHEA removed all labeling limits
Manufacturers may print only the ingredient list; any statement of effect is prohibited
Manufacturers may promise a cure if the ingredient appears in the Commission E monographs
q_0800.rationale: Dietary supplement manufacturers "may currently claim an effect but cannot promise a specific cure on the product label." The chapter adds that "herbal products are not FDA-approved drugs, and therefore their labeling cannot be relied on to provide consumers and patients with adequate instructions for use or even information about warnings."
q_0800.trap: (B) and (C) are the two intuitive extremes — total freedom or total silence — and the real rule sits between them. (B) pulls hardest for a student who has learned "supplements are unregulated" and generalizes that into a permission the law does not actually grant.

q_0801.stem: A manufacturer asks a nurse educator which features the FDA weighs when considering a prescription drug for OTC status. Which of these are criteria listed in Box 7.1? Select all that apply.
options: The condition must be diagnosed by a health care provider
Benefits of correct usage outweigh the risks
Limited interaction with other drugs
The drug is easy to use
The company will sell the OTC version at a lower price
q_0801.rationale: Box 7.1 groups its criteria under three headings — indication for use, safety profile, and practicality for over-the-counter use. "Benefits of correct usage must outweigh risks" is an indication bullet, "limited interaction with other drugs" a safety bullet, and "easy to use" a practicality bullet.
q_0801.trap: (A) is the exact inversion of the box's first bullet: the consumer "must be able to easily diagnose condition," so a condition that requires a provider to diagnose would disqualify the drug. (E) pulls because reclassification is loosely associated with saving money, but the box says nothing about price, and reclassification "may increase out-of-pocket costs."

q_0802.stem: A drug under review for OTC status has a wide gap between the dose that produces toxicity and the dose that produces benefit. How does that bear on its candidacy?
options: It favors reclassification, because Box 7.1 requires a high therapeutic index
It argues against reclassification, because a wide gap makes the dose hard to titrate
It is irrelevant, because therapeutic index applies only to intravenous drugs
